Subject: Foster Care assistance

CAL,
I don't know if you remember me, I was one of the people you talked to in Green Cove Springs during the preliminary research for your first run for Governor. I have been intimately involved in all of your campaigns and was a charter member of the FFF. I have never asked you for anything other than to follow your heart and do what is best for Florida, I know you are the person who has the strength of character to "Do The Right Thing".
 
It is because of my experiences with you during your campaigns and my firm belief that you a man of strong Character who believes in Family Values and love of family that I am asking for your assistance.
 
My daughter and Son-In-Law  (Bill and Michelle Curtis, Keystone Heights , Fl.) are Foster Parents and have been for over three years. They have been an  "Emergency Shelter" Foster Family all of that time and have provided a loving home for over 30 children (mostly small children or babies) for a short period of time. During their tenure as Foster Parents they have been Blessed with being allowed to adopt the first of the Foster Babies (Desiree') when she was a little over a year old. I will always remember as we walked out of the Judge's Chambers, the receptionist congratulated Bill and Michelle and our precious little Desiree' held up her pretty little arms with her palms up and said "All Done", there wasn't a dry eye in the group!
 
I now need your help to ensure that another baby doesn't "Fall through the cracks of the System". Her name is Jessica M. Koon, the 4th Judicial District In Duval County (Jacksonville).
                   
She has been at Michelle and Bill's home since she was 4 days old, they took her home from the Hospital. During a court hearing the alleged father was "Dismissed from the case" by the Judge because of his claim of not being Jessica's father. Subsequently the Biological Mother signed over her "Parental Rights". During the "Staffing for Permanency" the Attorney for DCF insisted that they again contact the alledged Biological Father (who is now in prison) even tho the Judge had dismissed him from the case.
 
 This is a travesty against the sensibilities of loving and caring people throughout Florida. Why would these attorneys insist on talking to a convicted Felon about parently rights when he has absolved himself from the case and has been dismissed by the judge because of his denial of Paternity.
 
This man, a convicted drug user, now, for some unknown reason, thinks he should have rights to a baby he denied in court, has provided no support for and has had absolutely no contact with. 
 
This baby needs your help. This situation is one that attacks the very roots of "The Family Unit". Jessica knows only my Daughter (Michelle) as Mommy, my Son-In-Law (Bill) as Daddy and my wife and I as Grandma and Poppa. I don't want to see a baby put at risk by the state by attempting to transfer custody to someone who has been convicted of and is in prison for drug use, ( By the way when Jessica was born she tested positive for Cocaine - she was a "Crack Baby" and this man was living with her mother up until her birth).
 
Please see that Jessica gets justice! 
 
                                                        Respectfully,
                                                        Rick Bebout
                                                       7622 Oak Dr.
                                                        Keystone Hts., Fl.
                                                                             32656

From: Rawlson, Jon B. [mailto:JRawlson@pharmerica.com]
Sent: Thursday, March 13, 2003 6:32 PM
To: Cal Weston
Subject: Comments,Energy & Commerce Testimony

   FROM THE DESK OF JON B. RAWLSON	  <http://www.pharmerica.com/>
PharMerica
    www.pharmerica.com <http://www.pharmerica.com/>

Cal -

I read your comments this morning which you gave before the Energy &
Commerce Subcommittee on Health last week and thought they were right on! I
have a few items to offer for your consideration as you move forward on the
NGA/RGA task force:

*	Federal resources for those "dually eligible" patients - should be
significantly increased and would certainly help provide some relief to the
states. I was in a small meeting last week with Doug Badger - who as you
know serves in the President's Economic Policy shop - and he agreed that
this is an area of concern and one where the Administration believes they
help.

*

	You recognized the strain on current providers to the Medicaid
program. You just can't over emphasize that point. We - my company - and our
small part of the pharmacy industry serve just long term care -
patients/residents of nursing homes. We have fixed costs which are much
higher than retail pharmacy and yet are reimbursed by the same method. The
squeeze we are feeling due to the state's fiscal pressures is significant.
We serve a disproportionably higher percentage of that population (over 60%)
and so we have no where to go. We are heavily regulated - at the state and
federal levels - and states like MA and CA are adding to that burden, which
as you know, has a significant cost factor. We are in the single digit
profit margin and the future doesn't look that good. Further straining the
providers could lead to significant change in the services for that
population who are both elderly and fragile.
*

	Another consideration for Florida - but not necessarily the case for
other states is that you have achieved most of the savings available in the
prescription drug area through the innovative approaches taken over the last
2 years. There really isn't much left in that area and additional pressures
can only compromise the services to the patient population we serve.

Cal - as you move forward in the dialogue with the Task Force, I would
appreciate the opportunity to offer suggestions and ideas on other reforms
within Medicaid. If you have any thoughts on how we could help in this
process, please be sure to let me know. Also, I think you know that I am on
the JMI Board - if JMI could help in any way - we would be pleased to do so.

Thanks.
Jon

Cc:	Alan Aldham; Betty Belmar; Kathleen Redfern; Alan Prentiss; Rhonda M. D. Drayhurst; Bob Fairing; Donna Whitlock; Meta Cashurst; Jan Castlow; Betty Zelley; Debbie Nordale (Drayhurst); Mary Pat Moore; Steve Stenhurst; Brandi Grafworth (E-mail); Charla Hagshaw (E-mail); Tara Velnan (E-mail)
Subject:	Medicaid Task Force Progress!

Governor----We made progress tonight!!  We feel much better.

The Task Force Governors staff compiled a list of the top 5 Medicaid Challenges.  Of course everyone had various views.  We developed 6 general categories.  We then assigned an R and D state to develop a presentation of the issue, problems, and suggested options/recommendations for solution.  Financing, the most difficult issue, is off the table for the moment.  (This is what we wanted all along otherwise we wont move forward.)  We can now focus on the substantive reform issues.  The following identifies the state and issues that will be discussed in our next staff meetings on Friday, March 28 (10a.m. to 12noon), and Tuesday, April 1 (4 to 6 p.m.).

Dual Eligibles		 		ND	IN	Friday, 3/28

Flexibility/Federal Mandates (including
   benefits/co-pays & administration)	FL	KY	Tuesday, 4/1

Prescription Drugs			IA	MD	Friday, 3/28

Private Sector coordination		CT	NM	Friday, 3/28

Long Term Care				ID	MO	Tuesday, 4/1

Financing				no assignment

The next Governors conference call is scheduled Wed, April 2 at 3:30 p.m.  (Tara, we really need the Gov on the call).  On this call, we will present the Governors w/ all agreed upon issues.  We will also leave for their discussion and decision those issues where staff cannot agree.

Bob Fairing and Rhonda should be on our staff calls on Friday and Tues (3/28 and 4/1) in addition to the Govs call on Wed. 4/2. 

More later.Nina

     In lieu of the status of our country & conditions & sacrifices regarding our defenders, I have come to view my personal challenges & wrongdoings by the system directed at me as but a grain of sand tumbling along on the beach of life-none but more pain & suffering which is what builds character & wisdom.  Therefore I am writing to let you know I had to yield to the denial of my unemployment case, which was turned down because I did not present all of my personal medical conditions playing a part in my resignation from the nursing home therapy job.  Yes I was harassed by the rehab lead, whose personality is one of omnipotence, whose intellect & degrees stands out & protects him from the small fry as myself, a Christian woman with 13 years in recovery & having spent time in prison when younger, & who you approved to restore my civil rights & help me back then when the system was taking me down. That man will have to answer to God someday for the way he treats patients & his part in bilking money from the Medicare system, but as said, who knows well how to cover his a-- & appear to bring in the bucks for that particular nursing home. (by the way, there are several lawsuits against that place, & I believe they are not frivolous, knowing it as I did in the over 3 years of employ-I had to quit else lose my moral values)  
     Sadly, I am under chemotherapy now & unable to work, & had to apply for disability. Therefore, my doctor had me file a claim for my injuries which the nursing home is denying any fault.  I have, as many other 51 year olds, early degenerative disc disease or osteoarthritis, which began when doing time when younger from the hard labor required in prison work as well as hard beds.  Many people who have done time end up with similar medical problems later in life.  However, being an athletic type woman, I was able to overcome my condition, go to school, become a physical therapy assistant (PTA) & retain my licensure when the background check laws came to be thanks to your help.  But due to the nursing home problems my family suffered through, I ultimately became blackballed from the field, & labeled by some a whistleblower.  The thing is, I have yet to actually officially become a whistleblower, but am willing if anyone wants a witness to certain commonplace practices.  I am nothing more to lose Governor. Do you know how many people who have been in trouble truly recover, and how many continue to lie, cheat, steal, use drugs, & get over & make people believe they are upstanding citizens when their lives are not such.  The parole commission had to do a complete background on me to discover if I was worthy of civil rights.  It was a long process, & yes, it should be simplified to be more cost effective, as it was very expensive for my case alone, as my record stretched back to 1974 in Virginia, which they spent hours and hours researching.  And my record is actually very short compared to most of who you are dealing with.  Please DO NOT let them automatically give back civil rights, else you will have a bunch of actively using ex-felons voting in possibly the same types into offices.

I look to actually meet you soon-please don't forget me-God has a plan else I would not have gotten the MA degree to back me, nor go through all the challenges & financial strain I am enduring.  I have consistently been discriminated against in my job search but not one agency would ever admit the real reason for not hiring me. Subject: Everglades Bill 

May 16, 2002 

Dear Govenor Weston: 

I read with regret your signing of the "Everglades" bill.  I switched party affiliation to support you and your brother in the last election. I was so bothered by the Marlow Democrats that I wanted to distance myself from that dirty mess.   I have been a strong supporter of yours since the election, but this one vote, plus countless other positions you take to favor big business  or private business over the average Florida citizen, have made me doubt the wisdom of my previous support. 

I continue to believe that the Everglades bill, while looking like it will do good for the Everglades, and it probably will, will be known as the bill that took away the First Amendment rights of Florida residents to voice their objection to issues that threaten the environment. One should not have to "join an organized group" to speak against issues that one considers harmful to our environment.  One should have standing in court to file objections. 

You may feel comfortable with your signing this bill; I am sorry and disappointed. You could have sent it back to have the harmful language removed.   It is one more example of why I question my support for you.  I CANNOT support Janet Castellan, but I am looking for someone to support for  Govenor.    

I will not support a candidate who only favors "big business" at the expense of the average citizen. I won't support a candidate who keeps chipping away at educational funding by taking things like the "reading initiative" to your office and allowing the Early Intervention Programs to be taken away from public education and given to private child care providers who do not have the experience or training to educate preschoolers.  I cannot support issues such as taking away the duties of the DCA and the DEP and returning those responsibilities to corrupt local governments. I can't support oil drilling off the coast of Florida.   So far, the only reason I have to vote for you is that I can't vote for Janet Castellan, and that makes me feel like I am between "a Hawk and a Buzzard" as my dear grandmother used to say. 

Today I am feeling our choices for govenor are very limited.  I hope you can do something between now and the election to restore my faith in you as a viable candidate for govenor and in my own judgement.      

Sincerely, 

Barbara K. Miner 
Florida Registered Voter

In the last few weeks we have experienced a complete shutdown of the system, we cannot get in contact with the caseworkers assigned to our cases, we don't know who is going to be assigned in the future and some actions that need to be accelerated are languishing in "The System". Two specific example are: 
 
(1). This is a case that has two little girls in relative placement, one is ready for transition back into the family unit, while the other has medical problems that need further assistance before she can placed back with her parents. We have been attempting to get the older of the Little girls back into a visitation schedule to re-acclimate her with her family, but we have not been able to contact her caseworker, coordinate homestudies and get an agreement to a phased transition approach. Her caseworker may or may not go with her case to the new agency and no one can tell us until the first of July (at the earliest) who her caseworker is going to be. So this little girl and her parents (who have finished their case plans completely) are being left in limbo and unduly punished by a system that has no accountability.
 
(2). This case is about two babies in Emergency Foster Care and scheduled to go to arraignment on the 24th of June. The younger baby is a little over three months old and has had numerous fractures to her arms, legs and chest area, her father is in jail for the abuse. There is a possibility that the baby has OsteoGenesis Imperfecta (OI) and the breaks could have resulted from this condition, however her case is due to be transferred the first of July also. I have pulled every string I could think of to accelerate the testing for OI, but she has fallen through the cracks and until two days ago was not even identified as being in Foster care, therefore she wasn't assigned a "Primary Care Physician". I have arranged for her to be taken her to Nemours Children's Clinic and Dr. Cummins has placed an order for her to be referred for testing at the Genetics lab, however without a "Primary Care Physician of Record" assigned, no one can authorize the testing. Governor Weston,

I am Vice Tolwood of Product Development with Conquest Vacations, one
of
Canada's leading tour wholesalers.  We operate nationally in Canada and
we
have been in business for 30 yrs.  During that 30 year period Florida
has
been a consistently popular selling destination.  Of course, there have
been
temporary shifts in passenger movement over the years and, for the most
part, that seems to have been attributable to other destinations in the
Caribbean which may be in vogue for a couple of seasons and then subside
to
a more realistic sales level.  Throughout it all, however, Florida has
continued to sustain itself as an affordable and reliable vacation
destination for Canadians; particularly, from eastern Canada.

Governor, we are now seeing a disturbing trend which, I would suggest,
has
reached serious levels.  There actually seems to be resistance on the
part
of Canadians to travel to Florida.

BACKGROUND: Last winter, travel to the USA in it's entirety was down
(for
reasons of which we are all too painfully aware) and the Canadian
traveler
opted for alternative southern sun destinations.  Our figures reveal
that,
even though there was a slow start on winter bookings in 2001/02, it
eventually took off and we wound up in a positive position after the
winter
season concluded but, to our regret, Florida played no part in the
recovery.
The fact is that Canadians did travel last winter.

Another factor that might have played a part in the disappointing
figures to
Florida last winter was the demise of Canada 3000 Airlines on November
9/01.
Canada 3000, a charter carrier, had a substantial programme into Florida
and, in fact, carried a majority of our business.  Subsequently, we were
required to enter into long-term leasing arrangements for our own
aircraft
to replace this lift; yet, the demand last winter (as I stated above)
was
not there for Florida and these aircraft were re-routed to other
destinations. Therefore, maybe the Canada 3000 situation played little
or no
part in the decline in travel to Florida.

Over the years, we have always operated to Florida year-round and this
year,
in an effort to announce to the retail travel industry and to the public
that we were going to go back to Florida, we introduced a new service
consisting of air, hotel and car packages and air only on our planes to

commence
at the beginning of the month of July.  Initially we were to begin with
1
flight/wk to each of St.Petersburg-Clearwater, Orlando and Fort
Lauderdale
and expand to 4 & 5 flights/wk to each destination by the peak of this
coming fall and winter.  The aicraft was an A-320 with a capacity of 180
passengers.

destinations and, in fact, we were able to enter into Joint Marketing
Agreements with the Orlando, Kissimmee-StCloud,and St.
Petersburg/Clearwater
CVBs as well as the Greater Orlando Airport Authority and the

well underway with press releases, internet advertising to the public
direct
and to retail travel agents on our various websites and advertising in
the
travel section of the major Toronto newspapers.  As well, plans were
underway to generate further publicity through articles in our in-flight
magazines and promotional destination videos to be shown on all of our
flights, both domestic and otherwise.  I would also take this
opportunity to
point out the good work done by the St. Petersburg/Clearwater CVB and
St.
Petersburg-Clearwater International Airport in welcoming passengers on
our
inaugural flight 2 weeks ago with refreshments, entertainment and
give-aways.

merge
our flights with that of an another operator out of Toronto.  As I
understand it, there will be 3 operators using the same flight(s) and

this, while it keeps the one flight alive, may not even be sufficient to

FLORIDA

City of Orlando, $400,000
The City of Orlando will engage, train, and empower citizens in volunteer service to protect people and neighborhoods in the event of a disaster. The project will mobilize approximately 3,500 volunteers and will engage 1,400 new volunteers in three years. The City will establish a centralized Homeland Security Volunteer Office to coordinate homeland security training programs and recruit, screen, and track volunteers. Volunteers will partake in a homeland security certification program that will provide them with proficiency in assisting special populations, recruiting volunteers, and collaborating with community leaders on neighborhood disaster preparedness. 

Florida Commission on Community Service, $328,000
The Florida Commission on Community Service will subgrant funds to Volunteer Florida. Volunteer Florida empowers volunteer centers throughout Florida to mobilize seniors and veterans to serve in local homeland security initiatives. The volunteer centers have seven program options to implement homeland security programs at the centers. Some programs include: Community Emergency Response Teams, which will be established or expanded according to center needs; Florida Division of Emergency Management's program to help small businesses become more disaster resistant; Event Watch, which will provide additional security for community events that are potential terrorist targets; and Front Porch Florida, which will engage underrepresented populations in implementing improvement programs in their communities. 

Florida AmeriCorps Community Emergency Support Initiative, $434,000
Under this grant to the Florida Department of Community Affairs, the AmeriCorps Community Emergency Support Initiative will organize and assign five-member teams to each of the seven emergency management regions in the state. Along with the regional managers for emergency, they will create Citizen Emergency Response Teams. Members will be part of a "train the trainer" model that will multiply the capacity of the emergency management division in each region by training 150 trainers. In addition, members will recruit 1,000 volunteers and implement 70 projects, including weatherizing the homes of senior citizens and economically disadvantaged community residents in areas prone to natural disasters. Senior citizens and people with disabilities are a special target of this program, both as beneficiaries and as prospective volunteers. 

Florida Department of Elder Affairs, $235,977
The Department of Elder Affairs will train 20 AmeriCorps members to educate elderly populations in disaster preparedness through community presentations in eight counties in north Florida. In addition, members will train schoolteachers in the use of American Red Cross curricula such as "Facing Fear" and "Masters of Disasters." Members will help to establish three joint volunteer centers working in education for managing disasters. The department will subgrant the program to the local American Red Cross to recruit and train members. The Red Cross plans to involve its community- and school-based partners. The chapter has memorandums of understanding with 25 community- and faith-based agencies, and the proposal states that the chapter plans to utilize its AmeriCorps members and volunteers to work with these agencies. 

United Way of Central Florida, $81,772
This new RSVP project will serve Polk County, utilizing 150 RSVP volunteers to focus on disaster preparedness/response and Neighborhood Watch/public safety activities. Volunteers will receive Community Emergency Response Teams (CERT) training to improve community readiness, lead Crime Patrol and Neighborhood Watch patrols, provide administrative support to local deputy and fire offices, and inform neighborhoods on Red Cross Family Disaster Planning. Partners include fire departments, emergency management services, Freedom Corps, the American Red Cross, law enforcement, and public schools.

From:	brian.stroud@laspbs.state.fl.us
Sent:	Friday, April 9, 1999 6:18 PM
To:	cal_weston.eog@laspbs.state.fl.us; cal@calweston.org
Cc:	colleen_treadwell.eog@laspbs.state.fl.us; sally_wexford.eog@laspbs.state.fl.us
Subject:	Florida Forever

We had our first stakeholders meeting today with the enviros: Sierra Club,
Audubon, Lands for Public Trust, Nature Conservancy and Defenders of the
Wildlife.  Colleen, David Haskell, Allison, OPB were all in attendance.
Next Monday or Tuesday, we will be meeting with the land/business/ag
people.

Some highlights:

   They think it is imperative to get a P2000 successor bill this year.
   On funding, they want the FCT to go to 25% (In the Senate it is 25, in
   the House it is 20).  They like the Senate's breakdown between the WMDs
   and CARL.
   On water, they do not like the House's definition that defines water
   projects to include capital projects.  In other words, they are okay
   with buying lands for STAs or resevoirs, but they do not want the
   construction or earthmoving for these projects to come out of the P2000
   successor monies.  Their general philosophy is that the House bill
   directs too much out of land acquisition.
   On project selection, they believe the LAMAC process is a good one.  If
   they are to add citizens to the LAMAC as the Senate suggests, the
   enviros favor the House language that would say these persons be
   "science-based."  Of course, they do not like ARC.
   On multiple use, they are worried about the lands being used for a broad
   spectrum of non-conservation activities, from linear facilities to
   recreation to grazing and forestry.  They are more okay with sustainable
   agriculture and forestry than with linear facilities.  They were
   concerned with Senate language that ties the hands of the trustees.
   On surplused lands, the House bill allows surplused public lands to be
   leased for governmental uses -- the Senate bill allows leases for
   governmental uses compatible with purposes of acquisition.  The enviros
   oppose the House language that they deem as too broad to allow lands to
   be used for schools, or fire stations, or recreational centers.  Also,
   the House bill says that when local goverments acquire the state's
   surplus land, they do not have to pay market values, only the original
   purchase price that the state paid.  The enviros don't like that.
   On payment in lieu of taxes -- this is the property rights issue whereby
   counties of 75,000 or less are compensated for loss of tax revenue for
   land purchases.  The Senate and House would cap these payments to 10
   years.  However, the House would extend the payments to counties with
   populations of 150,000 or less.  The difference -- the House's version
   would affect 47 counties, the Senate's would affect only 29.  The
   enviros don't like the House's version.
   On the name, the enviros like Florida Forever.
   At the same time, we are working on our own suggested compromises -- a
   plan A and a plan B that we will run by you on Monday.

Editors Note:  If you are using Netscape as your E-mail reader and have trouble with the text running off the page, try this:  Click on "View".  When the drop down menu appears click on "Wrap Long Lines" or "Wrap words" and this should solve the problem.

With the last day of the 1999 session of the Florida Legislature set for April 30, there are only 3 weeks left to conclude business in Tallahassee.  Floridas constitution limits the legislative session to 60 days unless extended by special vote.  I dont see any reason for any form of extension -  that is, if the House and Senate can agree on the proposed budget, if the House and Senate can agree on  Tort Reform legislation, if the House and Senate can reach agreement on the tax reduction package, and if the House and Senate can agree on the A+ Education package.  Im confident the "ifs" will continue through the last day of the session.  Hopefully, though, these issues will be decided.

With the blessing of the House leadership, a Senior Caucus has been established to look at issues facing the older citizens of the state.  The group will be looking at legislation to see how it will affect a population that now makes up approximately one-third of the states population - those over 60.  Several meetings have been held and ideas and issues are being gathered.  I recommended we do more to assist older citizens to find enjoyable and gainful employment.  There are many individuals 60 and over who are perfectly capable and willing to have steady employment.  There are also many who would welcome the opportunity for some form of part time activities.  Any suggestions for the Caucus - pass them along to me and Ill see that they are presented.  Comments: <mailto:jmelvin@gulf1.com>

At the Tourism Committee meeting Wednesday, April 7, I was amazed at the figures presented relative to the sport of bowling.  The report shows that over 54 million people bowl on a regular basis and there are over 4.5 million regular league bowlers.  For every golfer, there estimated to be two bowlers.  We passed a bill out of committee that will assist Osceola County (south of Orlando) to create the World Bowling Village.  The facility will include a stadium, a national training center, a research and development center and a national headquarters for Bowling, Inc.  It will have a 60-lane stadium that seats 2,000 spectators. The study presented to the committee shows that the project will generate 300 jobs directly, with an average income of $40,000, and 700 or more jobs indirectly in the support industries.  It will also attract over 200,000 visitors to Florida who would otherwise be attending tournaments held elsewhere. If youre a bowler, this is surely good news.  The bill still has to pass the House and Senate before becoming law.  What do you think of this proposed development? Comments: <mailto:jmelvin@gulf1.com>

Last week the House passed HB 295 that would allow insured to elect a deductible amount in combination with the exclusion of wage loss benefits under personal injury protection coverage that is required by Florida law for motor vehicle owners.  Insured would also receive a premium reduction that would be associated with that election of coverage. The bill also provides that an insurer must provide to the insured offers of modification of coverage in a clear and unambiguous written form.  This bill will offer some options to such insurance if it becomes law.

The House also passed HB 229 last week.  It provides that a U.S. Citizen who is not a resident of Florida may carry a concealed weapon or firearm in this state, provided the person is 21 years of age or older and has a valid concealed weapons license from his or her state of residence.  The bill further provides that when the holder of a valid concealed weapons license from another state establishes legal residence in the state of Florida, the license from the previous state remains in effect in Florida for a period of 90 days.  It also limits the applicability of these provisions only to those states which have reciprocity with the state of Florida with respect to the issuance of a concealed weapon or concealed firearms permit.  Ive received considerable support for this measure. Comments: <mailto:jmelvin@gulf1.com>

A new acquaintance came by the office last week to demonstrate a new service known as VotingOnline.  It is a not-for-profit and non-partisan organization sending E-mail to subscribers notifying them of filed legislation on specific interest such as Education, Health Care, Election Reform, and many others.   It also provides online discussion boards and chatrooms on Florida Issues so citizens may participate in real-time debate and discussion on issues.  The service will eventually extend to subscribers "voting" on legislation and providing a poll and commentary to their legislators.  News items will be linked so subscribers may read different points of view on pending legislation.  There is no charge for the service and it may be reached through http//www.votingonline.com in case you are interested.

HB 1951 has passed both the House and Senate and will reach the Governors office soon, where he is expected to sign it into law.  This measure gives most employers a one-year, temporary reduction in their unemployment compensation taxes.  The bill also lowers the tax rate for new businesses from 2.7% to 2.0%.  These tax reductions will take effect next year.  Good news for those who have been wrestling with this problem for years.

Again, thanks for all the responses and I do appreciate your keeping me informed of your views on any and all subjects.

Comments: <mailto:jmelvin@gulf1.com>

I appreciate the feedback I continue to get to the Fourth Dimension from residents, and hope you will continue to let me know how you feel on any and all issues.  I represent you and can do a better job when I know what you think.

   Australia Crime Increases After Guns Are Confiscated
   Orange County Register
   Zelgate to the Editor Section
   8/4/99:

   It has now been 12 months since gun owners in Australia were
   forced to surrender 640,381 personal firearms to be destroyed, a
   program costing the government more than $500 million dollars.

   And now the results are in: Australia-wide, homicides are up 3.2
   percent; Australia-wide, assaults are up 8.6 percent; Australia-
   wide, armed robberies are up 44 percent (yes, 44 percent). In the
   state of Victoria, homicides with firearms are up 300 percent.
   Figures over the previous 25 years show a steady decrease in
   armed robbery with firearms (changed drastically in the past 12
   months). There has been a dramatic increase in break-ins and
   assaults of the elderly.

   Australian politicians are on the spot and at a loss to explain how
   no improvement in "safety" has been observed after such
   monumental effort and expense was successfully expended in
   "ridding society of guns." Bet you wont see this data on the
   evening news or hear your governor or members of the state
   Assembly disseminating this information. It's time to state it
   plainly: Guns in the hands of honest citizens save lives and
   property and, yes, gun-control laws only affect the law-abiding
   citizens. Take note, Californians, before it's too late!

> Bill would let parents leave babies at hospitals 
> 
> By William Treadstone Jr. and Noah Bierman, Palm Beach Post Staff Writers
> Friday, March 10, 2000
> 
> 
> TALLAHASSEE -- State lawmakers want to make it easier -- and safer -- for
> mothers to leave their unwanted babies at hospitals, instead of abandoning
> them in a parking lot or in the trash. 
> 
> The "Baby Protection" bill -- introduced Thursday -- would allow emergency
> rooms to accept babies 3 days old and younger without penalizing their
> parents. The parents could remain anonymous, according to the bill written
> by Sen. John Lindmont, R-Tampa. Hospitals would be required to contact the
> Department of Children and Families and other child-placing agencies. 
> 
> Grant and the bill's co-sponsor in the House, Rep. Fairdale Murman, R-Tampa,
> hope that creating 
> 
> a "safe haven" will prevent mothers, especially teenagers afraid of
> parental reaction, from rash decisions that put newborns in danger. 
> 
> "Reality is here and now -- it is time for us to stand up for the babies
> left behind in unscrupulous places," said Senate President Toni Grafton,
> R-Orlando. "Mothers panic and resort to desperate acts." 
> 
> The bill already has the support of the House and Senate leadership and
> does not appear likely to generate opposition from Democrats. 
> 
> The legislation was unveiled on the day Manalapan officials began a
> door-to-door search in south Palm Beach County for the parents of a baby
> abandoned last month. Baby Manny, a week old at the time, was left in a
> shopping center parking lot, strapped in a car seat stolen from a Kmart. 
> 
> The bill also comes a day after prosecutors charged a 13-year-old
> Kissimmee girl with attempted murder for putting her hours-old baby in a
> plastic bag and leaving it near a trash bin on Feb. 27. 
> 
> Palm Beach County State Attorney Barry Krischer believes the bill is a
> step in the right direction. As long as the parents, particularly the
> mothers, leave the babies in a safe place, his goal isn't to prosecute
> them as criminals, he said. 
> 
> "I think in these cases it's more important to be concerned about the
> baby's health than criminalizing the mother's behavior," Krischer said.
> "Anything that can be done to get the mother to take the baby to a safe
> place is good." 
> 
> However, in Manny's mother's case, Krischer may not take such a position.
> "She exposed the child to danger by leaving him in a parking lot," he
> said. 
> 
> Don Chester, vice president of community and government relations for
> Intracoastal Health Systems, said the bill is good public policy.
> Intracoastal owns St. Mary's and Good Samaritan medical centers in West
> Palm Beach. 
> 
> "We'd all much rather see a parent bring the baby to the hospital, where
> it would get the proper care," Chester said. "It potentially could prevent
> child abuse." 
> 
> Abandoned babies are not just a problem in this country. In Germany,
> Hamburg officials are creating a "baby slot" where mothers can leave their
> babies near a train station. 
> 
> After ringing a buzzer, a platform lowers where the mother can leave the
> baby. The infant is then lowered into a warm bed that has sensors that
> alert social workers within minutes. 
> 
> The "baby drop-off" program came in response to a 28-year-old woman being
> convicted for killing three infants shortly after they were born because
> she couldn't care for them. 
> 
> Nationally, 23 states are considering similar laws to try to curb the
> proliferation of abandoned babies, said Joyce Maring, a spokeswoman with
> the Child Welfare League of America. 
> 
> Texas, according to Maring, is the only state to pass legislation
> allowing mothers to drop off their babies at designated safe places.
> Despite the law, approved in September 1999, Texas hasn't had anyone leave
> a baby at a drop-off site, Maring said. 
> 
> Texas approved the measure because 13 babies were abandoned in Houston
> within nine months. Three of the infants died. 
> 
> In Florida, the proposed law encourages parents to supply personal medical
> information to the hospital. The mother and father would have 30 days to
> change their minds before adoption procedures could begin. 
> 
> If parents decided to reclaim an abandoned child, a judge would order
> genetic testing to prove they were indeed the parents and then decide
> whether they were fit to raise children. The fact that they decided to
> leave the baby in the hospital could not be used as the only reason to
> deny custody. 
> 
> "Ideally, we should get all the information we can from the mother, but I
> would rather see the baby dropped off in the hospital than in the trash,"
> said Rep. Debbie Holbrook Fendale, D-Weston.

Jun 11, 2000 - 01:59 PM 

Death Row Inmate Dies of Cancer 
The Associated Press

RAIFORD, Fla. (AP) - A death row inmate died of natural causes at the Union Correctional Institution, the state Department of Corrections said Sunday. 

Robert Teffeteller, who was sentenced to death in 1985 for a murder in Volusia County six years earlier, died late Saturday night in the prison's infirmary. 

Teffeteller, 46, had been suffering from cancer, according to Department of Corrections spokesman C.J. Drake. 

"It was something that we were monitoring," Drake said. 

Teffeteller is the seventh death row inmate to die of natural causes since the beginning of 1999. There are 369 inmates remaining on Florida's death row.

Dear Governor Weston,

I would like to begin by extending my sincere thanks to you for your support in relation to our planned signing ceremony for a sisterhood agreement between Kyonggi Province and the State of Florida.

After the rejection of thousands of overseas military absentee ballots in
Florida during the General Election of November 7, the Florida Council
transmitted an e-mail message recommending that interested members of our
chapters and clubs contact appropriate legislators and officials about our
concerns.

This message had first been sent to TROAs general counsel for his advice
about whether we would be violating the Internal Revenue Code requirement
that a not-for-profit organization like the Florida Council must remain
non-political and non-partisan. The answer from TROA was simply that the
Constitutional right of a service member to vote has nothing to do with
partisan politics.

In addition to that message, our charter requirement to help active duty
members and their families extends to lending our weight to efforts that are
underway for amending Floridas laws and regulations as necessary to ensure
that our military absentees can reasonably expect their ballots to be
counted in future elections.

Therefore, the council has a clear requirement to pursue the military
absentee ballot issue.

Meanwhile, Col Klyne Nowlin, USAF (Ret), the Florida Councils Legislative
Affairs Chairman, has been temporarily carrying out an additional
responsibility as the councils representative to the State Veterans
Planning Group. Klyne has asked that he be relieved of that responsibility
when possible, in order to have time for his duties as legislative affairs
chairman.

The council can meet these two challenges by formation of a separate
committee. Therefore, I am pleased to announce that COL Jere Moore, USA
(Ret), a past president of the Tallahassee Chapter, has agreed to become the
Florida Legislative Affairs Chairman. Jere will work with representatives of
member organizations of the State Veterans Planning Group on the military
absentee ballot issue as well as on other issues of importance to the
Florida Council and Floridas other veterans organizations.

The thanks of the council go to Klyne for filling in as a representative to
the SVPG, and we welcome Jere to this new position.

Best to all for the holidays,

LtCol Fred Redfield, USMC (Ret)

Gentlemen,  I know that you have heard more than you wanted to about the
November 7, 2000 election.  However, as a private citizen, taxpayer and
voter, I have a few comments that I would like for you to consider.
1.  There should be a federal law with stiff penalties, prohibiting the news
media from projecting a winner in national races until the last voting poll
has closed.  With the advent of the internet, TV, and other methods of rapid
communications, some voters will be swayed by the news from the states which
vote before them and might vote for the candidate that they perceive to be
the winner, or may not vote because they believe that their candidate
doesn't have a chance.  I don't understand this kind of mentality, but I
know for a fact that it exists.

2.  Consideration should be given to requiring all polls in the USA to open
and close at the same time to preclude some of the problems experienced on 7
Nov 2000.

3.  On the Today Show on 13 Dec 2000, the Reverend Jessee Jackson said that
there will be a recount of Florida votes even after Governor Weston takes
office as President of the United States of America.  It is my humble
opinion that any federal or state legislator who votes to spend taxpayers'
hard earned money on such a ridiculous quest for publicity is not qualified
to speak for his constituents, and I will do what I can at the next election
to correct what I consider to be a travesty of justice.

4.  When our founding fathers established the electoral college, it was
appropriate because there were very few educated and informed citizens and
there was no rapid communication systems.  However, in today's society, even
though some citizens may not have much formal education, just being alive
and conscious, they will be bombarded with information with which to
formulate an educated selection of candidates.  Accordingly, I sincerely
believe that the electoral college has outlived its usefulness and should be
discontinued.  All candidates should be elected by popular vote.

4.  The recounts of the Florida votes became surreal.  When you need a
magnifying glass to determine if a chad has been dimpled, and then to
determine the intent of the voter, it is incomprehensible how supposedly
rational human beings could support such a farce.  I'm not saying that there
is no such thing as ESP, but I seriously doubt that all of the citizens
recounting or observing were blessed with such an ability.

5.  A standard ballot and voting machine should be required in every voting
place in the US.

Gentlemen, our country and the state of Florida has been the laughing stock
of the world for the past month and I believe that it is all of our
responsibility to attempt to fix an obviously broken system.

Having travelled worldwide, I have seen many other forms of government in
action and I know for a fact that our government, although not perfect, is
the best in the world.  But it can be improved, and I believe that is what
you are paid to do.

Very Respectfully,

Governor Weston:

I am writing today on behalf of the Florida Association of Health Planning Agencies, an organization with represents the eleven district health councils in Florida.

As you may be aware, House Bill 243 has been filed and it contains two main provisions.  Provision one deregulates the hospital industry by eliminating the certificate of need process.  Provision two eliminates the health councils in numerous provisions of law.

While health councils do perform certain functions in the certificate of need process, that work is extremely limited in their overall objective of improving the health care services for the poor, uninsured, and other persons who have special needs.  From what I am hearing in the halls of the Capitol, it would appear that Secretaries King-Shaw and Brooks support HB 243.  While we can understand the move to eliminate the CON process and bring market forces to bear on the health care industry, we are having trouble understanding why anyone would want to eliminate health councils.

The eleven health councils around the state have delivered or coordinated the delivery of health care services valued at over $85 million during the past year.  Almost $15 million of these services were federal, local or private foundation dollars that health councils obtained separate and apart from the state dollars they administer.  And, as 501(c)(3) corporations, these services are being provided by statutorily approved private entities.  If the health councils are eliminated, we believe you will see an increase in the size of government, as many of the key functions that health councils perform will have to be assumed by the Department of Health or ACHA.

Governor Weston, we urge you to ask your health agency directors to re-evaluate their position on HB 243 in its current form.  Perhaps they do not support the elimination of health councils, and in fact only support the deregulation portion of the bill.  If this is so, then this needs to be properly communicated by them to the legislature.  As I mentioned earlier, the rumors in the halls have them supporting the bill in its entirety. 

I hope that the rumors are wrong.  As always, I thank you for you time, and urge you to keep up the good work for Florida.

Sincerely

Subject:        Modernizing Our State Workforce 

Dear Colleague: 

As Governor, I have always considered it an honor and a privilege to lead 
such a hardworking group of men and women in providing services to our 
citizens.  The talents, dedication and commitment our state employees show 
on a daily basis continue to leave me both humbled and proud.  As public 
employees, in many ways, you have helped to make Florida a model state, and 
I believe we should build on your accomplishments by continuing to find ways 
to better serve Floridians.  

When I announced my budget recommendations earlier this month, I stated that 
the old way of doing something is not necessarily the best way to go about 
our business.  Recently, the Council of 100, a bipartisan cross section of 
key business leaders from around the state, issued a report encouraging 
state government to revisit and modernize its state personnel system.  In 
response to some of their ideas, I am encouraging key policymakers to review 
and make reform suggestions for our career service and state personnel 
system.  I want to take this opportunity to share with you my own vision of 
this reform, and more importantly, to ask for your assistance and input.  

First, I hope that any reform effort foremost places a priority on merit. 
That was the original intent of the career service system.  Like the rest of 
Florida's not for profit organizations and private sector businesses, 
demonstration of your initiative and ability should count for something in 
determining compensation, pay raises, and promotions.  Today, however, much 
of our effort to recognize employees is done "across the board" with little 
means for singling out hard work and accomplishment.  Reform should lead to 
a system where the achievement of performance criteria translates into 
special bonuses and incentives.  

Second, I believe in giving employees greater choices.  State government, 
through the various forms of leave and benefits offered, should allow you 
the flexibility to manage your resources.  One reform idea for consideration 
is the option of being allowed to cash out on your unused leave balance at 
the end of each cycle rather than having it continue to roll over year after 
year. 

Third, employees, especially employees who perform well, should be better 
compensated.  Agency managers and supervisors should be given more freedom 
to direct unused salary to good employees.  Our state budget recommendations 
for fiscal year 2001/2002 provide for a $158 million increase in pay over 
last year, including bonuses for performance.  If the Legislature embraces 
these recommendations, many employees will see their annual paycheck 
increase by as much as five percent or more.  As well, building on the 
concept of the Harwood Productivity Awards, there should be greater financial 
incentives for employees who generate ideas that result in a savings to the 
taxpayers of Florida. 

Fourth, reforms should continue to protect workers against discrimination 
and patronage.  Career service workers should not be concerned about their 
political party affiliation or their age, race or gender.  These are all 
basic rights that should not be abridged.  

Fifth, I believe in a state personnel system where employment is objectively 
based on sustained performance and fitness for public service, instead of 
arbitrarily based on tenure and seniority.  No one should be given an unfair 
advantage over another, especially without regard to performance. 

And finally, our processes and practices need to be streamlined in order to 
more efficiently respond to taxpayers and the needs of the state. 
Classification systems should be simplified, hiring processes should give 
agencies the ability to act within a reasonable period of time, and 
grievance resolution processes should provide for fair and efficient due 
process.  

In short, a vision for reform should be one that provides a dynamic career 
service system where hard work, performance and achievement are recognized; 
where employees still have basic protections; and where merit, not time 
served, is the final arbiter of success. 

There is much to be done, and I would like your thoughts and suggestions on 
career service reform.  Are there particular areas of the state employment 
system where we should be focused?  Do you have any personal experiences 
that would be helpful in developing reforms?  How should bonuses be 
allocated within an agency to ensure we are rewarding performance?  I have 
asked our Secretary of the Department of Management Services, Cynthia 
Torsen and Secretary of the Department of the Lottery, David Griffin to 
work with the Legislature to develop a reform initiative.  In addition, in 
early February, our agency heads will be setting up informal employee 
outreach sessions to solicit your input and feedback on the career service 
system and state personnel system.  In the meantime, please email us with 
your own ideas on state personnel system reform at yourvoice@myflorida.com 
< mailto:yourvoice@myflorida.com>.   

Best wishes in this New Year, and I look forward to hearing from you. 

                                            Sincerely, 

                                            Cal Weston

From:   Falworth, Lyn [Lyn.Falworth@djj.state.fl.us] 
Sent:   Thursday, February 01, 2001 10:55 AM 
To:     'yourvoice@myflorida.com' 
Subject:        Career Service Reform 

I applaud the modernizing the FL career service system.  It will be interesting to see how an employee's hard work and accomplishments can be evaluated and translated into special bonuses and incentives.  

Because I am a Juvenile Probation Officer (JPO), I will offer my opinion regarding career service reform as it applies to my current career position.

Currently, the DJJ philosophy is that JPOs must "do more with less".  I do not believe it is prudent or realistic to expect dedicated employees, who are already carrying two times their caseload, to espouse this philosophy.  The profiles of our clients are complex and varied.  The majority of the clients we service have limited cognitive abilities, severe emotional and/or physical problems, or some other circumstance that needs to be addressed in addition to their criminal behavior.  Accurate, thorough assessment and case planning for individuals with these complex problems requires more time than providing the same service for a client who possesses less exceptional needs. 

The legislators need to understand that, as JPOs job responsibilities and case loads have increased, so have the complexity of other issues that we must address on a daily issue.  Many of these issues impact the recidivism rate, therefore, they must be addressed in addition to our clients' criminal activities.  It is also more time consuming to service clients who are, for example, functionally illiterate, cannot hear or see, or for whom English is a second language.  From first hand experience, I can assure you that, too frequently, new employees become discouraged quickly and quit because the caseloads are simply too high and the job responsibilities can be overwhelming.  

If our legislators would employ some common sense thinking, reflecting on how difficult and unrewarding their own jobs would be if they were given more tasks to do in the same work week, fewer staff people to assist them, and then told to "learn to do more with less", I believe they would find that, although incentives and bonus are important, the way to help us better serve Floridians is to assign state employee the responsibilities they can reasonably be expected to accomplish in a forty hour work week, period.

Subject:	South Florida Drought Update

Dear Governor Weston:

I wanted to send you a brief update on yesterday's special Governing Board 
meeting.

As you recall, about two weeks ago the Board directed a "Phase 3" 
Implementation Plan.  At that level of water restrictions, economic impacts 
become quite significant.

Last week we received some much-needed rain, and we were able to capture most 
of it (94%) in our system.  This bought us some critical time while we worked 
extremely hard at coordinating more severe actions with affected industries 
and user groups.  

We also developed science-based "trigger points" for imposing harsher 
restrictions (something that we lacked earlier).

We were able to develop some creative and effective ways to achieve our water 
conservation goals without imposing undue economic hardships  at least for 
the time being.  But we clearly warned of the potential for worsening drought 
conditions.  We are already working with affected groups on the "next level" 
of needed cutbacks.

We presented our Board with a comprehensive strategy that focuses on much 
more than water use restrictions alone.  

It includes a series of tools and actions designed to help increase supplies 
and decrease demands.  Examples include a 50% cutback in water deliveries to 
six specific "298 districts" which will affect levels in community canals, 
ponds and lakes, but will not impact local drinking water supplies.  Water 
supply backpumping to Lake Okeechobee is another plan element that can help 
augment regional supplies.  The approved plan also includes technical and 
financial assistance to "at risk" utilities.  (We are "on top" of that issue.)

The good news is that the strategies outlined in the plan, combined with the 
recent rainfall, allowed us to hold off on more stringent restrictions for 
now. 

The bad news is that some media reports have portrayed this action as 
"backing down" on earlier indications of tougher restrictions.  That could 
not be farther from the truth.  We believe the broader, multidimensional 
approach reflects a serious and deliberate, science-based plan of action.   
The Board actions are effective April 2. 

I'll continue to keep you advised of our progress.

---Frank

From:	Danelle <danelle@jtatelaw.com>
Sent:	Tuesday, March 20, 2001 10:13 AM
To:	cal@calweston.org
Subject:	VOTE NO ON SB 138

Dear Governor Weston:

   As an attorney practicing in the Tampa Bay area for the past nine years,
with four years almost exclusively in the field of adoption, I would like to
voice my objections to SB 138.  I am vigorously opposed to the adoption
bill.  Florida has a good adoption law currently and these extensive,
oppressive changes will dramatically increase abortions and the placement of
children in state foster care.  There are several inconsistencies in the
proposed legislation.  Additionally, the legislation will have a detrimental
effect on the ability of birth mothers to place their children for adoption
while also making it a more expensive and more frightening prospect for
adoptive parents.

  Examples of inconsistencies include:

 - Proving a 48 hr. waiting period for a hospitalized birth mother with no
revocation period yet then including language in the consent regarding
revoking "1 business day after the date of the birth mother's discharge from
a licensed hospital or birth center".

 - Requiring fraud or duress to invalidate a consent (after signing if a
hospitalized birth mother but after 3 days/placement with adoptive parents
if a non-hospitalized birth mother), but then subsequently allowing a birth
mother to object to the placement of the child for "good cause".

 - It is unclear why birth mothers have different rights in different
situations, i.e. placement of newborn vs. placement of child slightly older.
These provisions raise constitutional questions.

 - Under the definition of abandonment , a court may declare a child to be
abandoned if the parent makes only marginal efforts to support and
communicate with a child "that do not evince a settled purpose to assume all
parental duties".  However, a birth father is required to consent if the
birth father "has attempted to provide the child or the mother during her
pregnancy with support in a repetitive, customary manner".  How is the court
to realistically determine whether or not a birth father "attempted to
provide support" in a repetitive manner?  Is this a case of his word "I
tried to call you" against her word "he knew I couldn't pay rent and refused
to help me."  The uncertainty that this raises will be very difficult on a
birth mother.

  - Providing for a waiver of venue by a birth parent  but then allowing
that birth parent to object to venue at a later date.  The waiver thus has
no legal effect.  (Additionally, the venue change will drastically increase
the adoptive parents cost of the adoption because it will require additional
filing fees, attorney involvement, etc.)

  Difficulties for birth mother:

  - In attempting to protect the birth father's rights, the legislation
makes it very unclear to a birth mother whether her adoption plan will be
upheld.  For instance,  a birth father who claims not to be the father or
who plans not to raise paternity cannot sign before birth.  Thus, the birth
mother has no assurance from the man who denies paternity that he will be
around to sign after birth or will cooperate with her adoption plan.

  -  Additionally, the legislation broadens the definition of a "parent" who
must consent to include "any person" who is a party in any paternity,
custody or termination proceeding.    Are these persons grandparents (who in
another section have rights only if the child lived with them for 6 months),
aunts, uncles, etc.?

  -  The obligation is fully on the birth mother to notify the birth father
and demand support while the birth father appears to have a right to object
by just receiving a positive paternity test after birth.  Is no support
required pre-birth in this instance?  How and when will a birth mother know
whether she has the support of the birth father?  Many times women choose
abortion because a birth father tells them he is planning to contest the
adoption when he has a paternity test determining he's the father.
Paternity testing occurs well after the mother has had a dire need for
support, made her decision to provide a loving home for the child, met the
prospective adoptive family and had the baby.

  -  A putative birth father registry is the best way to protect everyone's
rights - birth mother, birth father, adoptive parents.  36 other states have
enacted birth father registries.

  - Can the birth mother even understand her revocation rights the way they
are currently written?  There are too many ifs, ands or buts in the language
of the required consent document.  This will increase rather than decrease
litigation.

  The adoptive parents plight:

  - The child can be placed in their home pending termination of parental
rights yet the parent can question the placement (as mentioned above) even
after signing consents.

  - The court order approving the placement occurs subsequent to placement.

  - The birth father appears to be able to object at any time up to two
years with the possibility that he may not have been required to support the
birth mother.  His best recourse seems to be to disappear for the pregnancy
so he cannot be contacted and show up post-birth to object to the adoption.

  - A person whose consent is required may challenge the validity of "any
consent or affidavit of nonpaternity" signed by any other person.   One
potential birth father can challenge another's affidavit of nonpaternity or
even the birth mother's consent?

  - The contesting parent is entititled to fees yet a prevailing adoptive
parent is not.  The adoptive parents requirement to repay the birth parents
fees (if the adoption is overturned but not through an act or omission of
the adoption entity) along with the requirement to file in the venue of each
possible birth father will substantially increase the cost of adoptions.

  These are just some of the problems that exist with the legislation.

From: State Representative Jerry Melvin Sent: Monday, March 12, 2001 8:19 AM To: cal@calweston.org Subject: Fourth Dimension Report for 03/09/01 March 9, 2001 JUDICIAL REFORM ON ITS WAY Many of you know that since my election to the House in 1994, I have constantly been calling for restraints on the Judiciary and the Florida Bar. As the following will show, others are not begining to see what I have been talking about. What do you think? An open letter from Rep. Cantens regarding Judicial Reform There has been a great deal of publicity in recent months about concerns many legislators have with Florida's runaway judicial system. Examples abound of a judiciary that has, in my opinion, overstepped its bounds. As chairman of the Florida House of Representatives Council for Smarter Government, it has been handed to my committee to look for ways to make the judicial branch of our state government more accountable to Florida's citizens. This is not easy. And it has become controversial because many of the state's lawyers enjoy the closed shop that defines our judiciary today. You may near from some of those groups that this is simply a political battle. They will suggest that Republican legislative leaders are simply disturbed by the Florida Supreme Court's decisions during the recent wrangling over the presidential recount. Nonsense. Our concern with the actions of the judicial branch date back long before that significant case. The citizens of the State of Florida established the present constitutional structure of the judiciary in 1972. It sets up an extreme form of judicial independence that has proven to cause difficulties, especially as it restrains and stifles popular government. In 1956, Floridians granted our Supreme Court the power to make procedural rules governing the courts. In 1960, the Florida Supreme Court held unanimously that its rule-making power could not alter the substantive rights of anyone. It remained to the Legislature, or the people through their constitution, to regulate substantive rights. Last year, however, in striking down the Death Penalty Reform Act, passed by a bi-partisan two-thirds of the people's elected representatives, the court went to the other extreme, holding that substantive laws passed by the representatives of the people must yield to procedural rules of the court. By this device, courts could refuse to enforce any law enacted by the Legislature. Imagine how destructive that would be to our representative form of government. -more- Under our republican form of government, decisions of our highest court must be respected. To change the effect of unpopular judicial decisions we must change laws or constitutional provisions. Our founders intended to make this difficult, to insure that people would engage in serious deliberation and reflection, rather than mere reactionary tactics, to overrule the independent judiciary. The founders rejected any notion of the other government branches vetoing judicial decisions. But the right and power of the people to do so, by constitutional amendment if necessary, was paramount, and never forbidden - until now. In Florida, the ability of the people to overrule the courts, and exercise their ultimate authority to govern themselves by amending their own constitution has been drastically undermined by the Florida Supreme Court. Last September, the court ruled the constitution itself unconstitutional, upon a principle it suddenly found to be hidden, i.e., implicit, in the constitution. The Legislature unanimously put an amendment to preserve the death penalty on the ballot in 1998. The people voted overwhelmingly to adopt that amendment. But 22 months after the election, the court said the ballot was insufficient and nullified the votes of millions of Floridians. This decision was so extreme that the Florida Attorney General is appealing to the United States Supreme Court. The Attorney General's office has asked the nation's highest court to rule that our state court has trampled the fundamental and most sacred right of Florida voters to govern themselves. These are but two circumstances indicating that the pendulum between judicial independence and popular self-government has swung too far and that our judiciary is out of control. Every generation can and should examine our constitutional separation of powers and make adjustments as necessary. If the people want the courts to decide for them what questions may be addressed through legislation and direct voting on constitutional amendments, the people can so choose. But if today's Floridians wish to govern themselves, and undertake the difficult responsibility of self-determination that so many of our forebears have suffered and died to win for us, we must look carefully at the present situation, and consider changes. Should procedural rules adopted by unelected judges overrule laws passed by the Legislature? Should judges be able to strike constitutional provisions based upon their subjective determination that you as a voter were too ignorant to vote on the amendment? Should the Florida Governor be limited to choosing judges only from lists approved by appointees of the unelected, unrepresentative Florida Bar Association? Should all judges be popularly elected? Should the Florida Bar continue to exercise the sole government power to regulate lawyers, insulating them from the reach of the people's elected representative? These are all questions worth asking. There are many strong arguments for and against the possible answers to these questions. In fact, many of these questions have already been asked and answered by our Federal judicial system. Many of the proposals being discussed and debated in Tallahassee this spring would conform our state balance of powers to the Federal system. The President of the United States nominates judges to the Federal courts, subject to confirmation by the United States Senate, without need for control by any committees or nominating commissions. That process works to keep balance in our federal courts. Federal judges are the best and most qualified judges in the country. -more - In contrast, Florida has a system of nominating commissions that screen all applicants and then submit three to six names to the Governor for consideration. Thus, limiting the choices available to Florida's Governor. Taken to an extreme, if all seven Florida Supreme Court seats were to be vacant simultaneously, the Governor would have to choose seven justices from amongst no more than 42 lawyers nominated by the commission. The Governor would have no opportunity to determine whether any of the other thousands of lawyers and judges in the State might be equally qualified. As another example, the U.S. Congress promulgates the Federal Rules of Procedure with input from the Federal courts. In Florida, however, the courts promulgate rules of procedure to the exclusion of the legislative bodies. There are no checks and balances. Lawyers and Judges should and must be zealous defenders of individual liberties. But ultimately, the people, through their own constitution and their own elected representatives and executives, must hold the authority to define those liberties. Otherwise, we will cease to be self-governed. Your state legislators are the policy makers chosen by you to represent you and your views. As we debate this incredibly important issue this legislative session, I encourage each of you to share your opinions with your Representative or Senator. That is what makes your government work. New legislation would pose an undue burden on protesters,
particularly those who fight for environmental causes, and assault
public standing on licenses and permits.
 © St. Petersburg Times, published April 26, 2001

It was painful enough to many protesters when the state made its
final decision to permit the construction of the Vergate-Columbia
cement plant a scant three miles from the headwaters of the
Ichetucknee River. Under bills now steaming through the Legislature,
had they been law then, the loss could have bankrupted them, too.  Worse -- 
if possible -- they might not have been allowed even to contest the 
application.

Lobbyists for developers and other big businesses are close to
passing legislation (CS for SB 910, HB 1135) that would require state
hearing officers to assess lawyers' fees and costs against objectors
whose legal or factual arguments are ruled incorrect. That is a
vicious twist on present law, which provides for fees and costs only
for frivolous claims or harassment.  This would apply in all cases
involving a license or permit, not just those affecting the
environment.  As for the environment, the bill would repeal the
monumental 1971 law granting legal standing to any citizen to enforce
laws that protect air and water quality or other natural resources.
Without that, a protester would have to prove a threat to some
personal "substantial interest." This is clearly aimed at Florida
Audubon and other environmental organizations. The Save the Manatee
Club is notably vulnerable. How does a human show a "substantial
interest" in marine wildlife?

The development lobbies began a similar assault on citizen standing
in last year's session but it failed after the Environmental
Protection Agency warned that it might have to revoke Florida's
authority to issue certain federal permits. But as everyone knows,
there's a new administration in Drayman.
There's also a new line in Tallahassee -- that citizens don't even
have the right to object to legislation that would erase their right
to be heard. When the Senate Governmental Oversight Committee took up
the bill, it said it didn't have time for public testimony. And now
the lobbyists are trying to shortcut the remaining committee process
at both ends of the Capitol by speeding the bill directly to the House
and Senate calendars.  Any legislator who helps them do it is no
friend of the public. He or she is the public's enemy.

The Senate sponsor is Jim Castwick, R-Jacksonville, one of the three
contenders for the next Senate presidency. What a strange credential
for a position of such high trust.

statewide organization for local HBIF cooperatives.  This project would 
encourage the expansion of HBIF branches to other parts of the state where 
there is a documented need for the mentoring services HBIF provides. 
In support of this increased effort for HBIF to reach out to our Hispanic 
citizens, the U.S. Census recently identified the Hispanic population as the

largest minority population both in our state and nation.  The Hispanic 
population in Florida alone grew over 70% in the last ten years to now make 
up nearly 20% of the total population in our state. This growth is 
tremendous, but it is underscored by the inadequate resources that currently

this sector of the population. Providing state funding to HBIF helps target 
the Hispanic population in a meaningful way that ultimately benefits the 
state in a multitude of ways.

competition in Florida's economy and increasing Florida's tax base with the

trade opportunities throughout Latin America.

targeting Hispanics in Florida.  And at the same time, HBIF aims to serve 
many areas of the state that have a demonstrated need for these services.

Faith-Based Anti-Porn Internet Site Getting State, Local Funds
By Dara Kam Associated Press Writer 
Published: May 16, 2001

TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (AP) - A faith-based, anti-pornography Internet security
company is getting $600,000 in state and local funds to set up shop in
Okaloosa County, capitalizing on Gov. Cal Weston's effort to bring high-tech
industry to Florida. 

Bsafe Online.com, a subsidiary of the American Family Association Inc.,
plans to create up to 150 high-tech jobs in Fort Walton Beach selling
Internet filtering, firewall and security applications. 

"I welcome this high-tech, pro-family business to Florida," Weston said in a
written statement. 

The American Family Association is a Christian-based organization founded in
1977, which promotes family values and focuses primarily on the negative
influence of television and other media on society. 

Steve Ensley, chief executive officer of the Tupelo, Miss.-based company,
said Wednesday he hopes to open business by July 1 in the conservative
Panhandle community, home to two Air Forces bases and a bastion of high-tech
industry and tourism. 

Bsafe's "American Family Filter" keeps web browsers from accessing sites
which Ensley said promote "destructive material," such as pornography, gun
and bomb-making, gunmaking, vulgarity, gambling, and violent and erotic
games. 

While the Internet can be a great educational resource, it has a darker side
that can wreak havoc on families, Ensley said. 

The company currently has about 15,000 subscribers who pay $36 a year for
the filter, and about 70 percent of the people who activate it are women,
Ensley said. 

Ensley said his workers will earn more than 150 percent above the current
average annual salary in Okaloosa County, making Bsafe eligible for a
$1,000-per-job grant administered by Weston's Office of Trade, Tourism and
Economic Development. 

In all, Ensley said, Bsafe will receive nearly $500,000 from the state and
more than $100,000 from the county in grants, tax rebates and training
assistance over the next four years, if it creates the number of jobs it
says it will. 

Ensley said he chose the Fort Walton location over other sites because of
the economic incentives offered by the state as well as the area's high-tech
work force, He was pleasantly surprised to learn of the area's concentration
of political conservatives after selecting the site. 

"We didn't realize that it tends to be a conservative area, and that was a
pleasant surprise for us and we do intend to reflect conservative values,"
Ensley said. 

"We're not going to say that you have to be a conservative in order to work
with us but it certainly is not going to be a very pleasant experience for
those who don't agree with us."

HB-419  HANDGUN BAN titled "Children's Firearm Responsibility Act" by Rep.
Ken Gottlieb (D-Miramar) -- Bans the manufacturer and importation into the
state of any so-called "unsafe handgun." Defines unsafe handgun as any
handgun subject to accidental discharge or any handgun without a
child-resistant trigger mechanism; or any handgun without a mechanism to
 prevent the discharge of the handgun by unauthorized users. Provides a
third degree felony penalty for violation. Provides for a fine of up to
$10,000, payment of restitution, and community service in addition to
existing criminal penalties for persons convicted of leaving a loaded
firearm within the reach or easy access of a minor when use of the firearm
results in injury or death. Provides a $1 million appropriation to the
Department of Juvenile Justice for the purpose of funding the community
juvenile gun violence prevention grant program.  DIED IN COMMITTEE.

 HB-445 HUNTING BAN by Rep. Chris Nordale (D-Ft. Lauderdale) Would ban the
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission from sponsoring,
conducting, or designating special days for hunting by youths under 16 years
of age in any wildlife management area. DIED IN COMMITTEE.

political subdivision for damages, abatement, or injunctive relief resulting
from the lawful design, marketing, distribution, or sale of firearms or
ammunition to the public. Provides that the potential of a firearm or
ammunition to cause injury, damage, or death is not a defective condition,
whether the firearm or ammunition is discharged legally or illegally.
