From:	Stroud, Brian <brian.stroud@myflorida.com>
Sent:	Monday, July 23, 2001 11:55 AM
To:	'cal@calweston.org'; Maddox, Frank; Whitlock, Donna; Latster, Frank
Cc:	Redfern, Kathleen; Larkin, Nina; Briston, Michael
Subject:	Health Team Trip to Drayman

Last week, we met with members of the Weston Administration's
Medicaid/Medicare team and key Congressional staff involved with
Medicaid/Medicare reform on House and Senate side.  In addition, we met with
Speaker Hastert's top advisor on health policy issues.  Here's a brief
snapshot of findings.  Others on email may want to supplement if i've left
anything out.

On Medicaid Reform

Congress and the Administration are currently overwhelmed with Medicare
reform.  Medicaid issues will not take a front seat until the former is
completed.  However, with TANF reauthorization, they expect next year to be
the year for Medicaid issues.  

The Administration would rather do as much as it can in-house on Medicaid
first before going to Congress.  HHS is currently working on a Model
Medicaid Waiver -- they made clear that on waivers, HHS will grant the
greatest flexibility possible for innovation, but the initiatives must be
budget neutral. They also want better guidance from the states as to the
impacts of the waivers requested.  HHS will not predicate waivers based on
expansions.

As it relates to the NGA proposal as an option for reform (flexibility with
expansion), HHS made clear that they have a problem with what NGA proposed
and was well aware of our position, which they shared.  Mark McClellan, the
President's policy advisor on this, also agrees with our position -- they
are looking at Medicaid reform that would be based on "flexibility with
performance/accountability."  Using the same amount of funding to move in a
new direction.  We shared our position on the NGA proposal with all the Hill
staff that we met -- most seemed sympathetic and were skeptical that the NGA
proposal would get any traction based on budget realities.

We shared with them our views on Medicaid reform overall not displacing the
private insurance market, and adding more personal involvement and
responsibility to reforms much like welfare reform.  Both HHS and WH want
our specific input on the wavier and reform as this moves forward.  They
want ideas on how we show "performance."

On Medicare Reform

Everyone believes reform will happen this year -- with a bill emerging from
Congress in either October or November.  The House Energy and Commerce staff
assured us that all the proposals on the table right now have the federal
government fully picking up the cost of drugs for Medicaid/Medicare
dually-eligibles, which would amount to a $700 million fed/state savings
over time -- the over time is the key point here as the phase in is likely
to take a while.

There is also discussion on the Hill on Medicare reform adding some type of
means-testing component/looking at premium subsidies from the government to
be based on income.

On S-CHIP Coverage for Children of Immigrants

We made the pitch at a number of meetings and there is legislation currently
filed in Congress that would allow us to do this.  However, the proposal to
provide this coverage was met with some skepticism based on Congressional
dynamics.  We were told by Hill staff that the Speaker had some concerns
with the legislation and perceived it as a roll back on welfare reform
advances.  Mike did a good job stessing the importance of this to the
Speaker's aide and explaining why this was not rolling back the principles
of welfare reform -- part of Florida's allocation that we cannot draw
down/the "federal responsibility" for our borders and immigration.  All and
all, it was not a hopeful outlook.

On Florida Drug Formulary

Everyone in DC was interesting in our Pfizer agreement and how the formulary
works.  HHS did indicate that Pharma wants HHS to review our new law.  We
need to find a better way to package this initiative (pr-wise) for those who
are interested -- AHCA currently is passing out a powerpoint presentation
that they use, but its a little technical and not as comprehensive
Mike/Greg, can you work with Bob's shop/AHCA communications to have them
create a simple two/three pager that covers the major features of the law,
the agreement, how we are measuring performance, timing, efforts to move
forward.

On Nursing Home Initiative

HHS indicated they will be moving foward with some type of nursing home
quality initiative that is not all directly financial assistance, but would
have many components.  They were not in a position to share too many
details, but we did offer to have Florida be one of their showcase states --
based on our own reforms from this year.

suffered while taking part in those activities. 

The rules, which were issued jointly by the Internal Revenue Service, the 
Pension and Welfare Benefits Administration, and the Health Care Finance 
Administration (HCFA), directly contradict the intent of Congress in passing 
HIPAA. In fact, language in the Congressional Record notes that the law "is 
intended to ensure, among other things, that individuals are NOT excluded 
from healthcare coverage due to their participation in activities such as 
motorcycling, snowmobiling, all-terrain vehicle riding, horseback riding, 
skiing and other similar activities." 

The AMA and other motorcycling groups worked hard to get that language 
included in the Congressional Record after uncovering incidents in which 
employers were discriminating against motorcyclists, leaving them without 
coverage when they were involved in recreational activities. The AMA noted at 
the time that some health plans would provide healthcare benefits for 
employees involved in ILLEGAL activities, like driving a car while drunk, but 
cut off those benefits from many legal activities. 

These new rules are an outrage! And I, for one, as a registered voter and 
motorcyclist am appalled that I am being discriminated against in this 
manner. I pay my carrier roughly $200.00 PER MONTH for family health 
coverage, and have been doing so for over ten years. Now I am told they will 
be able to deny me reimbursement for medical care in the event that I am 
involved in a motorcycle accident? 

In fact, I believe this legislation will backfire horribly as individuals who 
are denied health care do to recreational injuries such as this will FOREGO 
treatment and rehabilitation due to inability to pay the astronomical costs 
demanded by medical institutions. As a result there will be an escalation of 
man-hours of labor lost to employers due to injuries and the aftereffects 
from those injuries. I believe there will also be an escalation of disability 
claims as a result of this legislation. 

This legislation benefits no one but the greedy insurance agencies who are 
paid to provide the very service which they now seek absolution from! No 
other service industry in this great country could ever get away with such 
trickery! Let's not allow this travesty to occur! 

Please join myself and the voting, motorcycling public, and the AMA (American 
Motorcycling Association) in making sure that this problem is corrected 
immediately and that the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act 
of 1996 is corrected to reflect it's ORIGINAL intent! 

Thank you in advance for your consideration of this matter.
J.D. Maring
Homestead Florida

Hi, Pam

Our very best public relations experience and advice is that the Governor
does NOT want Visit Florida responding to this issue! Anything we may say
would be suspect as tourism PR flak. It would be better for us to direct
media to the Governor's Office or to a Florida governmental department like
Fish and Wildlife for that entity to have a spokesperson lined up and ready
to respond.

This is a  lesson we learned when several European visitors were murdered
back in the early 90's. You do not want your tourism marketing folks
responding to the news media on such issues. You need an expert on the topic
who is not perceived to have a vested interest. 

During the tourist murders the tourism industry PR folks got together and
agreed that anything the then-Division of Tourism or CVBs or anyone in the
industry might say would be viewed as "chamber of commerce" flak by the
public and by news editors. But if the issue is addressed by someone who
doesn't have a vested interest, it is much more believable. Back then we had
the head of FDLE be the spokesperson to say that Florida was safe. Much more
believable from that source.

Remarkably there have been no news media calls on this shark attack.
Normally we would not advocate a proactive stance on something like this
media. It only generates more ink and more attention to the issue. 

Our recommendation is to get a marine biologist expert lined up and
available to speak to the media on the issue. His or her speaking points
might include:

1.) Literally millions of residents and visitors safely enjoy Florida's
beaches and beaches.  
2) The chance of shark attack is rare and remote. There is no reason to fear
going into Florida's Gulf or Atlantic coastal waters.
3) Sharks do not target humans. If a shark bites a human, it is because the
shark has mistaken the human for one of its traditional food sources.

The spokesperson may want to  give a few pointers (i.e., sharks generally
feed at dusk or at night; if you see a shark while you are bathing in the
ocean, do not panic, just swim to shore or walk out of the water).

If you want us to assist, we will be happy to call Mote or Sea World to see
if they can provide a spokesperson. Again, it must be someone with good
credentials who can speak well on the issue. Our recommendation is to use
them only in response mode to media inquiries.

Kindest regards,

Friday Night Greetings!

Here is an update of DCF happenings that you should be aware of:

1)  Federal Adoption and Safe Families Act Audit:

Representatives from HHS have been in the state all week to audit our
compliance with the Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA).  We volunteered
to be one of the first states in the nation to do this.  They are looking
at cases from 1999 in every state to determine a baseline for comparison
and implementation of the ASFA goals (safety/well-being/permanency)
nationwide.  We audited ourselves last year using their methodology in
order to prepare for this big event and begin corrective action in advance
of the formal audit report.  I attended our exit interview with the federal
reps this afternoon.  Three sites were visited:  Okaloosa County, Sarasota
County, and Miami-Dade County.  Overall, we did better than we expected
given that these were 1999 cases and substantial changes have been put in
place since then.  Our preliminary 2000 self-audit showed us scoring below
the 50% mark in all categories, predominantly due to our challenges in
Miami-Dade.  Although the federal numbers have not been finalized, they
reported that their numbers will come in much higher than we expected in
all categories.  (Example -- 89-90% in safety category; 66% is our expected
lowest score in the well-being category.)  In several categories we did
extremely well.  The best news is that the Sarasota site did extremely well
in all categories.  Chris and crew were present for today's exit brief too.
This will give us additional evidence that the reformation of child welfare
is occurring here in Florida by advancing this important initiative.  The
federal reviewers also commented positively on HomeSafenet; use of our
monthly situation reports to track progress; the role of the Community
Alliances and neighborhood partnerships; our movement towards
accreditation; and our training program.  Areas of weakness noted were lack
of mental health services for parents and children; inconsistency in
engaging the parents in the development of the caseplan; and lack of
infrastructure in the districts to do programmatic quality assurance and
contract monitoring.  The initial report will be out in 30 days.  I have
asked that they give us a heads up prior to releasing it so that we can be
prepared to respond.

2)  Palm Beach County Grand Jury Report #2:

The 4th District Court of Appeals ordered that the second part of the Palm
Beach County Grand Jury report be released today.  This is the report that
details the individual employee errors that contributed to the death of
Joshua Saccone.  This report was done in March, 2001 but the employees
involved (at the time all career service) fought in court to keep this
report sealed.  Judge Colbath denied their motion to suppress its release
and they appealed.  The appellate court ruled against them and it was
released today.  We have already taken the corrective action required (i.e.
firing them) and advised the media of the status of each employee named
when they called today.  Interesting enough, one of the employees was
reinstated by PERC and is on the job.  This should draw attention, once
again, to the Grand Jury recommendation supporting civil service reform.
Last week we filed our first report on our progress since the first Grand
Jury report was issued.  The response was well received and Judge Colbath
reported that he was very pleased with the progress shown.

3)  District Visits

I continue my visits around the state to each district to meet with local
community leaders/movers/shakers to share the vision and listen to their
concerns.  This week it was Daytona.  They are very excited about the
transition to community based care.  I promised them that you would visit
when they are fully operational (probably in December/January.)  The main
issue of concern in this community appears to be mental health.  They have
some very vocal advocates that made their thoughts known.  It continues to
amaze me how little is known about the Dept by the public.  Six visits down
and 8 more to go!

4)  Dependency Summit

We are very psyched that you will attend on the 29th!  There are now over
1700 people attending and we are being hounded for more slots.  Let me know
when you want me to brief you on this event.  We can work up bullets for
you if you wish.  It will be a great opportunity to highlight our progress
and your commitment to child welfare.

It's been a long and busy week for DCF.  Hope that all of you are well and
will get some great R&R this weekend.
(That means little or no Cal e-mails please!)

Per your request for information for Florida House.
 
The Andean region includes some of Florida's top export markets around the world.  Last year despite recessionary conditions  throughout most of the region, they still bought about 5.7 billion dollars in Florida products and probably as much as 3 billion in Florida services. Many of the products we sell them are high technology Florida origin products( see attachment # 2).  About  50% of everything Colombia buys from the US passes through Florida.
 
The Andean Trade Preference Act gives duty free entry to the US to Andean region produced products (see attachment # 1). Last year  approximately 3.3 billion dollar in Andean products passed through Florida. Thousands of Floridians are employed by the companies that import these products. For example the Colombian flower industry here employs over 10,000.
 
Repeal of the  ATPA would:
 
1- Impact heavily the already weakened economies of the region as it will affect about 35 % of the total products they export to the US. This in turn would deny them the reserves needed to buy US products affecting an already sluggish Florida export and services export.
 
2- It will damage further Florida logistic and transportation services sector that supports our two way trade not to mention the workforce that works for the importers
 
3- It will further fuel the economic pressures that are responsible for an unprecedented migration of Andean citizens to Florida, many of them undocumented.Further affecting our economy, quality of life, services, etc.
 
4- The ATPA also serves as an incentive for these nations to promote alternatives to cultivation of Coca and marijuana and to combat drug trafficking. Should the act be eliminated so will one of our key carrots to combat the drug trade.

Well Cal, it's like this:

I am an employee of the Department of Corrections.  I have near 20 years
service to the state-an amount that you wont even come close to meeting
half-way.  You wont work the trenches like we do.  You do not have to put up
with the destruction that your reforms have created.  You're the Governor and
everyone jumps and yells, "How high do you want me to go?"  You don't care
about us or the State of Florida any more than you did before you thought
about getting elected and you will forget about us 10 minutes after your last
possible day in office.  I voted for you.  I am a registered Republican and
am ashamed to be associated with your election.  I sure don't tell any one
that I voted for you.  Well enough of that part of my opinion.  It won't make
any difference anyway.

Just in case someone does read this and bothers to pass the info on:

The reduction of the Personnel Offices in FDC (as Michael Moore like to call
it) has had a devasting effect on us.  It is practically impossible to get
any service from the 4 Personnel Offices that still exist.  Most of them
figure that their jobs will soon be coming to an end and are unwilling to do
anything.  

The changes to the Business office are similiar.  They have been more
devasting when it comes to purchasing supplies.  Now we have to call the
(Un)Service Center where someone, who knows absolutely nothing about a
prison, makes a decision whether or not we need something we ask for.  If we
didn't need it, we wouldn't be asking and if you don't trust your local
supervisors' judgement, then you should get new supervisors.

As far as Staff Development goes, it doesn't.  Our Training situation did
need reform-everyone said so but it didn't need a shut down.  Speaking of
that, did you know that Mr. Moore wants to change our Basic Recruit Training
so that we are not interchangable with the County Sheriffs' Departments?  Of
course you know that.  If he succeeds, then he can lower our pay.  We have no
doubt that he will do that, if he can.  

About Merit raises.  We've been there before and it didn't work.  It created
dissention and distrust between Supervisors and Staff.  There were several
problems.  One of them was that the funds were limited.  As an example, a
Supervisor with 70 Officers assigned to his shift was allowed to award 3
merit raises/year.  Now how could anyone determine that a Supervisor was only
going to have 3 meritorious staff members.  Most shifts will have more than
that and some will have fewer.  Needless to say, the Supervisors gave the
raises to the "Good Ole Boys".  If you are going to insist on this, you must
do two things.  1)  There must be enough funding so that everyone on the
shift can get it.  That event is unlikely but possible so the funds have to
be able to cover it.  2)  There have to be some very strict and defined
regulations by which these funds may be awarded and the regulations must be
widely publicized so everyone has a chance.  This will mean a major overhaul
of the Career Service Rating System (RAPP).  As it is now, all the standards
can be answered by "Yes" or "No" which means that there is no room for
Meritorious ratings.  Also, a Meritorious rating system must grade the
employee against a standard - not against their peer group.

Dr. Nora Hoover, who ran the university's reading lab had developed the program at the request of Larry Sullivan, Principal of Interlocken Elementary School in Alachua County.  

The program is now operated by a non-profit corporation, The Literacy Trust, Inc. in Gainesville.  Dr. Hoover gave up her position at UF to devote her full attention to this program.  It involves training literacy experts and tutors who tutor a student every day for a minimum of thirty minutes.  Participation means that  a school makes a commitment to helping the most needy young students learn to read.

1/21/02
State overflows with road projects
Some economists doubt that additional spending will bolster sagging
economy

By Paige St. John, The News-Press Tallahassee Bureau

TALLAHASSEE - Gov. Cal Weston's economic stimulus package pumps so much
money
into highway construction that state administrators are uncertain
whether
contractors can handle the work.

They warn that high demand and limited supply are a bad mix -
threatening
inflation of Florida's cost of building roads.

The boost goes to an industry in boom.

In November, Florida awarded more road contracts than any other state.

With the stimulus package pushing state contracts to $2.3 billion,
Florida
will have a record $4.3 billion in state taxpayer-funded road work in
progress this year.

Labor statistics from the state Agency for Workforce Innovation show
employment in heavy construction has climbed steadily for two years, to
a
record 54,700 workers in November.

Some economists say the spending plan does little to the economy.
RELATED
STORIES
Scholarship program under review
Medicaid could face reductions in 2002
Road construction to tie up state's traffic

Although $668 million in contracts are to be awarded by July 1, only 15
percent, at best, can be spent in this fiscal year. It will be 2003
before
the work is in full swing.

"Stimulus packages are more about politics than they are about doing
anything for the economy," said James Gwartney, an economics professor
at
Florida State University who argues that there is little that state
governments can do to affect commerce.

"It is not likely they're able to do anything that's hugely important,"
Gwartney said.

"They might do a few things that are helpful," such as speeding up state
spending, Gwartney said, "but the gains there, it would be easy to
exaggerate."

The double-edged message of spending amid cuts became Weston's motto in
the
three months after Sept. 11 as he shepherded an $823 million stimulus
and
state security package through the special budget-cutting sessions of
the
Florida Legislature - for a net state spending increase of $59 million.

At the same time, Florida public schools were forced to give up $309
million. Human services programs were cut $111 million. Criminal justice
lost $87 million.

The cuts came out of the state's general revenue fund while the road
work
was paid for from Florida's transportation fund, fueled by the state gas
tax, motor vehicle registrations and title fees and borrowing against
Florida's future share of the federal gas tax.

Two years earlier, Weston and Florida's major road-building companies had
pushed a major package, Mobility 2000, that this year moved $320 million
from the general revenue programs to the road fund.

At the time, lawmakers cited Florida's "healthy" budget surplus.

With the tide turned and the general revenue budget on the rocks, the
road
building industry is fighting to prevent a reverse flow - to prevent the
Legislature from "raiding" the transportation trust fund.

The budget cuts eliminate 1,813 state government jobs.

Department of Transportation spokesman Dick Tarburn said the $529 million
road
building plan will add 17,850 jobs.

Not all of those jobs come with road building. Tarburn said the estimate
includes new jobs created after the roads are built. He cited the
reopening
of a Dunkin' Donuts and Publix grocery store pending the widening of a
highway in Tallahassee.

On a cushion

The industry is so busy that DOT district production planners harbor
concern
that Florida could push out too much new road work.

"The biggest problem we were concerned with was the lack of construction
companies to perform the work," said Jim Holgate, production management
director for the DOT's District 4 that encompasses Palm Beach.

"Right now, there's an enormous amount of construction work being done
in
South Florida," Holgate said.

The heavy construction industry isn't as rosy as it looks, cautioned Don
Sollie, vice president of regional operations for APAC-Florida, the
state's
second-largest road building company.

"We have some built in-cushion for downturns in the economy. Once that
cushion goes away, the amount of work in the marketplace is diminished,
and
we have to lay off people," he said.

Although public works projects are up, Sollie said, the bulk of the
business
for his company is private construction - and that will be lagging if
corporations reduce capital investments. Already, he said, Disney has
decided to stall a major hotel project that would have provided work in
Orlando.

"We feel the governor has done a magnificent job in providing that
cushion,"
Sollie said.

Uneven benefits

If the construction companies keep up with Florida's road projects, the
effect will be some of what the governor promised: jobs.

"The big concern is people - not companies we've got plenty of those;
not
equipment, we've got bulldozers and what not - but the people to do the
work," said Bob Burleson, president of the Florida Transportation
Association.

"The one thing we're all hopeful of is people laid off in the service
industries might finally take a look at construction and see that it is
not
something you do after you're laid off at Burger King. It's a great,
alternative long-term career," Burleson said.

"The wages and benefits are very good. And the best thing about it is,
it is
very stable. We don't experience the downturns in the same severity that
even building construction does."

Road wages are based on experience and location. Raking asphalt in
Escambia
County in the Panhandle pays $6.50 per hour, but $7.23 in Brevard on the
Space Coast and Lee counties.

But there is another hitch.

The majority of the road construction projects land in two Florida
counties,
Polk and Palm Beach.

Palm Beach, with the second-largest number of out-of-work Floridians,
will
receive $180 million of the work, including the biggest project, a $79
million widening of Interstate 95.

The project is so huge the district production management director
expects
national and international road firms to bid.

Projects in Polk County in the central part of the state total $153.8
million.

Other counties, such as Brevard, received no projects. Lee and Collier
counties received nearly $34 million for projects.

Betties----pls print for Gov and Kathleen.  Betty H.---does Gov have a call and work time available?
Governor----Congressman Hagshaws COS called today.  Dr. Hagshaw met with Sec ONeil re the Florida Non-Resident Alien banking regulation that Florida Bankers have been very worried about and that we have worked for about 1 year.  Below is a brief description of the issue and a short timeline.
Dr. Hagshaw would like to speak with you this week, about his conversation with Sec ONeil and hopes that you can light more fire in the Administration to get them to pull the proposed regulation.  Our office has had several contacts with the FL Bankers about this issue and with Treasury and the WH.  I get the sense that the Congressman would like this to be our number one issue.
Background.
Florida's bankers are concerned about an IRS-proposed regulation that would require banks to report all interest of $10 or more earned by non-resident aliens on their depositswhich the US government would then share with the aliens' home countries.  The U.S. government sees this as a way to better track possible terrorist assets while encouraging communication and coordination among nations fighting money laundering.
However, according to the Florida Bankers Association (FBA),  this regulation would force wealthy individuals to withdraw their funds from US banks and seek financial shelter elsewhere due to a fear of kidnapping or terrorism in their home countries if the scope of their wealth were disclosed.  Currently, Florida holds approximately $49 billion in foreign assets, the majority of which originates in Latin America.  If the IRS began implementation of the regulation, the FBA estimates that Florida would lose $18-$34 billion and 62,000-188,000 jobs in the first year alone.
Timeline.
-          By May 7, 01, Frank Bonner had talked to IRS, I spoke with Asst Sec at Treasury and Kathleen spoke with ONeils Chief of Staff.
-          May 17, 01, Frank Bonner attended a meeting with FBA and Senate Committee Staff (we set the meeting).
-         May 17, 01, Frank Bonner attended meetings with FBA and Treasury and WH staff.
-         The Governor wrote a letter on June 7, 2001 to Secretary O'Neill asking for a careful review of the regulation and for Treasury to look for a better solution to the problem of money-laundering/collaboration.
-         October 1, 01, the FBA and Florida International Bankers Association sent a letter to Secretary O'Neill including an impact study they had commissioned to look into the damages of this regulation (Tony Falbury completed the study).
-         October 17, 01, representatives of FBA, came to Drayman to meet with Pippa Malmgren and Marc Weinburger (Dept. of Treasury) to discuss the issue, and inform the Department about the implications of the regulation.  The same day, the group also met with Congressman Hagshaw, Congressman Harwood and staff from Senator Graham's office.

letters, the first from Senators Bob Baumann and Bill Ransome stating
their deep concerns and opposition to the proposed NRA rule. Our two
U.S. Senators, Florida's Congressional delegation and Governor Weston are
very concerned about the economic impact this proposal will have on
Florida.

American Bankers Association, (ABA) addressed to the Secretary, stating
his objections and concerns with the proposed NRA rule. As you know, the
ABA  represents bankers nationwide.

mailed soon.

government, the United States benefits in competing for international
deposits. If made final, the proposed I.R.S. rule would drive out
hundreds of billions of dollars in non resident alien deposits that work
to capitalize businesses and communities in our country and more
specifically, right here at home in Florida.

A significant flight of this capital will reduce the amount of credit
available to local communities, will adversely affect the liquidity of
many banks, and will make it harder for consumers to acquire loans in
those communities in our nation that have significant NRA deposits.

with you again soon to hopefully bring this matter to a close.

Federal Nursing Home Quality Initiative
 
Request for involvement - The Centers of Medicare and Medicaid Services and the Department of Health and Human Services are planning to have a multi-city Florida press event (possibly at a nursing home) starting April 25 -26. Plans are for Tallahassee on Thurs 4/25, then to Tampa/Orlando and Miami. They have invited the Gov, Lt. Gov, or some other Florida administration official to attend.  Sec. Thompson will announce the program on 4/24 in D.C. at 2 pm. Right after the press conference, data from the 6 states will be available on-line at the CMS website.
 
Background -- In the fall of 2001, Gov. Weston requested that Florida be included in Medicare's Nursing Home Quality Initiative 6-state pilot project along with Colorado, Ohio, Maryland, Rhode Island and Drayman. Gov. Weston was instrumental in getting Florida involved in this initiative.
 
CMS will publish new quality information on nursing homes in the 6 states to help make people aware of how performance differs across nursing homes. The quality information will be used by Medicare beneficiaries to make placement decisions as well as by homes to improve the quality of care. CMS plans to expand initiative nationally by mid- October 2002. 
 
Quality measurements -- The nine measures to be used for the pilot public reporting effort are -- Florida overall scores (avg for other states): 
 
Bed sores - 9% (8%)
Residents who need more help doing daily activities - 14% (14%)
Pain in long stay residents - 13% (14%)
Weight loss - 8% (8%)
Physical restraint use - 6% (7%)
Infection prevalence - 15% (16%)
Delirium in short stay residents - 3% (4%)
Pain in short stay residents - 27% (30%)
Improvement in walking in short stay residents - 34% (34%)
 
Florida was the same as the other states in 3 categories; lower in 5 categories; higher in 1 category.  While there are some slight variations, essentially all states ranked very similarly in all categories according to Mary Kay.
 
FLORIDA NOTES - AHCA currently produces a web-based nursing home guide since ...
 
State selection criteria -- The six states were selected because they will provide CMS with a diverse group of settings in which to test the objectives of the program-how effective is providing quality information to consumers in helping them make decisions about their health care. The criteria included: past experience or current interest in consumer reporting; a State's legislative mandate to report consumer information; the varied size of the states, both in terms of geography and population; urban and rural populations; the number of nursing homes in the state; the diversity of residents in the state; and the mix of chains and independently owned facilities.
 
Expected role of states -- The role of the states is to provide a friendly and supportive environment for the pilot and the release of data. Specifically, the states will stand behind the validity and importance of the measures, will communicate the importance and meaning of measures to public, will be prepared to respond to poor facility performance.
 
CMS support to pilot states -- create and implement public awareness programs and publish the quality information for their states; collaborate with nursing homes and help them use the information to develop and implement quality improvement projects; and evaluate the pilot efforts in collaboration with CMS.
 

PRESS RELEASE INFO-- 
 
CONTACT: Martin Bahl, Communications Media Specialist
 

FLORIDA ADDED TO MEDICARE NURSING HOME QUALITY INITIATIVE

 (February 20, 2002) Florida is one of six states participating in a Medicare quality improvement demonstration project designed to help people who rely on Medicare and Medicaid programs and their family members find the best nursing homes for their needs. 
 
HHS Secretary Tommy Thompson announced the Nursing Home Public Reporting Quality Initiative on November 19, 2001. Colorado, Maryland, Ohio, Rhode Island and Drayman are also participating in the demonstration project that reflects the administration's commitment to improving quality of care in all aspects of the Medicare and Medicaid programs.
 
"People covered by Medicare and Medicaid have the power to choose the best care to meet their individual needs, but they have to have more reliable information to choose quality care," Secretary Thompson said. "Our efforts today will help beneficiaries all across the country to compare the performance of their local nursing homes, and will provide the recognition that high-quality nursing homes deserve." 
 
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), a division within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, will release publicly reported quality indicators on nursing homes as part of the six-state demonstration during the month of April.  Plans call for all states to be part of the program by fall 2002. 
 
National Quality Forum, a Drayman, D.C.-based, nonprofit organization created to develop and implement a national strategy for health care quality measurement and reporting, has established the nine quality of care measures and reporting criteria. These nine measures reflect care given to those with chronic conditions: physical restraints, pressure sores, weight loss, infections, pain management, declines in activities of daily living, managing delirium, pain management and improvement in walking.  The data will be risk adjusted to account for differences in the types of patients who are in the care of nursing homes.
 
Florida was added to the pilot because of its high number of Medicare beneficiaries, diverse population and demographics. Florida currently has 721 licensed nursing homes accounting for 81,963 beds. Florida Medical Quality Assurance, Inc. (FMQAI), a quality improvement organization contracted by the federal government to monitor and improve healthcare for Medicare beneficiaries, will coordinate the project in Florida.
 
FMQAI will work with the nursing home industry in Florida on quality improvement efforts based on the publicly reported information. FMQAI is currently partnering with other quality improvement organizations in the pilot states, state agencies, trade associations, professional groups, patient advocacy organizations and academic faculty to develop the project in Florida.
 
Partners include the Florida Health Care Association, Florida Association of Homes for the Aging, Florida Medical Directors Association, Florida Association of Directors of Nursing Administration, Florida Association of Nursing Assistants and the Agency for Health Care Administration.
 
The new consumer information, which will be posted on http://www.medicare.gov, will expand and strengthen CMS' existing beneficiary-oriented comparison tools -- including "Medicare Health Plan Compare," "Nursing Home Compare" and "Dialysis Facility Compare" which are all also posted on the Web at http://www.medicare.gov <http://www.medicare.gov/> . The information is also available at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).

The following article was in Friday's "CongressDaily" regarding the federal
election reform bill, which is currently in Conference Committee between the
House and Senate.  There is a great deal of pressure on the Committee to
finish the bill quickly and a deal is likely in the next few weeks.

There are three provisions mentioned in the article below.  Following is an
update on those provisions:

1.  Poll Worker Training Funds--Both bills authorize funds for training poll
workers.  If the bill is completed this year, Florida would benefit from
funds disbursed during the fiscal year that starts tomorrow.

2.  Timelines--Both bills have very strict timelines for carrying out the
reforms.  Since Congress has delayed in passing the bill, many states have
voiced their concern that there will not be enough time to institute the
reforms before the 2004 election.  We voiced similar concerns to Conference
Committee staff during a conference call in July.

3.  State Database/ID Requirement--It is highly likely that the compromise
bill will include requirements for state-wide databases and identification
checks at polling places.  Most states are very concerned about this
requirement, since only five states have a database already in place.
(Florida has a database system.)

Thanks, Melissa

LOOKING IN
Preventing Future Floridas
     Prompted by Florida's disastrous primary Sept. 10, lawmakers on Capitol
Hill are scrambling to reach final agreement on a sweeping overhaul of the
nation's voting system.
     Florida's recent troubles have prompted House members to press for
quick action on long-stalled election reform legislation. The legislation
passed the House in December and won Senate approval in April but has been
stalemated in conference for months. At the instigation of Rep. Maxine
Waters, D-Calif., the House has now instructed conferees to reconcile the
two bills by Oct. 1 - next Tuesday.
     The rush to finally enact a bill is understandable. After all, two
years have passed since polling problems in Florida disrupted the
presidential election and revealed a nationwide voting system badly in need
of repair. Yet Florida's latest election fiasco suggests that hastily
enacted reforms have a tendency to backfire. The real lesson from Florida
may be: Proceed with caution.
     Florida officials invested $32 million in new voting systems and
equipment, but last month voters faced long lines, uncounted ballots and a
weeklong recount. (In the hotly contested Democratic gubernatorial primary,
former Attorney General Reno eventually conceded to lawyer Bill Ferris.)
The problems, according to a recent report: poorly trained precinct clerks
and confusion over new provisional ballots and touch-screen machines.
     "To say to states: 'We'll give you a little money for a new piece of
equipment,' and to throw it on their doorstep with no training resources
would be a major mistake," said Cathy Cox, the Georgia secretary of state
and chairwoman of the elections committee for the National Association of
Secretaries of State.
     Cox and other secretaries of state are eager for a bill, but they worry
that certain provisions now on the table will cause Florida-style problems
nationwide. Both the House and Senate bills set aside $3.5 billion over five
years to help states buy new equipment, upgrade election systems and
establish minimum standards for provisional voting and statewide
registration systems.
     But state officials fear that they will not receive federal funding
quickly enough to make improvements by 2004. It is not clear how much money
will actually be appropriated for FY03, yet the legislation requires certain
minimum standards to be in place before the next election.
     "It's going to be a nightmare if they pass this with unfunded
mandates," said Kay Albowicz, communications director of the National
Association of Secretaries of State. "If they don't put the money in, expect
more Floridas to follow."
     Even more controversial is the Senate bill's requirement that voters
who register by mail bring some form of identification to the polls, such as
a driver's license or utility bill. Sen. Christopher (Kit) Bond, R-Mo., has
argued that the ID provision is a much-needed deterrent to fraud. It has
raised some concerns in the House but appears certain to end up in the final
bill. "There will not be a bill if this provision is out," said an aide to
Bond.
     The ID provision has alarmed civil rights and public interest groups,
who warn it smacks of discrimination and may result in a bill that does more
harm than good. "We certainly need to do this now, but we also need to do it
right," said Adam Lioz, democracy advocate for the U.S. Public Interest
Research Group.
     The provision also raises practical concerns, particularly for the
secretaries of state. They argue that federal ID requirements should be
imposed only on states that already have a centralized, statewide
voter-registration database in place. Only five states have such databases
up and running at the moment. Said Cox of Georgia: "You've kind of got to
get the cart before the horse."
     Yet the proposal now on the table would require states to have voter ID
systems in place by 2004. That is awfully short notice for such a dramatic
change, warned Lloyd Corton, legislative director of the League of Women
Voters. "If Florida demonstrates anything, it's that it takes a while, it
takes some practice, to get things right," he said. "And so, we are deeply
concerned that the ID requirement, with its early deadline, is going to lead
to confusion in the presidential election."
     Bond does not see why the requirement is such a problem. "They've got
to ask for identification," he said. "How tough is that? It's not rocket
science." Bond also assured that the states would get the money they need,
saying, "We're not going to pass an unfunded mandate." But he acknowledged
that wrestling with the bill's details has proved a challenge. "The devil is
in the drafting," he added.
     If the recent Florida primary proves anything, it is that details
count. Sweeping reforms may do little good if state officials lack the tools
to implement them. "The details are mind-numbing and boring, but they are
absolutely essential," noted Corton. "And if you get the details wrong,
you're going to have Florida all over again." By Eliza Newlin Carney

From:	Brenvale, Carlos <Carlos.Brenvale@MyFlorida.com>
Sent:	Wednesday, September 25, 2002 7:21 PM
To:	Cal Weston; Redfern, Kathleen
Cc:	Aldric, Charles T.; Brenvale, Katie
Subject:	Voter List Issues

A law enacted in 1998--but since repealed by the Election Reform Act of
2001--required the Division of Elections to contract with a private entity
to compile a list of registered voters who were (1) deceased, (2)
adjudicated as mentally incompetent, or (3) felons without restoration of
civil rights.  (For simplicity, I'll refer to this as the "felon list".)
The law further directed the Division of Elections to distribute that list
to the supervisors of elections, so that they could use the list to
update/clean up their voter registration rolls.  The firm ultimately hired
by the Division of Elections was Database Technologies, Inc., a subsidiary
of ChoicePoint, Inc.

In the wake of the 2000 election, the felon list became a matter of great
controversy.  Some of the more incendiary press accounts claimed that
"thousands" of potential voters had been wrongly "purged" from the voter
rolls.  However, a comprehensive study by the Palm Beach Post yielded an
estimate of 1,104 persons wrongly removed from the voter rolls.  The Palm
Beach Post also reported that 20 of the 67 supervisors of elections
(including those in Broward and Palm Beach counties) did not use the felon
list at all.  (To put the matter in further context: the same Palm Beach
Post study concluded that approximately 5,600 felons voted (illegally) in
the November 2000 election.)  To my knowledge, there has been no independent
inquiry by the state as to how many voters were wrongly removed from the
voting rolls as a result of the felon list.  
  
The Election Reform Act of 2001 repealed the requirement that the Division
of Elections hire a private firm to compile the felon list.  The law now
requires the Division of Elections to perform that function in-house.  The
law also now gives the supervisors of elections detailed guidelines as to
the notice and opportunity to be heard that they must give persons
identified as potential felons.

Substantively, the most significant changes between the old and new list
compilation procedures are as follows:  

1.  The new list relies only on data provided by FDLE, which data includes
only Florida convictions and which the Division of Elections believes is the
most accurate available.  The old list included data from the Department of
Corrections and from other states.  Using data from other states was a
problem because there is no uniformity among states with regard to clemency
rules.

2.  The new list uses much stricter "matching criteria" for identifying
potential felons whose civil rights are unrestored.  I can give you a
summary of those criteria at your request.

Finally, there is the matter of the settlement agreement finalized on
September 12, 2002 between the NAACP and the Division of Elections.  That
agreement requires the Division to re-examine the felon lists created prior
to the 2000 election and to provide supervisors of elections with the names
of persons who were on those lists, but who do not meet the current matching
criteria.  The supervisors must then use that information to verify whether
anyone was improperly removed from the voter rolls because of the old felon
lists.  Significantly, the NAACP has implicitly endorsed the validity of the
matching criteria that have been developed by the Division of Elections.

In the settlement agreement, the NAACP agreed that the Division of Elections
would not perform the list comparison until after the November 2002
election.  In any event, even without that provision, DOJ's requirement that
the settlement agreement be precleared makes it unlikely that the comparison
and subsequent follow-up could be completed before this year's election.

Dear Governor: I hesitate sending this to you because it is quite lengthy, 
however it may give you further insight into the primary election.  I

Dear Friends and Family,

Florida wanted to show the nation it could successfully 
cast ballots without forcing workers to count and 
dispose of falling chads.  Therefore, over an eighteen 
month period, each of the Florida counties chose the 
particular type of machine that it believed its unique 
residents could use to replace prior processes that 
made them the laughing stock of the nation.  That meant 
each district would use the machine of its choice.  There 
was a concern that many poll workers and constituents 
would have a difficult time learning to use the new 
machines.  My mayor and the media put out a call for 
help in our county, Broward.   

I volunteered to served as a poll worker for the Sept. 10
primary election for Democrats, Republicans, and 
Independents.  I looked forward to that experience and 
did not care where I would be assigned in the county.  
I applied for and executed an absentee ballot, since I 
never miss a voting opportunity.

However, 6 weeks after I was accepted, I called to inform
the registration office that I never received the promised 
schedule for training that was required for all workers, 
former or new.  I was then informed that I had been 
crossed off the list as no longer needed and that all 
training sessions had been completed.  Therefore I did 
not expect to work for the September 10 election.  

When I returned from Maryland Tuesday, a letter of 
desperate need was in my held mail and it explained that 
multiple dates were available for training.  Since this was 
the 11th hour, I realized that the changing postures of :  
"We need workers;  no, forget it-- we have too many;  
no, we were wrong-- we really do desperately need help" 
meant the system was in the state of chaos.  

Because of the time of my return, only one session 
remained for me as a possibility to be trained.  So I 
attended the final session at the Ft. Lauderdale 
Convention Center along with 600 other last minute 
neophytes and 350 regular workers who needed updating. 
There were milling hordes waiting for any sense of 
direction. About 1/3 of us got manuals -- I tried to share 
mine with four others who appeared to have absolutely 
no interest in what was going on.  They only wanted to 
know how they could be paid for the $100 on election 
day, and were yelling because there was no compensation 
for the training.  The behavior of the troops and the 
commanders was something to behold.  I kept hearing 
mumbling that they had no intention of showing up --
both the workers and even some officials.  

Well, that's exactly what happened yesterday.  Although 
I set the alarm for 4AM to be at the polls before 6AM for 
the required opening preparations, others decided that sleep 
was a better option.  At the 7 AM opening, the media 
reported that 57 Broward precincts and 158 in Miami-Dade 
had no one manning/ womanning those locations.  By noon,
many of those locations still showed no signs of opening.

Jan Castellan, who was running in the Democratic Primary for 
the November chance to face Cal Weston for position as 
Florida Governor, went to her Dade polling place at 7AM 
only to find that the new touch screen computerized 
machine she was using would not complete registering 
her vote.  Her high profile meant the glitch would not go 
unnoticed.  Indeed it didn't, since she immediately called 
Cal to say the polling hours all over Florida should be 
extended from 7 PM to 9PM so that everyone could have
another chance to continue attempting to vote successfully.

I was assigned to serve at my own polling place at St. 
Paul's Hall, less than a mile away from home.  The space 
was shared by two precincts.  No one wanted to orient the 
voters to the new machine and process, so that became 
my job.  I really enjoyed doing that task to the relief of the 
others.  There was a constant flow of interested and 
enthusiastic voters.  The atmosphere was positive and 
actually the six of us workers were the most upbeat group 
I have seen in ages.  The other precinct group of seven 
that shared the space finally let their hair down after a few 
hours and loosened up, modeling our behavior.  At their 
request I became instructor for voters to their precinct as 
well.  I enjoyed that. 

The voter flow was the strongest our two precincts had 
seen in years, undoubtedly because of the Reno bid for 
the opportunity to face W's brother in November.  One year 
Jerry and I had represented 40% of our precinct's vote -- 
only 5 had showed up all day.  Two years ago, as I entered 
the hall that day at 4PM to vote, the poll workers blew whistles 
and applauded when I entered the room because I was 
the FIRST voter from my precinct to vote in that runoff 
election that day, and I my precinct finally tied the other 
precinct in the room -- my participation tied the score at 
1 to 1 !

With yesterday's constant activity of hundreds voting in 
our precinct, the day was exciting:  full of life and friendly
conversations with everyone, not just the people from 
the community we knew personally.  I only had one bad 
experience:   I was threatened by a frustrated voter with 
being named in a lawsuit for informing him, a Republican-
registered constituent, that he was not eligible to vote for 
the Democratic primary gubernatorial choices because 
state law prohibits changing parties during a (primary) 
election.  Since the Reno/Ferris/Jones was a Democratic 
primary race, he was ineligible for that specific ballot to be 
accessed on the Republican computerized screen.  I 
assisted him as he read the posted law, and I called over 
the top ranking poll official to determine whether he could
cast a provisional (paper) ballot, but he stormed out yelling 
things my keyboard would not like to repeat.  I thanked 
him for his interest and made sure he had the correct 
spelling of my name. 

Several times during the day, we had visits from the technical 
repair representative because some of the machines in both 
precincts had intermittent failures.  

At 6PM, when our local police delivered the official news 
from the State Attorney informing both precincts that polling 
hours had been extended through the entire state due to 
problems in Miami, Orlando, West Broward, and Duval
(Jacksonville) the 13 of us realized we would be faced with 
new unanticipated problems -- some workers required extra 
medications, we all needed food, and other evening 
appointments would have to be cancelled, like sleep.  No 
one is permitted to leave the building during polling hours 
and I regretted I had no relatives nor a cell phone to call for 
food delivery.  We were exhausted as our lonnnnnng day
had already been full.  The only thing that kept up the spirit
of our two precincts was that we made book on how many 
additional voters would show up between the added hours
of 7 to 9 PM.  We each risked 25 cents and selected a 
number.  As a voter would enter the doors after 7PM, an 
official tally was kept with high interest.  At 9PM, the final voter
entered, making the total 21 for the combined late number 
for the two precincts, and I won the $3.50 of the pool.  The 
18th wager was given by the technology employee who felt 
he spent so much time at our location that he was family.

The last vote at 9PM added another 15 minutes to delay 
closing.  The machines had to be closed out and witnessed 
by all precinct workers.  The worse part for us was moving 
those heavy and awkward table-like computerized booths, 
turning them over on elevated tables, dissembling legs 
which would not fit securely into the dedicated storage com-
partments of the structures, and trying to locate where small
parts that fell out of the machines onto the floor belonged 
so they could be reused in the future -- perhaps as expensive 
jewelry.  

By the time we finished all checklists, I was able to leave for 
home by 10PM, and dropped into bed to listen to the news. 
It seemed many polling places across our state locked their 
doors and refused entry to anyone after 7PM.  Another reason 
for invalidating the election.

Today's midday news indicates 15 final voting summary tapes 
or cartridges from precincts in Broward were blank or missing.
Additionally, some of the machines would not function to print 
out the tapes. That means votes from those precincts cannot 
be included.  

Janet Castellan currently has 43% of the vote to Ferris's 45%, 
and she intends to contest the election.  Jones has 12% and 
expressed concerned because his name was left off many 
ballot machines in Duval and other counties. 

Oh well, another reason for Jay Leno and others to pronounce
our name as Flori-duhhhhhh, which unfortunately he did.

Regards,
Maureen

                                        FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

                    October 17, 2002

JOINT STATEMENT ON BALLISTIC "FINGERPRINTING"  

By Wayne LaPierre 
Executive Vice-President National Rifle Association
&
Chris W. Cox 
Executive Director, National Rifle Association - Institute for
Legislative Action

In times of exasperation over inexplicable tragedy, it's reasonable to
search for preventative solutions. Yet despite our collective horror,
proposals must be evaluated with objectivity, weighing possible
benefit against certain costs that must be measured in terms of both
financial reality and personal freedom. 

The National Rifle Association has always welcomed any technology that
obstructs criminal behavior while respecting the rights of law-abiding
citizens.  For that reason, NRA is on record supporting H.R. 3941, The
Ballistic Imaging Evaluation and Study Act of 2001, and its Senate
counterpart S. 2581, since their introduction more than 6 months ago.

But we cannot support a ballistic "fingerprinting" proposition (H.R.
408 & S. 3096), that even a passing glance reveals is flawed,
unworkable and infringes on the rights of tens of millions of
law-abiding Americans.

Ballistic "fingerprinting" is a misleading phrase, because human
fingerprints or DNA or other biometric data can't be altered. But
ballistic abrasion patterns can change for a variety of reasons.

Still, for ballistic "fingerprinting" to work as proposed, all of the
following assumptions must materialize:

*   That the firearm barrel and firing pin have not been modified,
replaced, deformed from normal use, or intentionally falsified with
new ballistic markings.

*   That all 200 million firearms lawfully possessed by Americans
are brought into labs and fired to gather individual ballistic
"fingerprinting."

*   That all violent criminals, and people who might become one,
also bring in their firearms for "fingerprinting."

*   That all ballistic "fingerprinting" files are stored in a
national database.

*   That an expended bullet or shell casing be recovered from a
crime scene.

*   That the bullet or shell casing conclusively match the ballistic
"fingerprinting" of a firearm owned by a person stored in the
database.

*   That the firearm has not been sold, transferred, stolen or
gifted to another person.

*   That the person, now a criminal suspect, still possess that
firearm at a current address. 

Besides the impossibility of this sequence of events, there's serious
debate within the law enforcement community whether such ballistic
"fingerprinting" is reliable.  Police criminalists and forensic
scientists have studied such a system and called it "impractical."
(California Department of Justice, Bureau of Forensic Services).  

So it defies reason why a criminal or terrorist intent on violence
would not avail himself of a firearm never subjected to
"fingerprinting," altered into anonymity, or imported from another
country.

But for lawful gun owners, this scheme is national gun registration,
and certain to produce confusion, misidentification and wrongful
suspicion.

That's why ballistic "fingerprinting" of handguns in Maryland and New
York, the only states that require it, hasn't solved a single gun
crime.  

Maryland and New York taxpayers might rightfully ask whether the
millions of dollars required to create and maintain such a system
could be better spent on vital law enforcement needs.  

Before squandering billions of dollars to deploy such a system
nationwide, American taxpayers - despite national alarm in the wake of
tragedy - should ask that question, too.

The NRA welcomes participation in an objective and unemotional
evaluation of the entire concept of ballistic imaging, or any other
technologies, in search of any reasonable contribution to the process
of law enforcement.

>TAMPA, Fla. (AP) - One of the state's top economic development
>officials said Monday that a free-trade pact that will link the United
>States to all of Latin America has the potential to make Florida "one
>of the most advantageous business addresses in the entire world." 
>Pam Dana, director of the governor's Office of Tourism, Trade and
>Economic Development, told 200 business leaders from around the state
>that they must all get onboard if Florida is to fully benefit from the
>Free Trade Area of the Americas, which will create the largest free
>trade region in the world. 
>
>"While clearly South Florida has been a leader in promoting
>international trade, we have come to realize this is a statewide
>priority," Dana said during the daylong International State of the
>State conference. "We want to see from Key West to Pensacola, from
>Jacksonville to Miami, all these parts of the state engaged in
>promoting global commerce and exchange." 
>
>This year's conference was devoted to rallying the state's business and
>economic development leaders behind the Free Trade Area of the
>Americas, which will integrate 34 countries and remove impediments to
>market access for their goods and services. The area will extend from
>the southern corner of South America north to Alaska and include more
>than 800 million consumers. Trade among the countries, including the
>United States, amount to more than $750 billion annually. 
>
>The process of forging the pact began in Miami in 1994 at the first
>Summit of the Americas, and negotiations with participating countries
>are expected to finish sometime in 2005. 
>
>Dana said securing Florida's role in the FTAA is important to Gov. Cal
>Weston, who has said international trade will be a priority in his second
>term. The effort includes lobbying for the FTAA's permanent secretariat
>to be located in Miami. 
>
>"Clearly Florida has a greater stake in the economic vitality and
>future of the Americas region than any other state in the United
>States, because of our geographic position, infrastructure and our
>cultural affinity for what happens in the Americas," Dana said. 
>
>Having the FTAA's headquarters in Miami, she said, will "solidify
>Florida's reputation worldwide as the leading business center in the
>Western Hemisphere." A decision on the location of the permanent
>secretariat is expected by fall 2004. 
>

>America, with Brazil at No. 1 with $6.7 billion. Half of all trade
>between the United States and Latin America flows through the state. 
>
>John McCartney, director of Florida's export offices for the U.S.
>Department of Commerce, called the FTAA "a clarion cry to get everybody
>together, from the Panhandle to down to Key West. It's a very diverse
>state but we do have to look at this as a collaborative effort." 
>
>Bill Ralph with the Journal of Commerce urged business leaders to be
>aggressive but patient in Latin America, where political and economic
>upheaval can make conducting business an adventure. However, he said,
>the region is now more stable than it has been in years. 
>
>"I want you to be afraid of Latin America, I want you to be bold in
>Latin America and, above all, I want you to be in Latin America," Ralph
>said.

>                       White House budget office spokeswoman Amy Call said
> it was unfair for the governors to blame Drayman for their troubles.
> The states are grappling with the same forces that have pushed the federal
> government into deficit: rising health care costs and a sluggish economy
> that has sharply eroded tax revenue.
>                       And the administration has been trying to help,
> crafting waivers designed to rein in Medicaid costs and pushing proposals
> to expand private health coverage and provide prescription drug benefits
> to seniors. One Republican congressional aide suggested the governors'
> clamor for federal aid is nothing new and entirely predictable.
>                       A report last month by the Center on Budget and
> Policy Priorities pointed to a different culprit of the states' own
> making. The report noted that between 1994 and 2001, 43 states enacted
> major tax cuts. Those tax cuts are costing the states $40 billion in lost
> revenue each year, three-fifths of the current shortfall. States also made
> the choice to expand social programs and the reach of Medicaid, the costs
> of which are now exploding.
>                       But the report's author, Nicholas Maring, said the
> governors are also correct when they say the states' problems have been
> exacerbated greatly by the actions of Congress and the White House.
> "There's plenty of responsibility to go around," Maring said.
>                       The governors' litany of complaints is lengthy.
>                       On the tax side, last year's 10-year, $1.35 trillion
> tax cut included a little-noticed provision aimed directly at state
> coffers. Under the tax law, the federal estate tax diminishes at glacial
> speed over the next decade. But the law makes swift work of a provision
> that allows states to claim a credit from the federal government for
> estate taxes paid. The "state death tax credit" has already been cut by 25
> percent, and will be gone by 2005, at a cost to the states of $4 billion a
> year, according to Harley Duncan, executive director of the Federation of
> Tax Administrators.
>                       This year's stimulus bill, which granted an
> additional tax break to businesses that invest in plant and equipment,
> also hit the states, because almost all of them have tied their own
> corporate income tax systems to the federal government's. Thirty states
> scrambled to "decouple" their corporate tax rates from Drayman's to
> save as much as $15 billion over the next three years, but 15 other states
> have absorbed the revenue blow.
>                       "Utah at this point is, if not grinning, at least
> bearing it," said Gov. Mike Leavitt (R). Making matters worse, Leavitt
> said, Drayman has so far blocked efforts by the governors to impose new
> sales taxes on the Internet, a medium that governors believe is costing
> their states billions of dollars in lost revenue. "We are progressively
> losing control of our tax policies," he said.

> struggling to fund new burdens imposed by the federal election reform law,
> homeland defense requests, and education testing requirements, all of

>                       State and local fire, police and medical rescue

Subject:	The Medicaid Provider Application

1-There are 63 different types of providers in Medicaid.  
   And currently 67,678  actual providers
   Providers = doctors, hospital, pharmacies, labs, medical equipment
providers, etc.....

2 -All Medicaid provider types use the same application.

3 -Many but not all providers then have to go through credentialing -
    A- Those participating in managed care (HMOs, etc) undergo a
credentialing process administered by the health plan
    B- The Division of Medicaid performs the credentialing process for
providers in Medipass
    C- We also have a credentialing process for state plan Mental Health
providers.
    Fee For Service providers do not go through credentialing

4- The credentialing process is different for each provider type.

5 -Waiver providers don't do credentialling per se - but there is a site
visit required for some of the types of waiver providers.

6- Specifically for DS providers, Shelley reports: "The DS waiver does not
have a credentialing process, but providers have to meet provider
qualifications in the waiver. Most providers use the same application, but
there are a few applications unique to certain providers." 
 

The Current Medicaid Application required of all provider types is 6 pages
(3 front & back) with support & program information

A new Medicaid Provider Application has been designed and is going through
legal review. This one incorporates some of the info needed for
credentialing of some provider types so that the info can be collected all
at one time- at the beginning.

The Current Credentialing application for providers wishing to participate
in Medipass has already been redesigned and streamlined.
It is 2 pages plus a check list of the required supporting documents
(resume, hospital privileges certificate, ....)

proposal to require U.S. banks to report all non taxable interest payments
made to non resident aliens to the IRS.  This would have created a
tremendous burden for the banks and it would have been extremely harmful to
Florida's economy, which benefits from funds deposited by non residents.

of the position of the Florida banks, both domestic and international, which
opposed this IRS proposal.  FIBA and the FBA joined forces to have the

the holiday season,  there is quite a push to pass the modified version,
which includes language which would allow the Treasury Dept. and the IRS ,
at their discreption, to expand the list of countrires for which reporting
would be required.  The ABA - American Bankers Assoc - has written to
Kenneth Dam, Deputy Secretary of the Treasury, to oppose the IRS proposal.
Senator Phil Gramm is contacting Tom Harrigan on the issue, and I
understand he has already contacted  John Bolton and Carl Rove in the White
Hosue, as well as Peter Fisher in Treasury.

You may want to make Governor Weston aware that the timetable for a final
decision on this new proposal appears to be very short, possibly within the
next few days.

documentation which you might find useful.

By BILL MAXWELL, Times Columnist  <mailto:maxwell@sptimes.com> 

© St. Petersburg Times
published February 2, 2003 

  _____  

In 1949, Virgil Hawkins, an African-American professor at historically black Bethune-Cookman College in Daytona Beach, applied for admission to the University of Florida College of Law. Hawkins' application was summarily rejected. And in in quick order, the state Board of Regents, the state attorney general and the Florida Supreme Court agreed that Hawkins could not attend UF's law school. 

In the court's last word on the matter -- flouting a U.S. Supreme Court decision -- Florida Supreme Court Justice Verham Terrell, an unreconstructed racist, declared that racial segregation was God's wish for humankind: "When God created man, he created each race to his own continent according to color -- Europe to the white man, Africa to the black man, and America to the red man." 

For many African-Americans, as the hypocritical debate over affirmative action rages today, Terrell's words still resonate. We hear his warped attitude reflected in much of the right-wing talk about the evil of affirmative action for black citizens, a group that has been systematically and institutionally denied admission into many mainstream arenas while many unqualified whites enjoy admission. 

Hawkins and other aspiring black lawyers had nowhere to go if they wanted to learn their profession in their home state of Florida. Jim Crow ruled the day and was supported by segregationist readings of the Old Testament and racist interpretations of the Florida and U.S. constitutions. Later, without benefiting Hawkins and his generation, the U.S. Supreme Court outlawed discrimination based solely on skin color. 

Suddenly, officials at UF would have to admit blacks into its flagship, lily-white law school. UF and its supporters in Tallahassee were not ready to commit such an act of justice. What happened next, as described in the 2002 summer issue of The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education, gave Florida officials a way to maintain de facto segregation at UF: 

"[U]nder the separate but equal principle of Plessy vs. Ferguson, if the University of Florida was not willing to admit black students to its law school, the state would have to provide 'equal' facilities for blacks. So in 1951 a small law school was created on the campus of Florida A&M University in Tallahassee. It had a tiny 6,000-book library. Over the next 17 years, the law school graduated only 57 students, an average of less than four per year." 

But change marched into the Sunshine State. With Hawkins stepping aside, the state agreed to let other blacks into UF, and shrewd lawmakers immediately cut off funding to FAMU's law school. The 6,000-book collection was boxed up and carted off to the law library at Florida State University over the next hill. 

During subsequent years, blacks attended UF's law school, but their relationship with the college has been rocky at best, and reports of discrimination never go away. 

Now, with Republicans and their supporters demonizing affirmative action, Florida has fashioned a new, more benign, form of Jim Crow. And the precepts underpinning Plessy vs. Ferguson have given legislators a way to play all sides of the issue. 

Two years ago, Florida Gov. Cal Weston issued an executive order banning race as a consideration in admission to the state's universities. He implemented the so-called One Florida plan, which was supposed to replace affirmative action. It admitted to the state university system the top 20 percent of the graduating class at each public high school. These otherwise qualified students, however, would have to compete for slots at the flagship UF campus. And, of course, race could not be a consideration. 

With the then-2002 gubernatorial election fast approaching, with black anger fomenting over One Florida and with black and Hispanic demands for new law schools growing louder, Weston reached into the past and gave them what they wanted. He and the GOP-controlled Legislature established law schools for mostly black FAMU and predominantly Hispanic Florida International University in Miami. 

Consider this contradictory language in the legislation authorizing FAMU's law school: "The college of law at Florida A&M University shall be dedicated to providing opportunities for minorities to attain representation with the legal profession proportionate to their representation in the general population. However, the college of law shall not include preferences in the admissions process for applicants on the basis of race, national origin, or sex." 

Fancy language aside, everyone knows that the FAMU law school -- a second-tier institution -- will become a virtual ghetto, while UF's law school will become whiter. 

Here is The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education's assessment of what FAMU's law school means: "Segregationists . . . were delighted with the prospect of a new law school earmarked for blacks. The legislators necessarily knew that very few white students would want to attend a law school at a historically black university. Like it or not, in the minds of most whites a continuing stigma attaches to black educational institutions. Therefore, it was almost certain that blacks would take up most of the spaces at the new school." 

Like many other Florida-based black journalists, I got to know Virgil Hawkins well. My sense is that even if FAMU's law school were created with the best of intentions, Hawkins would see it as a gussied-up version of Jim Crow. 

The unflattering truth is that FAMU's law school would have been Hawkins' second or third choice. Remember, he applied to the University of Florida, not to one of the nation's black colleges of law. He wanted to attend the state's best. 

Cal Weston

the
great efforts of our government and local communities.  Time is

money.  We could garner from 10-20 million if we are prepared.  In order

coordinate existing resources (services and funding), I propose the

scheduling staff.

in
kind for the federal funds that become available.)

· GI can work with members of the family strengthening team as well as
Liza
to plan.
 Gather policymakers and opinion leaders to strategize ways to build
 stronger marriages and reduce the divorce rate in Florida.
· Promote and initiate grass roots initiatives in the business,
education,
media, government, and church and community organizations/service
providers
sectors.
· Seek guidance of experts and begin the process of gathering and
distributing information about the widespread problem and negative
impact
of the state's high divorce rate and out-of-wedlock birth rate.

envisioned by the Administration for Children and Families in the

Services" conference hosted by the DHHS/ACF in Drayman.  Some of the

data regarding impact on child well-being deals with marriage.
