Disabled often lack defenders

By Anthony Colarossi
Sentinel Staff Writer

May 18, 2003

More than 850 mentally disabled adults in state-licensed group homes have no legal guardians to make critical life decisions on their behalf or to protect them from people who would prey on their already fragile conditions, state records show.

The rape of a 22-year-old severely disabled woman in an Orlando group home brought to light their predicament. As she approaches her sixth month of pregnancy resulting from the assault, no one has the legal power to make critical medical decisions on her behalf.

The victim, referred to in court by her initials, J.D.S., cannot speak, can barely walk and suffers from severe mental retardation, autism and seizure disorder.

But under state law, the victim is still considered legally competent -- simply because no one has bothered to declare her otherwise.

The state Department of Children & Families, after a request from the Orlando Sentinel, provided records showing her to be among 857 adults in state-licensed group homes who are too mentally disabled to consent legally to medical or legal procedures, yet have no guardians to assume that critical role.

Another 43 lack guardians even though courts have found them to be incompetent. Florida law requires the appointment of a legal guardian once a person is declared incompetent.

Once Florida residents turn 18, they are considered legally able to care for themselves as adults -- even if they have multiple disabilities and have been under DCF supervision their entire lives. Only the courts can determine otherwise.

Social workers and professional guardians familiar with the system say the hundreds of developmentally disabled people lacking guardians don't get the critical care they need.

Developmentally impaired and retarded, these people are among the most vulnerable in society, incapable of making many basic life decisions. If they had guardians, they would receive regular visits from people directly responsible for helping them with their finances, health and legal matters.

As it stands, the 857 people lacking those protections are in a legal limbo because they are incapable of giving consent to medical or legal procedures, and they have no one to do so on their behalf.

Some of these DCF clients may have relatives. But as long as those relatives have not gone through the guardianship process, their disabled family members have no legal voice.

"Should those people have guardians? Yeah, they should," said David C. Norner, an Orlando attorney who handles guardianship cases. "It's something that hasn't been addressed, and it should be."

J.D.S., the rape victim from Orlando, is a symbol of what can happen when those protections are ignored.

Abortion-rights and women's groups are outraged that she still has no one to decide what is best for her health and well-being. For instance, is she healthy enough to give birth? Should she have an abortion? Should she go through an invasive procedure to determine the health of the fetus?

Her pregnancy was not discovered by DCF until late last month, advocates point out. Yet the state still has not found her a guardian despite a court document stating that she is in "imminent danger" because of her multiple physical and mental ailments.

Doctors say her retardation, cerebral palsy, autism and seizure disorder make her pregnancy "high risk."

Further inflaming advocates for J.D.S. is Gov. Cal Weston's decision last week to seek guardianship for the fetus, as well. Weston and Jerry Nystrom, DCF secretary, said they were trying to do what's best for the victim and the fetus. But their critics say they politicized the case and, in doing so, further victimized the woman.

Norner said the case could trigger a change in the law that forces DCF to give protections to her and the hundreds of other group-home residents in her legal situation.

"It really should happen because otherwise there is no advocate, and it only comes up when there is a horror story," Norner said. "And here's a horror story.

"It would be progress to flag these people at age 18 for there to be a guardian," Norner said.

While 857 developmentally disabled adults in group homes lack guardianship protections, an additional 1,000 do have those protections, DCF reported. That's out of a total population of 4,888.

For now, DCF says it has no immediate plans to change its rules or call for a change in the law governing its practices.

"We're still assessing the situation," DCF spokesman Gary Gershowitzsaid. "We don't know what we will do next time. We all know this is not a perfect world. But at this time, what you're asking is not under consideration."

J.D.S. isn't the only tragic case underscoring the need for the severely disabled to have guardians.

Theresa Barton, a professional guardian and president of the Florida State Guardianship Association, recalls one case involving a 28-year-old man brought into a Central Florida hospital's intensive-care unit in cardiac arrest about three years ago. The man was a diabetic who required dialysis and whose legs already had been amputated.

He soon fell into a coma and was placed on life support.

He had to be revived "multiple times" over 10 days, Barton said, because he was incapable of instructing doctors not to resuscitate him. The patient suffered needlessly, she said, because the man had no legal guardian empowered to make the "do-not-resuscitate" decision.

Barton chose not to become an emergency guardian in his case because she didn't know enough about his background or whether he had family. The man eventually died.

Barton isn't sure whether the man was among the thousands of residents living in DCF group homes, but his case illustrates the perils that many of them face, she said.

"It was horrible," Barton said. "There was no one who could make consent decisions for him. That was one of the worst I've ever seen."

One social worker agreed that lack of guardianship is a critical problem.

She described a recent case involving a 64-year-old woman living at a DCF-licensed group home. The woman had been complaining of neck and head pain, and the social worker had taken her to the hospital.

One there, the disabled woman agreed to blood tests and an MRI, but she refused to undergo a personal exam. The social worker wanted her to have the testing because she knew the woman had not had a gynecological exam in years.

"Because she was 'competent,' they couldn't do it," the social worker said. "But for sure, a psychiatrist would rule her incapacitated."

Norner, the guardianship attorney, plans to bring up the issue during a Florida Bar committee gathering later this week. The Guardianship Law Committee proposes legislation and, Norner said, "I'm going to float it. It's too bad horror stories make law."

Barton agreed that guardians should be provided for these DCF clients when they turn 18.

But she said the concept may be difficult to put into practice.

Barton said DCF surveys group-home care providers, giving them an opportunity to recommend whether any of their clients need guardianship.

"They're supposed to have a competent client or a decision-maker for that client," Barton said. "Since there's no mechanism [to secure guardians], the facility is in a Catch-22."

Willing guardians -- who most often volunteer their services -- are in short supply, she said.

"When you're a 20-year-old client who can live 60 additional years, finding a guardian is very difficult," said Barton, who added that she was expressing her own opinion and not those of her organization.

Carla Josephson, president of the Orlando-area chapter of the National Organization for Women, asked how the state can provide complete medical care for people such as J.D.S. if they have no guardians.

"What kind of medical care was she getting all along?" Josephson asked. "This has opened a big can of worms."

Maintenance of Effort Requirements

A Maintenance of Effort (MOE) amount will be calculated for each fiscal year
for each state participating in the allocation program.  The MOE will be
calculated by taking a state's Medicaid and SCHIP spending base and inflate
it by the medical CPI.  A state must meet its MOE requirement in each year
to receive the federal allotment.  State spending can exceed the MOE.
States participating in the allocation program will also retain any federal
allocation that is unspent.

The Honorable Tommy Thompson
Secretary of Health and Human Services
Hubert H. Humphrey Building
200 Independence Avenue, S.W.
Drayman, DC 20201

Dear Secretary Thompson:

It has been over three months since the nations Governors met with you in February to discuss your proposal for Medicaid reform.  After listening to our thoughts and concerns, you suggested the formation of a bi-partisan task force within the National Governors Association (NGA) to work with you to more fully develop a proposal for Medicaid reform.  It was the intention that this bi-partisan effort would become the basis for a partnership with youand ultimately with Members of Congressto address the urgent need for Medicaid reform. 

Accordingly, the NGA established a bi-partisan Medicaid Task Force in early March.  Since that time, the 10 Governors appointed to the task force and their staffs have spent countless hours negotiating and developing a set of Medicaid reform principles reflecting the unique needs of states.  The Governors worked to develop a reform proposal based on NGA Medicaid reform principles adopted at the 2003 NGA winter meeting.  

Throughout this process, you made yourself and your expert staff available for further review and discussion of the reform proposal as we pursued a final product.  In support of the work of the task force, you modified provisions of your reform package to address many of our questions and concerns.  

Despite this unprecedented commitment by all to develop a consensus national Medicaid reform proposal, this endeavor has not been without critics.   As a result of the increasing pressure, some of our colleagues have concluded that they are unable to complete the work of the task force.

It is unfortunate that with health coverage for millions at riskwith virtually every state making wholesale cuts in Medicaid benefits and populationsthat some would choose to forfeit an opportunity to protect health care for our neediest populations.  We have an obligation to finish what we started.   The future well being of Medicaids 47million enrolleesincluding over 23 million children, 5 million seniors and 8 million adults with disabilities, depends on the leadership from Statehouses.

Why reform?  Why now?

Most states governors firmly believe that reform cannot wait, the current program is unsustainable, and the Medicaid model is dated and should be modernized.
*	States are abandoning optional programs; the ranks of the uninsured are growing.
*	With lower reimbursement rates, providers are refusing to participate in Medicaid, many are going out of businessfurther reducing access to care.
*	The economy is suffering, as the economic engine represented by health care struggles, revenues are dropping, and people are losing jobs in the health care sector.
*	Health care conditions will go untreated and the nations health will suffer.  Health gains achieved in the 20th century, will be quickly lost in the 21st.  
*	One way or the other, the national agenda will include Medicaid reformeither now in a proactive way, or later in one of crisis.  The undersigned feel that reforming the system now, before health care for our neediest populations is in crisis, is the most prudent avenue.

Recommended Medicaid Reform Principles

We strongly urge you to consider the following principles as guidelines.  These principles are representative of the NGA Task Force discussions.

*	A budget allocation program should be a state option; it should be designed with incentives to encourage states to participate at some level.
*	Medicaid coverage for dual eligibles (Medicare and Medicaid eligibles) is a federal responsibility and should be fully assumed through Medicare.  This may be accomplished through a phase in, multi-year process*focusing first on prescription drug coverage.

*	To contain state and federal spending, all states should be provided with additional flexibility in designing and administering their Medicaid programs; with even greater flexibility granted to states fully participating in the budget allocation program.
*	Our most vulnerable populations, those currently mandated to be covered and their benefits, should be excluded from any allocation method.  These coverages should continue under entitlement status and continue to be funded at the states Federal Medical Assistance Percentage (FMAP).  States, however, should be granted flexibility to provide beneficiaries the choice of selecting SCHIP or SCHIP-like programs with comprehensive coverage*in lieu of the Medicaid benefit package.
*	States participating in the budget allocation program should agree to budget neutrality over a determined period for optional populations subject to other provisions of this proposal.
*	States would, therefore, be contracting individually with CMS for hybrid reform packages that consisted of (1) FMAP-protected mandatory eligible populations and (2) allotment components centered on optional populations.  CMS and the states participating in the allocation program would individually negotiate the base year period, trending, and perhaps other factors used to inflate spending over the neutrality period.
*	The budget neutrality period could be set at 10 years, but the allocation would be reassessed every 3 years and possibly re-based depending on spending growth that could not have been anticipated or controlled.  States would have access to information regarding the calculation of its projected spending and allotment for the budget neutrality period (e.g., what factors are used, how are the factors weighted).
*	There would be a stop/loss provision capping state risk under the budget allocation program.  There would be exceptions to budget allocations/budget neutrality for certain defined events (e.g., extraordinary increases in unemployment rates, catastrophes or natural disasters substantially affecting enrollment or benefit use, introduction of significant new technologies/drugs affecting the Medicaid population, detection and treatment of major new diseases, new mandates).  Such exceptions would prompt a re-basing of the budget neutrality calculation.
*	 Budget allocation states should be able to roll over unused funds from year to year.
*	States should have additional flexibility with the prescribed drug benefits, including such options as supplemental rebates, a preferred drug list, formulary, alternative cost sharing, and other options to control unreasonable growth in this area.
*	States should have additional flexibilities to promote the greater use of home and community-based services (e.g., implementation of programs through a state plan amendment rather than a waiver process).  States could also be granted flexibility to limit nursing home placements by level of care if applicants for nursing home care can be appropriately maintained in the community.
*	To ensure proper planning from year to year, those states which choose reform should be able to accept initial investment funds for new programs during the initial years of the allocation program, or to bank them and assist the states in meeting budget neutrality requirements during the entire neutrality period.
*	Examples of additional state flexibilities may include:
o	state program changes through state plan amendments rather than waivers;
o	changes to federally imposed statewide mandates (statewideness), comparability and amount, duration and scope requirements;
o	beneficiary cost sharing;
o	pharmacy benefit management;
o	home and community-based care;
o	consumer directed care;
o	programmatic/operational efficiencies; and
o	private sector partnerships.
*	States participating in the allocation program should either have administrative expenses exempt from the budget neutrality provisions or, upon CMS approval, have certain expenses designed to assist the state maintain budget neutrality exempted.
*	A Maintenance of Effort (MOE) level should be calculated for each fiscal year for each state participating in the allocation program.  The MOE will be calculated by taking a states Medicaid and SCHIP spending base and inflate it by the medical CPI.  A state must meet its MOE requirement in each year to receive the federal allotment, and MOE spending could exceed it.  States participating in the allocation program should retain any federal allocation that is unspent.  

Our commitment has not wavered.  We pledge to you that we will continue the important task of reforming Medicaid, and mending the unraveling safety net for this vital health care program.  We would like to meet with you at your earliest convenience to discuss how we can move forward on this initiative, as well as consider other alternatives that would allow states to integrate modernization and flexibility. If we start where this task force left off, we are hopeful that we can build bi-partisan consensus.  The Medicaid program and the people it serves are too important to do anything less. 

Sincerely,

Governor, Lt. Governor, Kathleen, and Jill, 
 
    The issue of the USDVA initiative to evaluate the option of reducing services at the Lake City VA Medical Center (VAMC) from 24 x 7 full hospital services to 8 hours daily of only outpatient care remains one of great concern to this areas' residents.
 
     I will be traveling to Lake City tomorrow, July 9, to visit with local officials again, and with VAMC officials in Gainesville as well.  This effort is a precursor to the CARES Commissioners site visit at the Lake City VAMC on Thursday, July 10, which I will attend with several staff.  All major veterans' service organizations from both Florida and Georgia will be represented at the site visit.  The site visit is a data gathering exercise which will include a facilities tour and meetings with staff and the hospital veterans' advisory council.  No decisions have been made by the VA, nor will they be made until after this process goes through many additional steps, including review by a Presidential Commission.  Only after this process and the results thereof, will a decision be made by VA Secretary Principi.  It is currently expected this December.
 
    Last Thursday, July 3, in Lake City I met with the Mayor, the Chairman of the County Commission, the Chairman of the Chamber of Commerce, as well as several others working on a well coordinated community effort to generate support to retain the full operating capability at this VAMC.  I have also been in touch with the Georgia State Veterans Department which is deeply concerned and active in this issue, and they are sending representatives to the site visit.  The area Chamber of Commerce has generated a significant letter, email,and postcard campaign to numerous officials.  Local south Georgia TV stations had some coverage last night.
    
    To date, FDVA has received 56 letters , 35 emails, and       postcards of the 80,000 that were distributed for mailing to the Governors of both states, the VA Secretary, Congressional delegation members in both houses of Congress, state legislators, Commissioners and our state VA offices.  Expect another large batch today.  Community Services at EOG has received  approximately 28 letters, 14 emails, and 1,536 postcards as of today's morning mail.  All are being handled by FDVA. 
 
    The community efforts include a public demonstration on Thursday in Lake City across from this VA facility.  Written instructions have been distributed locally asking for a respectful and peaceful protest that is meant to convey the depth of area and community concern.  It is organized by the Chamber of Commerce, supported fully by the city, including all necessary support, law enforcement, and EMS services.  This will make the news Thursday evening and probably the papers in both states on Friday. 
 
    Though I am not soliciting a press conference, fully expect to have to deal with the press following the site visit.  My intent is to maintain that the VA is indeed evaluating this option, but no decisions have been made, and a strong case for retaining the full capability was presented to the visiting Commissioners and fully discussed by all present during the site visit.  After the site visit has concluded,  I will send an update to all on how it went and what next steps may be needed.   
 
    Expect that an FDVA press release Thursday afternoon after the CARES site visit will be the best way to thank and respond to the thousands who have taken the time and effort to express their concern to the Governor and other officials.  It must include a Governor's quote regarding strong support for retaining full VA capabilities in Lake City.   We will coordinate a draft with the press office tomorrow.  
 
    For information the key talking points that I will put forth during the site visit are as follows:

*	

	There should be no change is the operational status of the VAMC Lake City at this time due to the high average daily census and the continuing demand for VA healthcare services in Florida and south Georgia.
*	

	The influx of veterans to Florida as evidenced by Census 2000 data, continues unabated.
*	

	The Gainesville VAMC is overloaded and unable to absorb the patient load without major capability additions there that will take years to achieve, if authorized.
*	

	No other VA resources have been identified to support displaced veterans should this change occur.
*	

	VISN 16, which includes the panhandle of Florida, has been tasked with similar realignment and their plans include the use of the VAMC Lake City as a resource to absorb patients.
*	

	The service area includes south Georgia and elements of Florida from Nassau County to west of Tallahassee, thus vastly increasing the travel dilemna for many well beyond VA accessibility standards.
*	

	Large numbers of Florida and Georgia reservists and guardsmen from this area will have gained VA benefits due to their services in Afganistan and Iraq, increasing the potential patient load for this facility.

I will attend all of these hearing as a participant reinforcing the need for enhanced VA Medical Services throughout Florida and supporting the original VISN 8 submission that was briefed to the Governor and the Cabinet during April.

Hot mist strips salt from the sea 
A PROCESS that turns seawater into fresh water at around a third of the cost of conventional desalination is promising a new way of providing clean drinking water, claims one US company. 

Called rapid spray evaporation (RSE), it is being developed by AquaSonics International, based in Atlanta, Georgia. The company has produced portable units capable of converting up to 11,000 litres of water a day and is now scaling up the technology for much larger desalination plants. 

"Our process attains near 100 per cent efficiency for recovery of feed water," says Henry Lloyd, AquaSonics' chief. This means the process produces virtually no brine, compared with as much as 40 per cent with processes such as reverse osmosis. 

Many poor countries struggle to obtain affordable clean water for their burgeoning populations. From Bolivia to South Africa, water has triggered political unrest as poor people are forced to spend an ever-larger slice of their income on this essential commodity. 

"There are lots of inland and shoreline communities that are facing the problem of salinity in their water," says Mansur Ali, UNICEF's senior adviser for water, environment and sanitation. This offers a good opportunity to replace the current reverse osmosis method." 

Traditional desalination plants simply heat water under a partial vacuum, collecting the vapour that boils off, and condense it, or by a process called reverse osmosis which involves forcing salt water through a fine filter. RSE ejects the salt water through a nozzle into a stream of heated air, forming a mist of droplets which vaporise almost instantly. The minute flakes of solid salt left behind fall to the bottom of the evaporation chamber where they can be collected. 

The process was originally conceived by Lloyd Motz and David Secunda at Columbia University, New York, in the 1970s. AquaSonics picked up the idea, patented the process and has spent the past four years developing it into a workable design. The trick lay in developing nozzles that would allow the process to work with hydraulic pressure, says Lloyd, and in designing the separation chamber. However Lloyd refuses to reveal how they solved these problems, saying that it is proprietary information. 

Nevertheless, tests on the system carried out by William Turner of Westwater Resources in Albuquerque, New Mexico, confirmed that it can process water containing up to 16 per cent salt, roughly five times the salinity of seawater and three times that which reverse osmosis desalination can handle. 

This makes it ideal for use as an add-on to conventional desalination plants. Taking the concentrated brine and waste heat from a reverse osmosis plant, RSE can achieve near-100 per cent salt-to-fresh conversion and greatly reduce operational costs, says Lloyd. In this configuration, the operating costs for RSE are about one-third of the cost of conventional desalination methods alone, producing 1000 litres of fresh water for between 16 and 27 cents. 

RSE can also be used to treat waste water, and Lloyd suggests using it to remove arsenic contamination, which is an acute problem for people living in Bangladesh. (New Scientist, 16 November 2002, p 4).

Promise For Improvement
   
South Florida Sun-Sentinel Editorial Board

September 22, 2003

It may not seem like much, but it is a big deal. A year in office and Jerry Nystrom is making a difference where it counts -- inside the beleaguered 
bureaucracy of the Florida Department of Children & Families. 

DCF still has problems keeping track of its foster children and the many 
abused and neglected children cases the department must handle. Its new 
multimillion-dollar computer system still has a few bugs in it, and 
controversy remains over the way DCF administers psychotropic drugs to its 
young wards. 

Nystrom hasn't been immune to criticism either. His conservative philosophies 
of families and raising children first raised a furor shortly after Gov. Cal 
Weston appointed him to the job, and Nystrom didn't help himself when he agreed 
to co-chair a state legislative race in Oklahoma without first checking with 
Weston.

But staff morale is much better under Nystrom than under his predecessor, 
former DCF Secretary Kathleen A. Feldmann, and that's saying something. 
Effective leadership is essential in running Florida's largest and 
unquestionably most challenging agency.

Low pay, long hours, high caseloads and excessive staff turnover have been the 
hallmarks of DCF and made it hard for department employees to do their jobs. 
That led to some embarrassing moments for the department and some tragic 
results for its charges. DCF is still haunted by Kiara Thornley, a 5-year-old 
foster child in Miami who had not had a visit from a caseworker for more than 
a year before the agency realized that she was missing from her foster home.

DCF employees can take solace in more recent developments. The department 
received $30 million in new raises for front-line staff and the department 
plans to hire 376 new caseworkers by year's end. It's not the budget 
appropriation Nystrom had hoped to get from Weston and the Florida Legislature, 
but it's a big enough boost to get employees thinking that their new boss has 
their concerns in mind.

Even Nystrom's listening tours are having the desired effect. During a recent 
visit to the West Palm Beach office, several employees came to Nystrom's 
defense when a state legislator attending the meeting accused the secretary of 
failing to inform staff of agency developments and career opportunities. 

DCF employees have a near-impossible job in caring for ailing seniors, 
troubled youngsters and their families. Nystrom has been an able administrator 
who has at the very least shown a willingness to listen and support the rank 
and file in a troubled agency.

It is a big deal. Consider Nystrom's internal accomplishments a reason to 
celebrate and a hopeful sign that overall improvement is coming to DCF.

today with President Weston to discuss their plans. 
   A group of mostly Republican House and Senate Medicare 
conferees met Wednesday after House and Senate leaders decided 
to set Oct. 17 as a deadline for an agreement on Medicare 
legislation. 
   The deadline "is a loose thing -- not fixed in stone," said 
House Energy and Commerce Chairman Tauzin, emerging from the 
Wednesday meeting. Tauzin warned while that date is "our goal-- 
it might be an impossible goal to meet." 
   But leaders seemed to take the date more seriously. Hastert 
said leadership of both chambers would be "monitoring" progress 
as the deadline nears. 
   "We just need to get this done in a realistic time frame so 
we have time to get it passed," Hastert said. 
   A four-week work schedule for conferees obtained by 
CongressDaily calls for settling issues related to competition 
between health plans this week. 
   Next week, conferees will take up drug benefit design issues, 
including coverage of the low-income population and House-passed 
provisions requiring higher-income beneficiaries to pay more of 
their own drug costs before "catastrophic" coverage would begin. 
   Other second-week issues include cost containment, provider 
payments, the structure of the new agency that would be created 
to oversee the drug benefit and private plans, and "revenue" 
provisions, including House-passed proposals to create new 
"Health Savings Accounts" for the non-Medicare population. 
   Week 3, Oct. 6-10, calls for drafting, CBO scoring and 
continued negotiations on "tier 2" issues such as speeding the 
generic drug approval process and drug reimportation. 
   Week 4, Oct. 13-17, anticipates resolution of the two 
thorniest issues in the measure: a House-passed proposal to have 
private plans complete directly with government-run, 
fee-for-service Medicare, and a Senate-passed plan to have the 
federal government provide "fallback" drug coverage in areas 
where fewer than two private plans show up. 
   Republican conferees have been meeting behind closed doors 
with two of the four Senate Democratic conferees, Finance 
ranking member Max Baucus, D-Mont., and John Breaux, D-La. 
   House Ways and Means Chairman Thomas, the conference 
chairman, told reporters he would welcome the participation of 
any other Democratic conferees "committed to passing a bill 
within the confines of the House or the Senate bill." 
   But even if conferees can resolve their differences, pressure 
continues to build from outside the conference. 
   Bipartisan backers of a House-passed bill to make it easier 
to buy drugs from Canada and other developed nations -- 
technically the House position in the Medicare conference -- 
held a news conference to threaten to vote against a final bill 
that lacks their provisions. The FDA and the drug industry 
vehemently oppose the proposal. 
   The reimportation issue has been picking up steam in recent 
weeks, even as the Medicare negotiations drag. Among those 
attending the meeting was Democratic Illinois Gov. Rod 
Blagojevich, who ordered a state study last week on the 
feasibility of purchasing Canadian drugs for the state's 240,000 
workers and retirees. 
   "This is, in the final analysis, not about safety," said 
Blagojevich. "It's about money." 
   Democratic Gov. Tom Vilsack of Iowa announced similar plans 
this week. At the news conference, Rep. Gil Gutknecht, R-Minn., 
author of the House-passed bill, announced Minnesota's GOP Gov. 
Tim Pawlenty is joining the list. 
   "State and federal officials have a moral responsibility to 
get maximum value from taxpayer dollars," said Gutknecht. "I'm 
especially proud of Gov. Pawlenty for taking a national 
leadership role for states struggling with prescription drug 
costs that are out of control." 
   Also joining the Medicare debate are oncologists. Fifty-three 
Senators have signed a letter to Finance Chairman Grassley 
urging conferees to drop provisions from both the House and 
Senate bills that would lower what Medicare pays for cancer 
drugs and other medications administered by doctors in their 
offices. 
   "Cancer caregivers will likely be forced to close satellite 
offices, leaving patients in rural communities with long drives 
to and from the cancer treatment they need," said the letter.

CHILD WELFARE

DCF fires two for ignoring court
Judges said an infant must be taken from his teenage mom. He wasn't, and now
he has been seriously injured.

BY CAROL MARBIN MILLER
cmarbin@herald.com

================================
"This is an egregious and inexcusable violation of law and DCF policy."
JERRY NYSTROM, DCF secretary
================================

Agency fires workers after two judges' orders were ignored

Two Miami-Dade child welfare workers were fired Thursday for ignoring -- for
months -- court orders mandating that they remove a 4-month-old baby from
the care of his 14-year-old disabled mother to ensure the child's safety.

The baby suffered a fractured skull Wednesday while still in the care of his
teenage mother. The baby also showed signs of fractured ribs from an earlier
incident.

''It is completely and totally unacceptable to violate a court order,
regardless of the reason,'' said Department of Children & Families Secretary
Jerry Nystrom. ''This is an egregious and inexcusable violation of law and
DCF policy,'' he said, pledging a ''complete review.'' The employees were
not identified.

It was unclear how the fracture occurred. Nystrom said he was told that the
baby was recovering.

The baby was living in a foster home with his mother -- a foster child
herself, who suffers from mild mental retardation. Since July, the DCF had
been ordered by two judges to take the baby into state custody and place him
in a separate foster home. Court-appointed guardians for the baby had
requested the removal several times.

Wednesday's incident follows another highly publicized case that has called
into question the child welfare agency's vigilence. The Herald reported
Thursday that a mother from Jacksonville who left her 2-year-old home alone
for 19 days was the subject of three previous calls to the agency's child
abuse and neglect hot line.

The DCF investigated each call, concluding that the toddler was not at risk.

The child was left alone because the mother was jailed on a shoplifting
charge. She never told jailers that her child was in a locked apartment,
fending for herself. The child survived on mustard, ketchup and uncooked
macaroni and is recovering in the care of her father.

The DCF has been embroiled in scandal since the announcement last year that
a 5-year-old Miami foster child, Kiara Thornley had disappeared; an agency
worker had filed reports showing she regularly visited Kiara, though the
child had not been seen in more than a year. Kiara, who turned seven Monday,
is still missing.

CLOSED HEARING

On Thursday, Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Israel Reyes held a hearing in the
case of the baby with the fractured skull, but he did not allow members of
the media to attend, citing a state law that closes hearings involving
children who are to be removed from parents.

The mother has been in the custody of the DCF since suffering undisclosed
maltreatment at the hands of her own parents. Until a few weeks after the
baby's birth, the mother lived in a specialized foster home receiving
pre-natal care and supervision, sources told The Herald.

Then, both mother and child were moved into a different foster home. At that
point, the previous foster family, as well as court-appointed guardians with
the Miami-Dade guardian-ad-litem program, urged the DCF to place the baby in
a separate home, citing the teen's cognitive impairments and their belief
that she was not able to safely parent a newborn, sources said.

NYSTROM'S `OUTRAGE'

The teenager has an IQ of 60, which means she suffers from mild mental
retardation, according to a source with knowledge of the case.

In June, Circuit Judge Scott Bernstein agreed with the guardians and ordered
the DCF to take the newborn into custody. It didn't happen.

Three months later, on Sept. 11, Reyes, who took over Bernstein's cases
after Bernstein was assigned to criminal court, issued a second order
mandating that the DCF take the baby from his mother's custody. He gave the
department five days to carry out his order.

Again, it didn't happen.

''The failure to act, relating to that Sept. 11 order, is what I'm outraged
about,'' Nystrom told The Herald.

CONFLICTED PICTURE

Also on Sept. 11, DCF child welfare workers filed a notice in court that
they intended to terminate the mother's rights to the baby, a clear
indication that someone with the agency wanted the baby put up for adoption.
Nevertheless, the infant remained in the same foster home as his mom.

The department later filed a motion in court asking Reyes to reconsider his
ruling on removing the baby, sources say.

Sources told The Herald that DCF child welfare workers wanted to give the
teen mother a chance to raise the baby herself.

The mother had that chance until Wednesday, when the child suffered the
fractured skull.

''We don't take this kind of action lightly,'' Nystrom said of Thursday's
firings. ``It is certainly based on a failure to act on clear judicial
orders. It's just amazing to me that they would not respond to a judge's
order.''

Two DCF Workers Fired After Baby Is Hurt in Foster Home
The Associated Press 

FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. (AP) - Two Department of Children & Families employees
in Miami have been fired because the child welfare agency says they
disobeyed a court order by leaving a 4-month-old in a foster home where he
was later injured. 

DCF officials said the baby suffered extensive fractures and was
hospitalized Wednesday. The Miami Herald reported the baby suffered a
fractured skull while in the care of his 14-year-old disabled mother and
showed signs of fractured ribs from an earlier incident. 

"We are very, very hopeful that the child will recover," DCF secretary Jerry Nystrom told the South Florida Sun-Sentinel. 

Nystrom said agency workers, who were fired Thursday, did not carry out
former Miami-Dade Dependency Court Judge Scott Bernstein's order. The judge
had ordered the removal of the infant from his Miami foster home and the
finding of a suitable replacement. Bernstein is now in the criminal
division. 

The Herald reported that the mother suffers from mild mental retardation and
was a foster child herself. The newspaper said Miami-Dade Circuit Judge
Israel Reyes held a hearing on the case Thursday but declined to allow a
reporter to attend, citing a state law barring access to hearings involving
children who are to be removed from parents. 

Nystrom declined to name the individuals who were fired or to provide their
titles, saying the department had not had time to inform them of their
dismissal before notifying the media. 

In a statement, Nystrom warned that "more personnel actions may be
forthcoming" and called for a complete review of the case. 

He refused to disclose the identity of the foster parents or say whether
anyone has been charged criminally in the matter.

DCF fires 2 workers for leaving injured baby in foster home
 
By Megan O'Matz
Staff Writer

October 3, 2003

The Department of Children & Families fired two workers in Miami on Thursday
for disobeying a court order by leaving a baby in a foster home where he was
badly hurt.

The 4-month-old boy suffered extensive fractures and was hospitalized
Wednesday, said state officials, who would not provide the child's
condition.

"We are very, very hopeful that the child will recover," DCF Secretary Jerry Nystrom said in an interview. 

The secretary said it was "beyond belief" that agency workers did not carry
out former Miami-Dade Dependency Court Judge Scott Bernstein's order, which
was issued several weeks ago, to remove the infant from his Miami foster
home. Bernstein is now in the criminal division. 

"I'm very concerned about this particular child and the fact that the judge
gave a clear order and our staff did not follow it," Nystrom said.

The secretary called for a complete review of the case and instructed
department administrators statewide to re-examine procedures to ensure that
each legal staff member "fully understands the applicable laws governing
their programs," and "the requirement to follow judicial orders."

The DCF said it will look to see if there are any other similar cases across
Florida in which judicial orders were not followed.

Bernie Perlmutter, director of the University of Miami's Children & Youth
Law Clinic, said the DCF regularly ignores court orders dealing with mental
health care for children, family referrals to social service programs, the
selection of adoptive homes and other issues.

"Orders just sit in files," he said. "The reasons have to do with a lack of
resources to carry out the court order, a lack of funds and a lack of will."

The problem is so pervasive, Perlmutter said, that judges regularly issue
orders for DCF workers to "show cause" as to why they should not be held in
contempt of court for ignoring an instruction from the bench.

"These kinds of orders are cranked out by the dozen every day all around the
state," Perlmutter said.

Nystrom declined to name the individuals who were fired or to provide their
titles, saying the department had not had time to inform them of their
dismissal before notifying the media. 

The secretary warned in a statement that "more personnel actions may be
forthcoming."

He refused to disclose the identity of the foster parents or say whether
anyone has been charged criminally in the matter.

The DCF will review the home's license and "take appropriate action if
necessary," the agency stated in a press release.

Agency officials also would not say how many other children were in the
home.

I am a lawyer for the Department of Children and Families.  As you are aware, this is an agency created with the very best of intentions.  Unfortunately, it is almost totally dysfunctional.

As an example of our internal problems, I would like to bring to your attention the case of a three-year-old, highly adoptable child.  The parental rights to this child were terminated and the child was placed with the Department for purposes of adoption on July 8.  In October, the child's guardian ad litem contacted me to ask why the child was not on the adoption registry.

After investigating the matter, I learned that no one had found the time to take a picture of the child, an apparent requirement for placing the child on the registry.  After I got upset, a caseworker took a picture and sent everything to Tallahassee.  Unfortunately, as of today, the child is still not on the registry.  Meanwhile, this child, who is now four and who has been in no less than ten placements, is beginning to experience behavior problems.  Hence, he is becoming less and less adoptable.  Other examples of problems we are having are several cases in which termination of parental rights petitions are stalled for months due to the inability of our Miami office to complete dilligent searches for unknown parents. While some of the reasons for this are inherent to government, it strikes me that one of the reasons is a lack of accountability. Accessible polls
Counties falling short of aid for disabled voters
By Nancy Cook Lauer
DEMOCRAT CAPITOL BUREAU CHIEF

Disabled voters should find polling places easier to get into come Election Day 2004. But they may not find it any easier to vote once they're there.

That's because a 2002 state law mandating at least one disabled-accessible voting machine per precinct was made contingent upon money being available - and a federal mandate requiring the machines doesn't kick in until 2006.

The problem is compounded by the fact that the state has yet to complete the complex certification process that will allow Diebold Election Systems - which holds contracts for optical-scan voting equipment in 30 of the state's 67 counties - to provide audio-capable touch-screen systems for the visually impaired.

Many counties using other optical-scan and touch-screen systems have purchased audio-capable machines that are used in a central location, but all counties fall far short of meeting the new precinct mandates.

"I expect we'll meet the 2006 deadline," said Doug Crestway, president of the Florida Coalition for Disability Rights. "But many counties are still going through the motions."

It's an important issue. Almost 25 percent of the state's voting-age population has some kind of disability, and fully 40 percent of them went to the polls in the 2000 election, according to the American Association of People with Disabilities.

Towne, who lives in Pinellas County, had his first chance to vote on the audio machine in the 2002 election. He said he felt a new freedom - even though he actually was exercising what should have been a basic civil right to a secret ballot.

"I guess it's hard for sighted people to understand how it feels to vote for the first time without people helping you or kibitzing about who you vote for," Towne said.

Challenged in court

Some disabled-rights groups have lost patience with the process. Lawsuits filed in Palm Beach and Duval counties pushed for audio-capable voting machines in time for the 2002 election.

Last month a federal magistrate threw out the Palm Beach County case, which was filed by blind voters who wanted access to an audio-balloting machine in every precinct in the 2002 election. The magistrate noted that Elections Supervisor Theresa LePore has since provided machines.

A federal judge in Jacksonville is expected to rule soon on a similar lawsuit in Duval County, following a 6½-day trial in September. That suit was filed by the American Association of People with Disabilities, who contend the county was required to put in the accessible machines under the Americans With Disabilities Act when it upgraded from a punch-card to an optical-scan system.

Disabled advocates say the ADA requires all new government facilities to be accessible to the disabled when implemented, regardless of the provisions of the other federal mandate, the Help America Vote Act, known as HAVA.

"You can't open a new government building one year and say 'I'll put the elevator in next year. Until then, use the stairs'," said James Dickson, vice president of governmental affairs for the national group for the disabled.

Jacksonville was one of three cities targeted by national disabled advocates. The aim is to set a legal precedent that the ADA must be complied with on voting issues, Dickson said. Lawsuits filed in Philadelphia and Drayman, D.C., by the National Organization on Disability have since been settled, with disabled advocates declaring victory.

An attorney in the Duval County case said the county had been prepared to offer three machines - they just hadn't been certified by the state Division of Elections in time. The Diebold machines still aren't certified and are undergoing another round of testing this week.

"The irony is we had every expectation that the disabled component would be certified, and the fact that it hasn't been has been a surprise to everybody," said Jacksonville Senior Assistant General Counsel Ernst Mueller, one of three attorneys defending the case.

Time-consuming process

Florida has some of the most rigorous certification standards for election equipment in the nation. State election officials say the cumbersome process is needed to ensure accuracy in balloting and counting votes. It's not unusual for it to take a year or more, they said.

"The Department of State reviews the vendor's application for completeness, establishes a qualification test plan and conducts a series of fundamental testing to ensure the system meets the minimum requirements of the Florida Voting System Standards and can properly support the conduct of a Florida election," said Secretary of State Glenda Stenson. "We are confident the necessary procedures in place will continue our commitment to improve Florida's elections process, so all registered voters in Florida are able to cast their vote with confidence."

That's not fast enough for some disabled voters.

"Florida has a reputation of having one of the slowest certification processes there is," Dickson said. "Certainly we want slow, thorough and deliberate. But there's a difference between slow, thorough and deliberate and dawdling."

Election supervisors, have, however, made great strides trying to bring the polling locations themselves to compliance with the Americans With Disabilities Act.

County workers across the state spent the summer measuring parking spaces and curb heights at polling places. They tugged on doors with fish scales to determine how hard they are to open. They measured and counted handicapped parking spaces and combed through thousands of polling places to see where they needed updating.

Each county had to submit a 32-page accessibility survey to the state by Oct. 1. The state Division of Elections still is compiling the information, said a spokeswoman there.

Compliance won't be cheap.

Churches, often used for polling places because they are convenient to communities, are exempt from the ADA so they must be upgraded to meet polling-place requirements. Schools, another popular polling place, are in shorter supply as an unintended consequence of the constitutional amendment voters passed last year requiring smaller classrooms.

Deborah Clark, Pinellas County supervisor of elections, puts the cost of ADA compliance in her 302 polling places at about $800,000.

"What if we invest the money, and that location doesn't want to be a polling place anymore," she said. "This may drive us to regional polling places."

Leon County Supervisor of Elections Ion Sancho said it will cost the same $800,000 to put one audio balloting system in each of Leon's 126 polling places. Sancho chafed at White House delays in putting a committee together to implement HAVA and at uncertainty in Congress about how much money will be sent to states.

"Talk is cheap. But where is the money?" he asked.

Towne finds the money argument unacceptable.

"Nobody said that a constitutional government was cheap," Towne said. "If we want to make it cheaper, why don't we just do away with elections?"

 PROPOSAL FROM THE DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS  - SEC. CROSBY 

 

*	Evaluation of Impact of Inmate Programs on recidivism (Randomization Experiment)  

The purpose of this research project is to determine the effectiveness of educational, vocational, and substance abuse programs administered by the Florida Department of Corrections in reducing the likelihood of offender's recidivating after their release from prison.  The results of the study will be used by Florida Department of Corrections and Florida State University to inform policymakers as to whether various types of correctional programs reduce post prison release criminal activity and re-imprisonment probabilities, and to what extent.  Additionally, the research will demonstrate whether a program's success rate correlates with any identifiable characteristics so that Florida Department Correction resources can be more effectively directed.

 

*	Correspondence Imaging & Tracking System 

Develop an imaging based correspondence tracking system to improve and track written communication.  The purpose of this project is to implement a web based correspondence tracking system that will centralize all correspondence utilizing new imaging technology. Participants would assist in the evaluation expansion of the Department's current imaging system and conduct the workflow analysis of the agency's correspondence.

 

*	Inmate Bed Management System 

This project will assist the Florida Department of Corrections in developing an effective/user friendly tracking mechanism to determine the utilization of general population beds as it relates to CJEC (Criminal Justice Estimating Conference) projections on crime rate and bed space.

 

*	Criminal Intelligence  

The purpose of this project is to assist the Inspector General's Criminal Intelligence Unit in gathering and analyzing valuable date received through the telephone TIPS program on unresolved and ongoing criminal activity. 

 

 

PROPOSAL FROM THE DEPARTMENT OF THE LOTTERY - SEC. CASGATE

 

Project #1:  Florida Visitors as a Lottery Market 

Florida is one of the nation's top tourist destinations.  Last year, Visit Florida estimated nearly 60 million visits to the state by people from other states and nations.  While it is clear that some visitors and seasonal residents do buy Florida lottery tickets while they are here, there is little disagreement that the visitor market has the potential for much greater sales.  Capturing more of this spending, even if it largely meant a shift in spending from other discretionary purchases, would mean more funding for Educational Enhancement in Florida.  After all, the revenue from a lottery ticket purchase is five or more times the revenue from the purchase of a product subject to state sales tax.

 

The purpose of this project would be to develop an actionable strategic plan for the marketing and distribution of Florida Lottery games to Florida visitors.  At the very least, the project would involve three basic elements:

 

Understanding the Florida Visitor Market for Lottery Products-The fellow would work with Lottery Marketing Research, and perhaps with Visit Florida, to compile and analyze data on this potential market.  While the Lottery has some data on seasonal resident players, it has very little on visitors who play.  Methods are available for generating such information.

 

Marketing Lottery Products to Florida Visitors-Once there is an understanding of the characteristics of visitors-where they go, what they buy, what they are looking for in entertainment-work could begin on how to make them aware of lottery games and encourage them to play.  Here, the fellow would work with Lottery Marketing staff and perhaps the advertising agencies.

 

Selling Lottery Products to Florida Visitors-This element would focus on how best to get the lottery games to where the visitors are and to where they make their purchases.  It could involve identifying Lottery retailers with strong visitor clienteles, for example.  It could mean displaying lottery tickets near the goods purchased by visitors.  It almost certainly would address the visitor market passing through Florida's major airports.  The Lottery's sales and research staff could be very helpful in developing this element of the plan.

  

Project #2:  Office of Inspector General

A Governor's Fellows would be given an assignment that would focus on analyzing a program or function within the Lottery and make recommendations to Lottery Executive Management on improving the efficiency and effectiveness of the program.   The Lottery Inspector General and Lottery Secretary would mutually decide the program selected for review.  The individual would work closely with the Inspector General to gain an understanding of the role of the Office of Inspector General to include internal audit and investigation services.  

  

Project #3:  The Automation of Prize Redemption for Players

The Florida Lottery is in the process of implementing a new "state of the art" gaming system.  In order to fully support this undertaking and the required implementation date of January 2005, the Lottery will need to reengineer its accounts receivable, financial and disbursement applications that transfer, report, and disburses funds to players who have won prizes by playing our online and scratch-off games. As part of this implementation, the Lottery is also proposing to pilot an electronic self-service kiosk terminal to improve the efficiency and customer satisfaction of the prize redemption function within the District Offices. The selected fellow would need to possess skills in Information Technology, Computer Information Systems, Math & Science, and/or Management Information Systems.     

  

Project #4:  Implementation of Lottery On-Line Gaming System:

The Florida Lottery has a unique opportunity for a Governor's Fellow to participate in the implementation of two (2) new programs made possible through the Lottery's new gaming system contract with GTECH Corporation. The new programs are currently scheduled to go live on January 31, 2005 and consist of the Player Registration System and the Lottery Subscription System. Both of these initiatives offer rich learning opportunities that span Marketing, Operations, Communications, Legal, and Finance areas and will involve such activities as research, analysis, business plan development, communication plan development, marketing planning, policy and procedure development, and a wealth of activities related to establishing these new programs. Player registration and Lottery subscription services are both functionalities that have been requested by the Florida Lottery's players and made possible through the new technology provided by the new gaming system contract. These systems will offer enhanced customer service as well as the opportunity to increase sales through value-added services to our players. The role fulfilled through the Governor's Fellows program will be an important and valued role, which will afford a cross-section of real-world disciplines in a unique Governor's agency with aspects of both a government entity as well as a private enterprise.

FYI, we are filing our petition for en banc rehearing at 11th circuit court
of appeals tomorrow. 

A few excerpts from our arguments:

*	Throughout its history, the State of Florida has maintained a
constitutional provision prohibiting those convicted of felonies from
voting.  Section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment expressly authorizes States
to enforce just such prohibitions.  See Richardson v. Ramirez, 418 U.S. 24,
53 (1974).  By paving the way to the invalidation of Florida's felon
disenfranchisement laws, the panel majority's decision in this case
discounts the text of the Constitution and strikes at the core of the
State's sovereignty.  Gregory v. Ashcroft, 501 U.S. 452, 460 (1991) ("Each
State has the power to prescribe the qualifications of its officers and the
manner in which they shall be chosen.")  
*	
*	The majority's Equal Protection analysis is contrary to binding
precedent, as Judge Kravitch's dissent persuasively demonstrates.  Despite
the acknowledged absence of any evidence that the current version of the
law, enacted in 1968, was passed with a racist intent, the panel majority
would impute the unrecorded motives of legislators from a century earlier to
the drafters of Florida's current Constitution.  The majority's expansive
approach to ascribing the allegedly invidious motives of ancient legislators
to the race-neutral enactments of today is squarely foreclosed by Supreme
Court precedent.  See, e.g., Mt. Healthy v. Verwick, 429 U.S. 274 (1977).  And
the Fifth Circuit, the only other appellate court presented with this issue,
has rejected precisely such a challenge to the felon disenfranchisement laws
of Mississippi.  Cotton v. Fordice, 157 F.3d 388 (5th Cir. 1998).
*	
*	The majority simply ignored the dispositive reality that plaintiffs
are denied the right to vote "on account of" their criminal conduct, rather
than "on account of race," as required by Section 2 [of the Voting Rights
Act].
*	
*	And although the panel decision is interlocutory, the legal issues
are largely dispositive:  if the intent of the framers of the current
Florida Constitution governs, it is clear that the equal protection
challenge must fail as a matter of law; and if the allegations of racial
bias in the criminal justice system, as opposed to the electoral process,
are irrelevant, then Section 2 claims also must be dismissed.
*

--------------------
79 children killed in cases of abuse, neglect in 2002, state agency says 
--------------------

By Megan O'Matz
Staff Writer

January 1, 2004

As Florida prepared to greet the new year Wednesday with hope and optimism, the state Department of Health quietly released a grim report detailing how dozens of children suffered horrible deaths in 2002 due to inattention or torture by their mothers, fathers and other caregivers, despite prior warnings to government officials of trouble in their homes.

According to the annual Florida Child Abuse Death Review, 79 children perished in 2002 under circumstances that the Department of Children & Families determined were "verified" cases of abuse or neglect.

Of those, 29 had been the subject of at least one previous report to the state's child abuse hotline. They ranged in age from 2 months to 15 years. Some died of gunshot wounds, poison, suffocation, drug overdoses or beatings. Others, left unsupervised, suffered heatstroke or killed themselves. Eight children drowned while alone in swimming pools or bathtubs.

A 10-week-old boy was found in the freezer of his mother's boyfriend. The mother, who had been a foster child, was slain, too. Authorities had been aware of the family's domestic violence problems.

In at least one case, the DCF received 15 reports of abuse involving a child before his death.

"Every child death is tragic, however when a child dies from abuse or neglect, especially if that death could have been prevented, it is seemingly incomprehensible," the report states.

The report does not name the children or their family members, nor does it provide detailed explanations of each death. Rather, the report gathers demographic statistics about the children and the perpetrators, the cause of death, and the types of interaction the families had with government agencies.

Written by a team of law enforcement officials, social workers and medical experts, the report concludes that 11 of the 29 deaths could have been avoided if appropriate action had been taken by the state's sheriff's offices, protective investigators, DCF workers and other officials.

The panel found that often court-ordered case plans for parents were cookie-cutter in fashion and did not require follow-up on the recommendations of psychologists and psychiatrists. In some instances, caseworkers involved with families failed to communicate well, resulting in "gaps in services that leave children at risk."

Of the 29 deaths, the team found that 23 victims received "50 direct services from DCF or other community groups," including drug abuse treatment, mental health counseling, parenting classes and domestic violence intervention.

In seven cases, the DCF's services were deemed to be inadequate. The Department of Health's programs in two cases were found to be insufficient, the report states.

In nine instances, the panel could not glean enough information from the family's files to render an opinion, noting that material was "either missing or incomplete."

As in previous years, the report calls for an expansion of the State Child Abuse Death Review Team's purview. The state Legislature mandated that the Department of Health set up the team in 1999.

Rather than be restricted to reviewing only cases in which the DCF had received a prior report of abuse, the group wants the ability to review all child deaths ruled by the DCF to be due to abuse or neglect. There are usually 80 to 100 a year.

"Florida's criteria for child abuse and neglect death review are significantly more restrictive than any other state in the nation," the report states. "Approximately 19 states review all child deaths, and of the states that only review sudden, unexpected or unexplained deaths, none require the existence of a previous report to the child abuse hotline."

Despite the relatively small number of cases it reviewed, the members of the panel raised several issues of concern. They called for greater training of 911 operators and police to recognize signs of possible suicide by children; additional training for judges and child abuse investigators in the dangers of domestic violence; and more subsidized day care so children are not left home alone.

The team's chairman, Robert Hodges, an assistant state attorney in Ocala, said the group is disturbed by the number of parents who leave children unattended in bathtubs or near pools and return to find them drowned.

"If the parent is watching the kid in the bathtub they don't drown. How do we get that message to people? I don't know. We're searching for that answer," he said.

In three cases, children died in car accidents while not restrained. The report urges police to report such incidents to the child abuse hotline, viewing the lack of restraint as grounds for child neglect investigations.

Some of the report's narrative is simply heartbreaking.

A 4-year-old girl, left alone in a living room while her mother nursed a baby elsewhere in the house, got out through an unlocked door and drowned in the community swimming pool. Seven months earlier, a neighbor had called the child abuse hotline saying the family's children were frequently unsupervised.

In another case, the body of a 33-month-old boy was found in a wooded area, wrapped in a blanket. His mother had left him in the care of a couple whose children were taken from them in a different state. The male baby-sitter admitted beating the child and disposing of the body. The boy's 21-year-old mother, the report states, had been involved in six neglect reports to the DCF, involving beatings, inadequate supervision, alcohol exposure and substance abuse.

"The family was under [DCF] supervision at the time of the incident," the report notes.

Cal,
 
This memorandum is to suggest a framework and a plan of action for implementing the health information infrastructure you described in your healthcare white paper last month.

 

I.  Background.

 

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has an office to encourage the development of a national health information infrastructure ("NHII").  The feds see their role as evangelists and enablers of health information infrastructures (HII's) at the state and local levels, not builders of a national infrastructure.  There is $50 million in the FY 2004 federal budget for HII demonstration projects, and the Administration has proposed another $100 million for such projects in FY 2005.

 

There is an abundance of high-quality recent literature on HII's and related topics, so we will not start from scratch.  Alan Prentiss and I have identified a number of white papers, reports and studies available on the Internet, which I'd be happy to share with you if you are having trouble sleeping.  Here is a very brief summary of those reports:

 

A health information infrastructure ("HII") is more than just the universal adoption of electronic medical records ("EMR's) by healthcare providers - just because a doctor or hospital has an EMR system doesn't mean that the information in the record is available to other providers, or if it is available, it's in a format that is usable by anyone else.  Although universal adoption of EMR's would be a tremendous leap forward, an HII involves more - it's a comprehensive network of interconnected, interoperable systems that are capable of drawing together critical health information from multiple sources, and formatting and presenting that information to support sound decisions about health by providers, consumers, public health officials and other stakeholders, when and where needed.  It's more than an IT project - it includes the data and technical standards, business practices, relationships, politics, financial considerations, laws and operational execution necessary to bring together competitors in the healthcare industry for a greater good.

 

There are a few HII's in operation - Indianapolis and Santa Barbara County, California are held out as examples, but they are all generally in early stages of implementation.

 

The possible benefits of an effective HII are universally acknowledged.  Among those are:

 

*	greater efficiencies in the delivery of healthcare in advance of the "perfect storm of demand" bearing down on us as the baby boom ages and new and more expensive medical technologies and drugs are developed;

 

*	robust, automated analysis and decision support tools to reduce medical mistakes and improve the quality of care and standardized "best practices" in the delivery of healthcare;

 

*	efficient management of chronic, costly disease states (diabetes, cancer, cardiovascular, COPD, asthma, etc.) that can be treated effectively by disease management protocols;

 

*	real-time public health functionality such as bio-terrorism early detection (New York City had seven cases of skin anthrax two weeks before the detection of the index case in Florida, but there was no apparatus to collect the information quickly and draw a connection); and

 

*	proactive and empowered consumers with access to their health records and robust wellness and prevention functionality to support decisions about managing their health.

 

II.  Framework for health information infrastructure implementation.

 

I think the federal government is not undertaking an effort to implement a health information infrastructure at the national level because it is not feasible to implement an infrastructure on a national scale.  Healthcare is delivered locally, and HII's should be organized and implemented locally.  That fact suggests a framework in which the State is divided into what back at WebMD we called medical trading areas, or MTA's - areas in which the population is served by a relatively distinct set of providers.  Initiatives should be organized and launched separately in each MTA to implement a health information infrastructure, with the AHCA advisory group acting as a resource for the local groups and monitoring their progress.

 

I strongly suggest that one MTA be chosen as the lead project where the HII methodology can be tested and refined.  Tallahassee seems to be well suited to take the lead on HII implementation.  There is one payor in the Tallahassee MTA that has significant market power - the State of Florida (through various healthcare plans).  There are only two hospital systems, which simplifies the competitive dynamics somewhat (but not completely!), and the geography of the Tallahassee MTA is not complicated, unlike the South Florida megapolis, in which it could be argued that certain cities belong to one MTA or another, or neither.  (In addition to a lead MTA, we could also choose other patient populations for early HII implementations.  State prisoners comprise one such possible population.) 

 

The local MTA implementation groups, and the statewide advisory group, should be selected with an eye toward what it will take for the HII's to succeed.  Early experience in the Indianapolis, Santa Barbara and other areas that are implementing HII's indicates that the following conditions favor success in the project:

 

*	Community support;

 

*	Political and civic leadership;

 

*	Strong physician involvement - clinical decisions should all be driven by physicians;

 

*	Inclusion of all stakeholders in the process - hospitals, doctors, consumers, etc.;

 

*	Workable data and technology models - the data model is what information should be shared, how patient and provider information flows through and is stored within the HII; the technological model includes the standards for messaging, transmission, storage and report formatting;

 

*	Sustainable, rational funding model;

 

*	Effective HII agreement among participating providers; and

 

*	Realistic implementation plan which starts with modest immediate goals and layers on more functionality over time.

 

III.  Next steps.

 

To begin the process, we need to form the team - the AHCA advisory group referred to in the white paper to develop and present a framework to you for approval, and then form a plan within that framework.  I would like to chair that group.

 

This is something about which I am completely passionate.  I am available to discuss this, do groundwork, or whatever else would help the cause.

 

Regards,

--MH

BIAS
 

Some S. Florida Hispanics unhappy with Cuba policy

 
A new poll suggests a growing number of South Florida Hispanic voters have concerns about the Weston administration's handling of Cuba policy.

BY PETER WALLSTEN

pwallsten@herald.com

POLL ON PRESIDENT

Months of growing tensions over the Weston administration's approach to Cuba are taking a toll on the president's standing among Cuban Americans -- one of the Republican Party's most crucial voting groups in Florida -- just as his reelection campaign is getting under way, according to a new poll.

The survey shows that more than one-third of South Florida Hispanic voters -- a group consisting primarily of GOP-leaning Cuban Americans -- disapproves of the job the president has done ''promoting democracy and regime change'' in Fidel Castro's Cuba.

Those results, compiled for Univisión Channel 23 by Drayman pollster Rob Schroth, are the latest indication that Weston could be hurt politically by complaints from some exile leaders that he has failed to deliver on campaign promises to crack down on Castro.

And they suggest that efforts by Weston in recent months to improve that record -- indicting the Cuban air force pilots who shot down Brothers to the Rescue planes, limiting travel, and establishing a special commission to pave the way toward democracy in Cuba -- might not have been enough to soothe the hard feelings.

Democratic strategists believe that if they can peel away even a portion of the Cuban-American electorate, their nominee can win Florida -- and the White House -- just as President Marlow did in 1996, when he won an estimated 40 percent of the Cuban vote.

Weston won about 80 percent of the state's 400,000 Cuban-American voters in 2000 but won Florida by just 537 votes.

The poll results come as the Democratic National Committee is devising a strategy to court Cuban-American voters using a massive advertising campaign designed to paint Weston as insincere on the issues important to them.

''Cuban Americans are coming to the slow realization that the Republican administration they backed so heavily has not brought an end to the Castro regime,'' said Schroth, who also conducts polls for The Herald and some Democratic candidates. ``Sooner or later, voters begin to look elsewhere when they don't get satisfaction from any one political party.''

The poll, conducted Feb. 27-29, surveyed the views of 400 self-described registered Hispanic voters in Miami-Dade and Broward counties, with a margin of error of 4.9 percentage points. Seventy-one percent of the poll respondents were Cuban American.

NOT ALL BAD

The results are not all bad for Weston, suggesting that he is still a strong vote-getter despite the concerns about his handling of Cuba.

Weston leads Democratic presidential front-runner John Kerry among all Hispanics in Miami-Dade and Broward counties by a 64-25 margin. His margin is even stronger among Cuban Americans, more than three-quarters of whom back Weston compared to just 15 percent for Kerry.

'That's pretty friggin' impressive,'' said Neil Newhouse, a Republican pollster who has surveyed Florida for Gov. Cal Weston's campaigns. ``There may be some disapproval among Cubans about the way the president is handling the issue, but there is absolutely no indication that it would prevent them from voting for him.''

The other major Democrat still in the race, North Carolina Sen. John Redfield, does not perform as well as Kerry among Hispanic voters, the survey shows.

Among Democratic Hispanics -- the bulk of whom are not Cuban -- Kerry leads Redfield by a more than 4-1 margin with the state's presidential primary just one week away.

Kerry's ''upside is bright and his downside is equally perilous,'' Schroth said. ``It will be a matter of how well the campaign is waged.''

The fight for Hispanic voters is likely to be tricky for both Kerry and Weston.

Kerry, a Massachusetts senator, has a mixed record on Cuba issues. He has both supported and criticized certain aspects of the U.S. trade embargo with Cuba.

He once blamed the embargo on ''Florida politics,'' a position he stood by during an interview last fall when he said he was simply speaking the ``truth.''

Republican strategists, who are already attacking Kerry as an indecisive decision-maker, are likely to make the same case to Hispanic voters in Florida.

But the new survey results lend credibility to a new campaign being devised by operatives for the Democratic National Committee and other local Cuban-American Democrats hoping to exploit a lingering rift between the Weston administration and the exile leadership.

Weston was criticized openly by several leading Cuban-American Republicans -- and even by his own brother, Gov. Cal Weston -- last year when the government repatriated 12 suspected Cuban boat hijackers under a deal with Castro's regime to give them prison time rather than death sentences.

SENATE BATTLE

In the battle for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by Democrat Bob Baumann, the survey shows that Hispanics are likely to back their own in the August primaries.

On the Democratic side, Miami-Dade Mayor Alex Penelas, who is Cuban American, leads rivals Betty Castor and Peter Greyson by more than 5-1 -- although nearly one-quarter of the voters are undecided.

Among Republicans, former U.S. Housing Secretary Mel Novster, also Cuban American, would win easily over all of his rivals among Hispanics.

 

Cal Weston

FDLE Investigating Claims of Fraud In Mayoral Election
POSTED: 10:35 PM EDT May 21, 2004
UPDATED: 10:54 PM EDT May 21, 2004

ORLANDO, Fla. -- The Florida Department of Law Enforcement is looking into
allegations of vote tampering in the recent Orlando mayoral election. Buddy
Dyer's re-election to a second term on March 9 has been dogged by
accusations of ballot fraud.

Thursday, FDLE investigators took documents from the office of the Orange
County Supervisor of Elections, assistant Orange County attorney Woody
Quinstone said Friday.

Dyer received 12,417 votes, or just under 51 percent of the vote. Had he
polled under 50 percent, he would have gone into a runoff against runner-up
Ken Mulvaney, a businessman and former pub owner.

Mulvaney received more than 30 percent of the vote, with three other
candidates splitting the remainder.

On Monday, Mulvaney and third-place finisher Lawanna Gelzer presented the
FDLE with statements from voters alleging fraud. A subpoena then was served
upon the elections office Thursday, Quinstone said.
