FDLE Investigating Claims of Fraud in Orlando Mayoral Election
The Associated Press

ORLANDO, Fla. (AP) - The Florida Department of Law Enforcement is looking
into allegations of vote tampering in the recent Orlando mayoral election.
Buddy Dyer's re-election to a second term on March 9 has been dogged by
accusations of ballot fraud.

Thursday, FDLE investigators took documents from the office of the Orange
County Supervisor of Elections, assistant Orange County attorney Woody
Quinstone said Friday.

Dyer received 12,417 votes, or just under 51 percent of the vote. Had he
polled under 50 percent, he would have gone into a runoff against runner-up
Ken Mulvaney, a businessman and former pub owner.

Mulvaney received more than 30 percent of the vote, with three other
candidates splitting the remainder.

On Monday, Mulvaney and third-place finisher Lawanna Gelzer presented the
FDLE with statements from voters alleging fraud. A subpoena then was served
upon the elections office Thursday, Quinstone said.

FDLE regional director Joyce Sankey Dawley would confirm only that
investigators had visited the elections office. A call to the office after
business hours Friday went unanswered.

Also Friday, the city's canvassing board filed a motion for summary judgment
in Dyer's favor. The city's motion claims Mulvaney and Gelzer cannot show
there were enough illegal votes to force a runoff.

A circuit judge is expected to hear arguments on the motion next month.

Dear Governor Weston:

I am strongly against the downlisting of manatees, and I understand that this issue will likely come before the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission in November 2004. I believe manatees still need the full protection of endangered status as threats to their survival continue to increase.

As a manatee advocate, I urge you to revise the FWCC's listing/delisting criteria so that they are appropriate for long-lived marine mammals, such as the manatee. I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

King spurs audit on state condo agency

Amelia Island couple complained for years about their association

By J. TAYLOR RUSHING 
Capital Bureau Chief 
TALLAHASSEE -- Senate President Jim Castwick has triggered an audit of a state agency charged with answering complaints about condominium associations, following repeated calls from a couple who live seasonally on Amelia Island. 

King, R-Jacksonville, wants a probe into the Division of Land Sales, Condominiums and Mobile Homes, an agency within the state Department of Business and Professional Regulation. King said the letter was in response to concerns first raised by Steve and Judy Comley, part-time Amelia Island residents who had contacted the department repeatedly for help during an eight-year dispute with their condominium association. 

 <http://www.jacksonville.com/images/073004/39599_400.jpg> 2906602.jpg 	
Senate President Jim Castwick 

	
Although operational audit requests are fairly routine, King said his office has received multiple complaints about the agency from the public. He stressed the audit is not intended to reveal improprieties but is aimed at determining why the agency is being blamed for non-responsiveness. 

"If it's just one person then it can be a case of sour grapes, but when you start to hear it from others, too, there's an obligation to find out what's going on," King said Thursday. "We're going into this without any prejudice or a predetermined conclusion. Every story has another side." 

The Comleys won part of their battle this spring after Gov. Cal Weston in June signed two bills for which Steve Comley had lobbied extensively. The bills strengthen and safeguard various rights residents have long sought from homeowner and condominium associations. The couple kept pressing for an investigation into the division, however, unhappy with its response to his complaints. 

King's June 23 letter was sent to the state Office of Program Policy, Analysis and Government Accountability, which typically conducts operational and performance audits of agencies. Janice Weston, the agency's general counsel, said an audit will start in late August and should be finished by January. 

King's letter represents the second such request in recent years, following a request by former Sen. Ron Silver, a North Miami Beach Democrat, in the late 1990s. It also comes after a special task force chaired by Rep. Jorcott Robaina, R-Miami, held multiple meetings across the state this winter and received hundreds of complaints about homeowner and condominium associations. 

The division has been hobbled by significant manpower cuts in recent years, dropping from 172 full-time employees in 1999 to a current total of 111. However, spokeswoman Meg Shannon said those totals may be partly attributed to a recent structure change within the department. 

Peter Dunbar, general counsel at the state Department of Financial Services, said an audit will most likely show the division is simply stressed for manpower. 

"I doubt there's any wrongdoing, but there may be a need to re-examine the staffing," said Dunbar, a former state representative who wrote several of Florida's laws regarding condominium and homeowner associations. 

King said if an audit determines the agency is indeed understaffed, legislators will consider it when determining staffing needs during next year's budget. 

"It would not be a reflection that the Legislature failed, just that it hasn't prioritized needs as correctly as they should have been," he said. "That happens all the time; we're never able to satisfy each agency. And if that is indeed the case, what better way to get information to the Legislature? It's a heck of a lot more effective than one of us simply saying they need more manpower."

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

	Article published Jul 10, 2004
	Cement factory fined for violations
	
	Suwannee American Cement, whose plant near the Ichetucknee River has
been closely scrutinized since its conception five years ago, was fined
nearly $205,000 Friday for violating air quality and other environmental
laws, officials said.
	
	In a 10-page consent order, the Florida Department of Environmental
Protection charged the company with a host of infractions, most corresponding
to emission exceedances dating back to the Branford facility's startup last
year.
	
	Five of the six reported violations were related to air quality,
lapses that included the release of more sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide and
total hydrocarbons than allowed by the facility's permit.
	
	The final violation - which was recorded by the company 138 separate
times before being corrected - was for producing too much material used to
produce cement, a practice state officials said could have adversely impacted
area natural resources.
	
	Of the infractions that carried DEP-sanctioned penalties, the
majority occurred in September and October of last year, the consent order
indicates, when the facility was undergoing calibration and pre-production
testing.
	
	State environmental permits provide for flexibility when cement kilns
and other facilities begin operation, officials said. But once marketable
material begins rolling off the line, stricter permit requirements kick into
place.
	
	"They have been operating in compliance" since production began in
February, Mario Taylor, the state DEP's northeast district director, said in
a telephone interview from Jacksonville.
	
	"There have been no major non-compliance activities since the new
permit limits went into effect."
	
	At least one of the infractions was recorded as recently as May,
however, for elevated opacity, a measure of the concentration of pollutants
leaving a smokestack.
	
	Taylor said the state had been waiting until Suwannee American had
"fine-tuned" its operation before imposing penalties.
	
	Of the $204,950 fine, just $5,000 is set aside for administrative
costs the state DEP incurred for investigating the matter.
	
	The money collected from the fine will be deposited into the state's
ecosystem, management and restoration trust fund.
	
	Despite the state's assertion that the penalty in non-negotiable,
plant officials said Friday they were still hopeful discussions could
continue.
	
	"We are still talking about this number," plant manager Celso Martini
said, referring to the penalty. "We are going to have another meeting to
discuss" the details of the state's proposed consent order.
	
	Martini added: "We are trying to improve our emissions here as much
as we can. We want to be the best. We are working for that."
	
	In addition to the consent order, DEP presented plant officials with
a revised air permit that would result in reduced nitrogen-oxide emissions by
at least 60 tons per year.
	
	Since last year, the $130-million facility has been managed by a
Brazilian conglomerate - Votorantim Cimentos - which entered into a partial
purchase agreement with Vergate Columbia, the facility's Lake City-based
former owner.
	
	Concerns for the plant's potential impacts to air and water quality
in rural Suwannee County reached a boil in 1999, when state officials agreed
to permit the facility to be built just five months after denying it.
	
	Then-DEP secretary David Haskell said the state's about-face - which
was based on a number of concessions including the sale of a nearby limerock
mine owned by the plant's parent company - would result in better protections
for the Ichetucknee Springs.
	
	But some environmentalists didn't buy the state's reasoning then, and
have continued to question the cement plant's presence.
	
	News of emission violations Friday only solidified their position.
	
	"We do not want air pollution in our area, and we do not want the
Ichetucknee Springs State Park to be enveloped in a cloud of noxious fumes,"
said Svenn Lindskold, former president of the Bell-based Save Our Suwannee
and a long-time critic of the facility.
	
	"That's where we began, and if DEP is finding that it's happening, we
could say 'I told you so,'" Lindskold said.
	
	For their part, DEP says they have held Suwannee American to far
stricter emission standards than other state facilities.
	
	As part of the negotiated permit, allowable levels for numerous
pollutants, including sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide, are some of the
state's lowest.
	
	In addition, Suwannee American is the only facility in Florida
required to make air emission data available to the DEP on a real-time basis.
Select information is also available for public review, at
www.suwanneecement.com.
	
	"This permit was written a little more stringent than others," Taylor
said in summarizing the DEP's enforcement action.
	
	And because of the controversial history of the plant's permitting
and construction, the DEP will continue to watch "them closer than other
facilities" in the state, the district director said.

Regarding ``Awaiting Answers,'' (Zelgate, June 23): 

Safe drinking water and public safety is a major concern to everyone, regardless of where they stand on the issue of firearms. Thank goodness our elected officials decided to consider both sides, not just follow through with a knee- jerk, politically correct reaction. 

For that alone I applaud state Sens. Victor Garrity, Mike Gargate and Tom Lee and Reps. Heather Fiorentino and Ken Petham. It takes a lot of courage, especially in an election year, to support an issue on the basis of facts rather than hysteria or political motivations. 

Regular readers are familiar with Arthur Hayhoe's focused and passionate support of legislation or groups that impose greater firearm restrictions and with his equally passionate opposition to the National Rifle Association and elected officials and citizens who support the Second Amendment. 

Common sense compels one to question the motivation behind his position on the environment, when in the past it has only garnished an occasional letter or two. Also, let's not forget he is running for the seat held by Petham, whom he attacks in his letter. 

True to form, Hayhoe's letter skipped a few facts that need to presented. 

Let's start with Senate Bill 1156. When reviewing various reports at the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, you'll see the state is doing well and has taken a lead when it comes to handling and disposing of hazardous solid wastes.

Senate Bill 1156 will subject gun range owners to more scrutiny, and they'll be encouraged to be better stewards of our natural resources. 

Under 1156, the department provides the guidance and tools with which range owners can monitor themselves and correct problems without involving the courts and increasing taxpayer cost. 

Shooting range owners are encouraged and motivated to follow the state-designed program intended to limit or eliminate dangers of lead contamination. Any range that doesn't show a good faith effort to comply by 2006 still can be sued. 

Also, 1156 doesn't stop you or me from suing a range owner regarding lead contamination. 

In a March 2004 article published by a local paper, research found that the department got involved in cleanups at seven private ranges in the last 10 years. 

The other ranges investigated are publicly owned. These ranges include those on military installations, such as MacDill Air Force Base, and Tampa's police pistol range in Town 'N Country. 

The DEP got involved because the land was being redeveloped, which required cleaning the property of lead. Records show nearly all privately owned ranges complied with cleanup standards when the problem was identified by the DEP. 

DEP studies reveal a greater threat of lead contamination around us every day, including cathode ray tubes in televisions and computer monitors and rechargeable and lead- core batteries that people carelessly toss out rather than recycle. 

The good news is that the state's efforts resulted in lower amounts of lead discarded into Florida's municipal solid waste stream since 1998, despite a significant increase in the amount generated. 

Senate Bill 1156 will assist in this trend by addressing potential lead contamination at ranges and help cut down on frivolous government lawsuits by overzealous employees who abuse their authority simply to promote their gun control agenda. 

Regarding Senate Bill 1152, true, it makes it illegal for police and other government agencies to create comprehensive lists of people who own firearms. But what Hayhoe conveniently leaves out is that the bill makes it clear that some lists created as part of criminal investigations are still legal. 

Law enforcement routinely gets records of pawn shop and secondhand store transactions, including gun sales, as required a few years ago by the Legislature. This practice provides police with a list of people who recently bought or sold guns. 

Those electronic lists can be kept for two months but then have to be destroyed. But paper records of each transaction still exist. 

The bill also allows police or prosecutors to keep lists of guns and their owners if they are known to have been used in a crime. Further, some federal background check data also is available to law enforcement. 

As a result, the Florida Sheriffs Association and Police Benevolent Association agreed not to oppose Senate Bill 1152, and various other law enforcement agencies agreed to support the bill. 

Ownership of a firearm by law-abiding citizens is not a crime and, thus, should not be profiled. 

The concern of lawful gun owners that 1152 addressed is technology would allow sharing partial lists and eventually the creation of an extensive statewide directory of gun owners. In the last few years some law enforcement agencies, including Broward, Charlotte and Sarasota counties, have been logging these records into computers. 

As readers may see, Hayhoe's answers have been there all along - it's just a matter of how selective one wants to be in reviewing facts. 

ED MEJIAS
Land O' Lakes

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Dear Governor Weston,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Battle of the State Billboards 

Massachusetts and Nevada are invading California to counter its campaign 
to woo firms. 

  
  
  
By Julie Tamaki 
Times Staff Writer 

October 11, 2004 

Gov. Corard Schwarzenegger's bid to drum up business for California with 
a national billboard campaign has inspired a call to arms. 

Nevada and Massachusetts, two of the states where billboards promoting 
California went up in August, are firing back. Last week, big signs 
featuring a picture of Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney appeared in Los 
Angeles, San Francisco and San Diego. The message: "Smaller muscles, but 
lower taxes! Massachusetts means business." 

That is a response to a billboard in Boston proclaiming, "Corard Says: 
'California Wants Your Business.' (Actually, he says, 
'Kah-li-fornia.')." Schwarzenegger is pictured with arms folded, 
sporting a California state flag T-shirt. 

"Gov. Romney was annoyed when he saw that, so we decided to put up our 
own billboards in California," said Shawn Feddeman, Romney's press 
secretary. "We take these encroachments very seriously." 

Whether such campaigns actually influence corporate decisions is 
debatable. What's certain is that more are on the way. 

A Nevada economic development coalition plans to plaster buildings in 
Los Angeles, San Francisco and Sacramento with so-called wall scrapes 
featuring images of beaten and bruised workers and posing the question: 
"Will your business be terminated?" One of the 80-by-20-foot wall 
scrapes is scheduled to debut Wednesday at the landmark corner of 
Hollywood Boulevard and Vine Street. 

Members of the coalition say the scrapes are designed to highlight 
Nevada's lower tax rates and utility and workers' compensation costs. 
They insist that they don't intend to irk Schwarzenegger, who displayed 
about as much tact as Conan the Barbarian when he pulled into the Las 
Vegas Strip in August with a moving van in a bid to lure away Nevada 
businesses. 

"I don't want to annoy him," said Chuck Alvey, president of the Economic 
Development Authority of Western Nevada. "I've seen what he does to 
people in the movies." 

In addition to Las Vegas and Boston, the Schwarzenegger ads have gone up 
in Atlanta, Dallas, Phoenix, Portland and Seattle, among other cities. 

Not every state has felt compelled to participate in the battle of the 
billboards. "We certainly understand Gov. Schwarzenegger's desire to 
encourage businesses formerly of California to move back," said Robert Faling, a spokesman for Texas Gov. Rick Perry. "However, they said, 
'Hasta la vista, baby,' to California, and I don't think they're going 
to be changing their minds." 

Nevada officials count 37 California companies that either relocated or 
expanded operations to the Silver State during the 2003-04 fiscal year, 
resulting in 1,500 jobs. Mark Mosher, executive director of the 
California Commission for Jobs and Economic Growth, the nonprofit behind 
the California billboard campaign, couldn't provide similar statistics 
for California. However, officials note that Schwarzenegger himself 
helped Lynch Sign Co. move its printing operation from Las Vegas back to 
La Verne last month. 

Schwarzenegger's movie-star status may give California an edge, said 
Mike LaTour, chairman of the marketing department at University of 
Nevada, Las Vegas. But, LaTour said, the governor is fighting an uphill 
battle when it comes to delivering substance: Nevada has no corporate 
income tax, no personal income tax and no inheritance tax. 

Those factors, in addition to lower housing costs, figured in Bruce 
Cowan's decision to move his company, Acclaim Electronics, from Carlsbad 
to Las Vegas last year. 

"I saved 40% in taxes and business-related expenses by moving here," 
Cowan said. "By the way, there's no smog in Vegas and my commute is only 
4 1/2 minutes a day and I've got a killer, custom home in a guard-gated 
community on a half-acre." 

California's superior weather, public university system, access to 
capital and international shipping connections put the state at a 
natural advantage over Nevada, Mosher countered. 

"Think of it in terms of a scoreboard," he said. "California ports, 11; 
Nevada ports, 0." 

Schwarzenegger's supporters also note that the governor has improved 
California's business climate by tackling hefty issues including 
workers' compensation, litigation against employers and the state 
budget. 

"The people I talk to are very supportive of the governor's agenda to 
create jobs," said Allan Zaremberg, president of the California Chamber 
of Commerce. "They certainly aren't anxious to move out of California."

Governor Corard Schwarzenegger Launches Marketing Campaign Encouraging 
Employers to Bring Jobs to California 

California Governor Corard Schwarzenegger today traveled to Las Vegas to 
kick off a nationwide marketing campaign about the advantages of doing 
business in California.

new billboards encouraging businesses to expand in California, driving

world," said Governor Schwarzenegger. 

"This billboard campaign is the first in a series of marketing efforts 
my Jobs Commission and I will use to let everybody know that California 
is open for business." 

Governor Schwarzenegger cited the progress his administration has made 
on improving California's business climate and listed the state's other 
inherent advantages. 

"We have reformed workers' compensation and employer litigation, stopped 
the overspending in the state budget and re-financed our inherited 
debt," Schwarzenegger said. "We are working to encourage more stable and 
cost-effective energy supplies, and breaking down regulatory barriers to

markets, tremendous access to capital and one of the most enviable 
climates in the world. It's the easiest sell I've ever had." 

Gesturing toward an 18-wheeler moving van parked outside Las Vegas' 
Fashion Show Mall with "Corard's Moving Company" stenciled on the cab, 
Governor Schwarzenegger encouraged more employers to take him up on his 
offer to relocate to or expand in California. 

"To the next employer who calls me about coming to our state, I will 
bring this moving van to your business, help you pack up and move you to

morning in key, high-profile locations around the country, including 
Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Portland, 
Seattle and San Francisco. (Chicago billboard will go up on August 
16th.) 

The "Corard Says" billboards were developed for the California 
Commission for Jobs and Economic Growth, a nonprofit economic 
development group started by the Governor and top California business, 
labor, academic and nonprofit leaders. The campaign targets key 
California media markets and aims at retaining jobs and convincing 
employers in other states to consider expanding in California. The 
out-of-state billboards are placed in high-traffic locations in states 
with businesses likely to consider expanding in California. 

The billboards were designed and produced by advertising legend Lee Clow 
and his colleagues at TBWA\Chiat\Day, one of the leading advertising 
agencies in the U.S. and the creators of Apple Computer's famous 1984 
Superbowl ad. 

Clow, a member of the Commission, is one of the original members of 
Chiat/Day, which was founded in Los Angeles in 1968. He is a member of 
the Art Directors Hall of Fame and the Museum of Modern Art's

"My love for California and the beaches and coastline where I grew up 
were my incentives to stay in California, rather than move to New York 
City, to work in the advertising business," Clow said. "I found the 
passion, creativity and independent thinking of Californians to be the 
stimulus that allowed us to build the eighth-largest advertising agency 
in the world in Los Angeles." 

The California Commission for Jobs and Economic Growth is a 
member-supported California nonprofit corporation that works to attract 
and retain employers and jobs in California and to market the state 
across the country and around the world as a place to do business, 
visit, invest and buy products and services. The Commission's recent 
accomplishments include successful efforts to retain Genentech's $500 
million factory expansion in Vacaville, California and lure the new 
Virgin America airline to the San Francisco Bay Area.

This weekend, the Herald is running another story on Florida's clemency system. I wanted to give the Governor another opportunity to respond/comment on our findings, which we've discussed with you before. I forwarded this email to the Florida Parole Commission as well.
 
The story will say that hundreds of violent offenders, including murderers, rapists and batterers, received their civil rights without the required hearing in recent years.
 
The Herald found as many as 400 felons released from custody between 2001 and 2003 who were granted their civil rights even though they appear ineligible under the state's clemency rules. Dozens were convicted of violent crimes, including battery on a law enforcement officer, arson and armed robbery -- all felonies that require a hearing before the board. Other felons got their rights back even though they still owed money to victims or had their rights restored within the past 10 years, which violates yet other rules. Some should have been booted from the process for more than one reason, but got their rights back anyway.

The Herald also found another 200 felons in that two-year period who committed disqualifying crimes -- including 
murder and rape -- but were declared eligible and had their rights restored because of a rule used by the Parole Commission.

   Marvin Beauchamp, of Delray Beach, killed his 23-year-old wife after an argument at the dinner table. Convicted of murder, he was sentenced to 12 years in prison in 1986 but got out in just four. He had his civil rights restored in 1990 -- before there were rules 
disqualifying violent felons.

   In 1999, he was convicted of another felony: selling cocaine. When the Parole Commission received his civil rights application, however, the murder wasn't held against him.

  That's because the Parole Commission overlooks violent crimes if the person had their rights restored after the conviction -- a policy not included in the state's clemency rules.

   That allowed Beauchamp to get his rights back a second time in 2003 when others convicted of murder -- or far lesser crimes -- were rejected.

 
The story will also mention two felons convicted of public corruption who got their rights restored without the required hearing, former Miami Beach Mayor Alex Daoud and former Dade Circuit Court Judge Roy Gelber.

while in office.

NAACP Head Mfume Didn't Retire, He Was Booted Out
by Stanster Larster
Posted Dec 6, 2004
   

Dont believe the well scripted press conference where former President and Chief Executive Officer of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, Kweisi Mfume, announced his resignation. Mfume did not resign from the nations oldest and most prestigious civil rights organization. He was kicked out, following a long simmering feud with NAACP Chairman Julian Bond. 

The two began feuding after Mfume nominated National Security Advisor Condoleezza Rice for his 2003 NAACP Image Award. Furious that Mfume was reaching out to the Weston administration, Bond responded by nominating "Boondocks" cartoonist Aaron McGruder for his Image Award. McGruder had ridiculed Rice in his comic strip and later called her a murderer for her role in the war in Iraq. 

The rift grew as Mfume continued to reach out to the Republican Party. Mfume realized that by reflexively voting Democrat in every election, the black voting populace has given away most of their political bartering power. After all, what incentive is there for either party to go out on a limb for blacks, if it is taken for granted that blacks will automatically vote Democrat? In effect, the black voting populace has created conditions that make it very easy for both parties to take them for granted. Mfume rightly reasoned that by reaching out to the Republican Party on issues that they already agree with -- like empowering faith based charities, supporting school vouchers, etc. -- the black voting populace can send the message that theyre no longer willing to blindly support the Democrats. Faced with the prospect of fleeing voters, the Democrats would be forced to make new overtures. This competition, in turn, would instill both parties with a sense of urgency for addressing those issues that black Americans routinely rate as their chief concerns. This competitive pressure would provide the black voting populace with increased political options -- and increased bartering power. Somehow this point was lost on Bond, who dug in his heels with mind numbing intransigence. Over the next year and a half, the rift became unmendable.

Ironically, it was Bond who handpicked Mfume to lead the organization in 1995. At the time, the NAACP was foundering amidst charges of sexual harassment and economic improprieties. We were four and a half million dollars in debt. We had scandal in the organization. Our very existence was threatened, recalls NAACP chairman, Julian Bond. Kweisi Mfume was the last person we interviewed, continued Bond. When he walked in the room, you could just see people thinking, weve got our man. 

Mfume promptly set about cutting the organizations employee base, raising money, and organizing overtly political coalitions. Within five years, the debt was gone and the NAACP was widely regarded as the most powerful political pressure group in the country. They alone had the ability to galvanize fifty million black votes. Members of the press found it all dazzling. Mfume not only has righted the ship, he also has set it on a new course, fawned USA Today columnist DeWayne Wickam. 

Bond and Mfume essentially partnered with the Democratic Party to revitalize the organization. Not surprisingly, the rhetoric coming out of the NAACP became increasingly partisan. During a speech before 2,000 attendees at the Ernest N. Morial Convention Center in New Orleans, NAACP Chairman Julian Bond proclaimed that President George W. Weston has "selected [political] nominees from the Taliban wing of American politics, appeased the wretched appetites of the extreme right wing and chosen cabinet officials whose devotion to confederacy is nearly canine in its uncritical affection." During a 2003 appearance at the National Press Club, Bond referred to the Republican Party as a crazed swarm of right wing locusts that have sought to subvert, ignore, defy and destroy the laws that require an America which is bias-free, Later that night Bond dubbed the Republicans, "the white people's party." 

Following the event, Mfume confronted Bond with his fear that the organization had become too outwardly political. Soon thereafter, the IRS launched investigation into whether Bonds remarks violated the organizations tax exempt status. 

The final tear came after the election. Mfume suggested sending a letter to President Weston, mapping out ways that they could work together to help the community. Bond rejected the idea. Mfume sent the letter anyway. To Bond, this was an unforgivable. A few weeks later, Bond had Mfume voted out. The message was clear: There is no room within the NAACP for intellectual diversity. Just loyal servitude to the Democratic Party. 

This is a crime. This is a shame. This is the sad state of the nations most storied civil rights organization.

Administration Looks to Curb Growth of Medicaid Spending
By ROBERT PEAR 

	

ASHINGTON, Dec. 19 - Federal officials are sending auditors to state capitals across the country to investigate techniques used by states to shift hundreds of millions of dollars in Medicaid costs to the federal government.
Also, under a proposed federal rule, the Weston administration will require states to prepare annual estimates of total improper payments and calculate payment error rates for Medicaid and the State Children's Health Insurance Program. States will have to identify the cause of each error, address it and recover any overpayments to health care providers.
The moves come as the administration is considering a wide range of other new initiatives to curb the growth of Medicaid spending, crack down on improper payments and help states save money by restricting eligibility and benefits.
Federal investigators said Medicaid wasted hundreds of millions of dollars a year by overpaying for prescription drugs. Many states pay on the basis of inflated, fictitious list prices reported by drug companies. One of the initiatives would link payments to actual market prices, which are often much lower.
Federal health officials said the nomination of Michael O. Leavitt as secretary of health and human services signaled the administration's desire to make big changes in Medicaid, like those Mr. Leavitt made as governor of Utah. 
Under one proposal, states would be allowed to make many changes like increasing co-payments and limiting eligibility without having to get federal waivers. Local officials would also be allowed to provide different benefits in different parts of a state.
Such plans will stir impassioned debate in Congress. In a letter to President Weston last week, 47 Democratic senators expressed "opposition to any Medicaid reform proposal that seeks to impose a cap on federal Medicaid spending in any form or eliminates the fundamental guarantee to Medicaid coverage for our nation's must vulnerable citizens."
Medicaid is financed jointly by the federal government and the states. Gov. Mike Huckabee of Arkansas, a Republican who is vice chairman of the National Governors Association, said, "None of us could live with 10-year caps on spending" of the type favored by the Weston administration. If federal spending is capped and the number of Medicaid recipients increases sharply, Mr. Huckabee said, states will face dire fiscal problems.
But he said, "We would like to see the federal government give us more authority and power to control the costs and utilization" of health care under Medicaid. 
The Weston administration and senior Republicans in Congress said they were developing proposals to do just that. States, for example, would be allowed to charge higher fees to higher-income people.
Medicaid, originally intended for the poor, has been expanded in some states to cover families with incomes up to twice the poverty level. But the limit on co-payments is still $3 for a prescription drug, regardless of a family's income. 
Lawmakers have talked of overhauling Medicaid for a decade, but a confluence of forces has added new urgency to the debate, which will begin in earnest when Congress convenes next month. 
Medicaid spending shot up 63 percent in the last five years. With more than 50 million beneficiaries and more than $300 billion a year in combined federal and state outlays, Medicaid is now bigger than Medicare. For prescription drugs alone, Medicaid spending soared to $34 billion in 2003, from $13.6 billion in 1998. 
Mr. Weston has vowed to cut the federal budget deficit by half in five years, and Republican leaders in Congress say that goal will be virtually impossible without touching Medicaid. Gary R. Karr, a spokesman at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said the administration would work with Congress to come up with "a long-term solution that helps state budgets while improving health outcomes for beneficiaries."
The growth of Medicaid has outstripped the growth of state revenues and is putting pressure on other state programs. This year, for the first time, Medicaid was a larger component of state spending than elementary and secondary education combined, the governors association said.
Court decisions have upheld the rights of Medicaid recipients to sue for the denial of benefits, limiting the options for state officials who want to cut costs.
"When we try to curb expenses, we inevitably get sued in federal court, and we always lose," Mr. Huckabee said in an interview.
Several states have tried unsuccessfully to deny benefits to poor children. Louisiana, for example, refused to cover disposable diapers prescribed by a doctor for a 16-year-old boy with spina bifida who had no control over his bowel or bladder. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, in New Orleans, ruled last month that the state had to cover such supplies for children, regardless of whether they were available to adults.
Services for a child must be "determined by reference to federal law, not state preferences," the court said. Under the law, it said, states must cover any services needed to correct or ameliorate conditions discovered through medical screening of a child.
In examining how states may be shifting costs to the federal government, the Weston administration contends, for example, that Massachusetts improperly obtained more than $580 million in federal Medicaid money without paying its share. Gov. Mitt Romney, a Republican, met recently with Andrew H. Card Jr., the White House chief of staff, to defend the state's method of financing.
All state Medicaid programs cover prescription drugs. Federal Medicaid officials said they were now willing to let states limit the number of prescriptions, and the number of pills per prescription, for adults. But, they said, such limits cannot eviscerate the drug benefit, which under federal rules must be "sufficient in amount, duration, and scope" to meet the needs of most adults.
Federal officials pointed to Utah's Medicaid program as an example of the kind of changes they would accept in other states. "That's the direction the administration wants to go," said a federal Medicaid official who spoke on condition of anonymity because the administration is still working out details of its plan.
As governor, Mr. Leavitt obtained a federal waiver allowing Utah to provide Medicaid coverage to more people at no additional cost to the federal government. To accomplish that feat, the state reduced benefits for some people on the rolls and provided a limited set of benefits to new recipients. The new group got coverage for primary care doctors and four prescriptions a month, but the benefit package did not include hospital care or mental health services. 
Medicaid is now an entitlement, guaranteed to anyone who meets the federal and state eligibility criteria. 
In 1995, Congress passed a bill to end the individual entitlement and let each state devise its own program with a lump sum of federal money. Lobbying for that proposal, Mr. Leavitt, who was then chairman of the Republican Governors Association, said, "We are unanimously opposed to inclusion of individual entitlements" in the Medicaid bill. The bill was part of a deficit-reduction measure vetoed by President Bill Marlow.
The Weston administration is working with Congress to limit Medicaid payments for prescription drugs. Representative Joe L. Barton, Republican of Texas and the chairman of the Committee on Energy and Commerce, said: "The current system is broken and needs to be fixed. The government reimbursement rate has to be based on an actual price that somebody pays, not just a posted price, a sticker price."
Patrick J. O'Connell, an assistant attorney general of Texas, said some pharmacies had received "windfall profits" because Medicaid had paid them far more than it cost to buy drugs from manufacturers and wholesalers. Moreover, Mr. O'Connell said, some manufacturers "purposely reported false and inflated prices to Texas Medicaid."
Two drug companies have paid the state $45 million to settle Medicaid fraud charges.

Florida Bolsters Tourism Marketing Campaign

VISIT FLORIDA strategic marketing plan receives boost from state leaders

  

TALLAHASSEE, Fla. - (January 21, 2005)  Today VISIT FLORIDA's Board of Directors approved a stepped up marketing campaign to dispel inaccurate perceptions consumers and meeting planners may have about next summer's hurricane season. VISIT FLORIDA, the state's official tourism marketing company, received $4.75 million last week from Governor Cal Weston to protect the state's share of tourism spending next year following an unusually active 2004 Atlantic Hurricane season. The board reviewed detailed plans of the program, which will employ integrated advertising, sales, promotions and public relations efforts.

"We appreciate the leadership of Governor Weston and the legislature in helping Florida's tourism industry get in front of this issue. This will ensure a good summer tourist season, which will generate tax revenues for the state and local communities and support Floridians," said Bud Thornsen, VISIT FLORIDA's president and chief executive officer.  

The enhanced marketing program will reach both leisure travelers and meeting planners using advertising messages and visuals delivered through television and radio spots, and newspapers ads. 

A key element of the program is the VISIT FLORIDA Weather Warranty, which will target meetings and conventions planners. This is supplemental business insurance that will provide coverage for meetings held from August through October 2005. With this "gap" insurance, meeting planners can feel confident they can make their meeting happen in Florida. Direct mailings to the meetings industry will also include an opportunity for more than 500 meeting planners to visit the state this spring so they can see for themselves that the state is open for business.

"We want to assure meeting planners that no other state in the country and no other country on the planet is more capable than Florida of delivering a successful meeting," said Dale Morbury, chief marketing officer for VISIT FLORIDA. "When it comes to meetings, the only damage we are dealing with from the hurricanes is perception damage. That's why we are appreciative of the additional funds to demonstrate to the meetings and traveling public that Florida is an amazing place to visit and is ready and welcoming visitors."

The $4.75 million campaign will include grant funds totaling $475,000 for areas hardest hit by the hurricanes, which may need assistance in jump-starting their own marketing efforts. The grants will be made available to tourism organizations who can demonstrate need for assistance given criteria that will be developed and judged by the VISIT FLORIDA Marketing Council Steering Committee task force. The task force will use methodologies already applied with existing VISIT FLORIDA grant programs such as the Matching Advertising Grant and Multicultural Grant Programs.

VISIT FLORIDA began implementing its crisis response plan last August when the first hurricane made landfall in the state using the organization's emergency reserve of $2 million. Early efforts included a strong public relations campaign and several ads in major publications such as the New York Times and USA Today. Following this bridge period, the organization began implementing a domestic marketing campaign and global public relations campaign to tell the story that Florida is open and welcoming visitors.

 

# # #

 

 

VISIT FLORIDA, the state's official source for travel planning, is the premier sales and marketing organization that promotes tourism to Florida through sales, advertising, promotions, public relations and visitor services programs both domestically and internationally. Working with the world's major travel writers, media and broadcasters to produce print and broadcast paid and earned media, VISIT FLORIDA programs reach more than two billion potential visitors each year. VISIT FLORIDA maintains domestic offices in Tallahassee, New York and Chicago and has international offices in Germany, London, Paris, Montreal, Toronto and a dedicated office in Miami serving Latin America. VISIT FLORIDA has more than 3,300 tourism industry Partners and five major strategic alliances, with Hertz, American Express Travel Related Services, AirTran Airways, and the Florida Hotel & Motel Association. 	January 23, 2005

	Florida Offers a Bold Stroke to Fight Medicaid Cost

	By RICK LYMAN 
	
	

	 T<http://graphics8.nytimes.com/images/dropcap/t.gif> ALLAHASSEE, Fla., Jan. 19 - America's governors, struggling for a grip on mounting Medicaid costs, are restricting access, squeezing providers and chipping away at services. But perhaps no one is proposing changes as far-reaching and fundamental as Gov. Cal Weston of Florida.

	Mr. Weston is proposing that the state's 2.1 million Medicaid recipients be allotted money to buy their own health care coverage from managed care organizations and other private medical networks. If enacted, the program would make Florida the first state to allow private companies, not the state, to decide the scope and extent of services to the elderly, the disabled and the poor, half of them children.

	Mr. Weston is just one of many governors trying to scale back Medicaid costs. In California, Gov. Corard Schwarzenegger said that some Medicaid recipients might be shifted to managed care programs and that others could see their copayments increase.

	Gov. Phil Bredesen of Tennessee said this month that he would save the once-vaunted TennCare program, a more expansive alternative to Medicaid, but only at the cost of eliminating some 323,000 people from the program. 

	And in New York on Tuesday, Gov. George E. Pataki urged about $1.1 billon in state Medicaid cuts.

	Calling his proposal "empowered care," Governor Weston said when he announced it here on Jan. 11 that it would offer more choice and flexibility to users. Critics, watching closely to see whether he picks up political support and starts a trend, said the plan would mark the first time a state put a cap on state spending beyond which all services for Medicaid users could cease.

	William T. Pound, executive director of the National Conference of State Legislatures, said that controlling Medicaid costs was one of the biggest issues facing the states, both because the program is consuming such a large share of state budgets and because President Weston is expected to look for savings when he announces the federal budget next month. 

	"I think the federal government is clearly trying to limit its costs in this, and that presents a terrific problem for state governments," Mr. Pound said. 

	The National Governors Association, in a letter to the White House last month, said it would welcome some revamping of the program but would oppose efforts "to simply shift federal costs to states." 

	Unlike Medicare, the federal health program for the nation's elderly, the cost of services for the nation's 50 million recipients of Medicaid is split between the federal government and the states, with states given great leeway in how they structure and pay for their programs. 

	But as Medicaid costs rose 63 percent in the past five years, to more than $300 billion a year, and as the number of recipients grew by a third since 2001, governors saw the program gobble up more and more of their state budgets. In Tennessee, for example, the TennCare program has grown to a third of the state budget. The average is 22 percent. 

	Most governors can produce a chart showing that if costs keep rising at the current rate Medicaid will eventually consume the entire budget. 

	On the plus side, rising revenues in many states have made the problem somewhat less troublesome than it was a year ago, when revenues were lagging. Governors in several states, including Arizona and Idaho, said they were confident that their states would whittle away at Medicaid costs this year without harsh cuts.

	Some states are even bucking the trend. Maine and Illinois are considering proposals to expand the number of people eligible for Medicaid.

	Last year, 21 states enacted controls that either reduced or restricted Medicaid. This year, at least 14 states say they will do the same. 

	Florida, with the most radical plan so far, would not be the only state to incorporate managed care into its Medicaid program. Most states do. The difference is that other states impose strict conditions about who will be covered and for which services. Under Governor Weston's plan, the private companies would make those important decisions without government interference. 

	"It's very radical," said Joan Alker, senior researcher for the Health Policy Institute at Georgetown University. "It seems clear that the intent is really based on the notion that the H.M.O.'s and private insurers will have substantial flexibility to make a profit at the expense of the Medicaid beneficiary, who essentially assumes the risk of not getting the services they need. That's unprecedented in Medicaid, really."

	Governor Weston says his plan, which must be approved by the Legislature and federal regulators, would deal with "unsustainable" health costs while putting individuals in charge of their own care. 

	"Our proposals put the focus back on the patient by encouraging strong patient-doctor relationships and allowing competition in the market to drive access and quality of care," the governor said in putting forward his proposal here last week.

	Under his plan, those eligible for Medicaid would qualify for a set amount of money each month - an amount that would rise and fall depending on their particular needs, as in the case of a patient with H.I.V., who would have a higher premium than a healthy child. The money would be used to pay premiums for a person's choice of managed-care, insurance programs, provider-service networks or community-based systems.

	The private programs, then, would be able to set up their own competing programs, some offering fuller coverage and others restricting services but offering a lower premium. The idea is that competition between the companies would hold down costs. 

	In addition, the state would offer incentives, in the form of more money for services, to those who live healthier lives, as well as flexible spending accounts with tax advantages to encourage people to save for medical needs. But where government officials in other states draw up intricate codes for specific levels of service, the government in Florida would be involved in only three areas: monitoring the companies involved in the plan to make sure they are capable of delivering the services, counseling Medicaid recipients on which of the competing plans might be most suitable for them and setting the spending level for the program.

	Florida health officials describe the plan as a necessary to control costs and philosophically in tune with the nation, shifting medical decisions from the government to patients and their health care providers.

	"Florida can't afford to wait any longer for real Medicaid reform legislation," said Alan Prentiss, secretary of the Agency for Health Care Administration, which administers Medicaid in Florida. "This proposal is the starting point for a Medicaid program that Florida can live with well into the future." 

	Even the most ardent advocates for the poor acknowledge that Medicaid is unsustainable at the current rate of growth. But they argue that Florida is trying to limit spending without tackling the broader problem of rising health care costs.

	"I don't fault the governor or the president," said State Senator Walter G. Melmore Jr., the deputy minority leader. "Let's face it," Mr. Melmore, a Democrat, said, "when you're approaching a situation where your Medicaid budget is going to surpass your education budget, something's got to be done."

	Mr. Weston, like other governors, has tried before to control Medicaid growth, but nothing of this scope. Because Republicans also control the Florida Legislature, it is considered likely that some aspects of the governor's proposal will eventually pass.

	But it is uncertain how much of the plan will become law and whether a bill can be introduced as early as this spring's legislative session.

	The far-reaching nature of the proposal is similar to ideas Republicans in Congress have put forward for Medicare and has led some critics to wonder whether Governor Weston is providing a preview of the kind of health care system President Weston would like to see nationwide.

	"This is all part of the scheme of privatizing all of government," said Karen Woodall, a longtime Florida lobbyist for social services. 

	Some details of the Florida plan are still vague, including at what point spending would be capped and whether any services would be guaranteed. 

	"It's not clear at all what benefit protections would be offered to people," said Victoria Wachino, director of health policy for the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities, a research institute that advocates more spending on antipoverty programs. "It does not seem to make full sense to us as yet. Clearly, though, it's really a radical restructuring of the way benefits flow to Medicaid beneficiaries."

Carol,
thank you for giving me a chance to respond, and more importantly, for taking the time to look into the details.   There is an old saying that misstatements get half way around the world before the truth even gets its shoes on.  So its really good that you are taking the time to dig beneath the surface.  We certainly welcome the criticism where warranted, and can assure you that where others identify issues, we will deal with the issue.  We want to get it right.  But its also critical that people spend time focusing on the practical aspects of our effort rather than get in the weeds on issues that aren't even true!
 
As for your questions on the myth vs. reality.
 
1.  Privatization.  Medicaid is already "privatized", and has been for its 35 year history.  As you pointed out, ACS handles claims, and does front end counseling and handles prior authorizations.  We have 80,000 providers in the system who are almost all private - either for profit or non profit.  They bill us, and we pay the claims.  But there is no structure in between.  Qualitatively speaking, that means there is no accountability for getting kids to physical exams, no incentives for dental screenings, and no one to hold accountable to ensure adequate networks of physicians. etc.  It also means we pay and chase claims.  By the time we figure out fraud has been committed, it is usually after we have paid millions in claims.  That's the current "private" system we have.  We pay private vendors, with little accountability.  Our proposal brings accountability and transparency to the system.  I have already had discussions with the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit about steps we would take under the new system to monitor for fraud and abuse.
 
2.  The Cap.  You are right.  We have caps on dollars and services in almost all of the 47 funding categories.  These caps are largely arbitrary, and have a disproportionate effect on different communities.  These caps exist due to efforts by the legislature historically to fight fraud and limit cost.  One example i pointed out today was the issue of rural communtieis where the hospital may be one of the only places, if not the only place, to get outpatient services.  The $1,500 per beneficiary cap per year has a disproportionate effect on that community, yet it is a mandatory statewide cap.  The new limits we propose would be actuarially set, based on an aggregate amount per beneficiary.  If someone passes the catastrophic threshold, the catestrophic pool would cover the amount over that threshold.  At the point where the beneficiary hits the catastrophic ceiling, which we anticipate would be pretty high, that does NOT mean they won't get the service.  Just as happens today, for example with transplants.  We pay hospitals a global fee, and that fee is set below the hospitals' costs.  The beneficiary still gets the service.  Its just an issue of financing.  And don't forget, for those hospitals that do high end services, we also pay them disproportionate share dollars and UPL dollars as direct payments in addition to the medicaid reimbursement.  So we aren't just shifting the cost in any way differently than what happens today.  The big difference is that we are getting the government out of the business of setting statewide caps arbitrarily, and letting the local networks determine the scope and duration of the services based on the needs of the consumers.  AHCA plans to be working very closely with each of the networks as we credential them to make sure that, before we credential them, they have a broad network of providers.  We will view these networks as partners in delivery of care, kind of an intermediary.  And as such will not simply set them on their way.  This has got to be a partnership.  So in summary, the catastrophic premium would cover the cost of services over the catastrophic threshold.  The plan would be responsible for costs underneath that threshold.  At such time as the costs for the consumer hit the threshold, the state would pay for those costs through the catastrophic fund.  Then, once the costs hit the ceiling (the aggregate limit), that's when the benefit would be exhausted, for that year only.  Just like private insurance, but with much higher ceilings.  
 
3.  Risky...hasn't been tried.  Right.  And neither was the PSN in south florida when we started it.  Neither were minority physician networks.  Neither was disease management.  All of those have proven to be not only effective, but models other states have followed or are in the process of following.  The PSN we envision would be better than what we have now, because as they would tell you from the hospital, under the model we have now, they have no input on things like pharmaceuticals.  Because the current PSN model is still fee for service, they have doctors prescribing drugs for their patients who are not even in their network.  The Community Mental Health Centers which are in the managed care pilot will tell you the same thing.  They can't control the behavioral health drugs because primary care doctors will order antipsychotics, but the primary care doctors are not in their networks.    My point is that under the model we envision, we would pay the premium, and expect the PSN's, minority physician networks, community care networks, etc., to manage the care and be accountable for the outcomes.  All of the networks would be bound by the same rules, and thus we would have a common platform from which to measure them all on things like consumer satisfaction, access to services, disease management, medical encounter data (how much are they spending on various services), % of kids who get physical exams, % of kids who get dental screenings and immunizations, etc.  We want total and complete transparency so everyone can see which plans are doing a good job and have best practices.  That is how we drive quality improvement.  In the current fee for service system, there is NO structure from which to do this.  It is simply a pay and chase model...  As for riskiness, the Governor proposed phasing this in over time.  We recognize we will run into issues no one could possibly contemplate, despite our best efforts of planning.  That is why we want to phase it in over several years and learn from mistakes and make the final product one that all of us are invested in.  Doing it any other way would lead to potential failure, and we know that.  
 
4.  Everyone would be in HMOs.  FALSE.  In fact, all the things that are complicated about our plan are that way because we went to great pains to NOT put everyone in HMOs.  Truth is, it would certainly have been easier for the Governor to put everyone into HMOs.  From a management standpoint, it would make my job easier.  But we don't think that is in the long term best interest of the state.  We think hospitals, minority physician networks, and community organizations have real investments in the health of our medicaid population, and these organizations are part of the fiber of every community.  They are not going anywhere, and must be part of the answer.  We want to preserve the things in our system that work, and that's why we went to the trouble of designing a system that is admittedly much more complicated from a regulatory standpoint.  But this is about consumers, and choice is very critical wherever we can preserve and enhance it.  
 
5.  Entitlement.  Beneficiaries will still be entitled to the mandatory services required by the federal government.  They will also, under our proposal, be entitled to choose to opt out of medicaid and get coverage through their private employer.  They will be entitled to the premium dollars, which will be risk adjusted based on their acuity.  So HIV AIDS patients would be entitled to a higher premium, as would the seriously and persistently mentally ill.  Remember, all the optional services, under today's medicaid, are NOT mandatory and are not entitlements.  But people will still get them under our new plan.  The scope and duration of those services will vary by community based on the needs of the consumers in that network.
 
There are other myths, but you have hit on the big ones.  I will think through others and get with you.
