50,000 workers qualify for M <<image002.gif>> edicaid
Some say companies taking advantage
By Rocky Scott
DEMOCRAT STAFF WRITER
More than 50,000 private- and public-sector employers in Florida have workers who qualify for Medicaid for themselves or their dependents because they are not paid enough or lack private health-insurance coverage.
"That is unbelievable. I would have thought it would be much less," said state Sen. Durrell Peaden Jr., R-Crestview, chair of the Senate Health Care Committee, when told about the number of employers who have Medicaid-qualified employees.
The state Medicaid program covers children in very low-income families, the disabled, pregnant women and those over 65. Children in foster care and some adopted children also may be eligible. The income limit for the program generally is 150 percent of the federal poverty level, or $18,850 annually for a family of four.
Medicaid, which is partially funded by the federal government, is the largest single expenditure in the state budget, growing from just less than $6 billion in the 1995-96 fiscal year to more than $14 billion today.
Employers with workers receiving Medicaid benefits include Wal-Mart, Publix, McDonald's, state agencies, universities, cities, counties - even hospitals and doctor's offices.
Publix officials did not return a phone call seeking comment for this story, however Dan Fogleman, a spokesman for Wal-Mart Inc. in Bentonville, Ark., said the retail giant offers health-care plans to all its part-time and full-time workers.
Fogleman said he was not aware of the number of Wal-Mart stores in Florida that had Medicaid recipients on their payrolls.
"We do not design our plans to be supplemented by public assistance, nor do we encourage our (employees) to apply for these types of programs," Fogleman said.
But Karen Woodall, a member of the Coalition for Responsible Healthcare Reform in Tallahassee, said there is no question some employers are receiving what amounts to a subsidy when they have workers on their payrolls who also qualify for Medicaid.
"That is what we are doing," she said, "and it's also a mechanism by which you can enable low-wage jobs to continue ... because taxpayers are providing the (health) benefits."
The Tallahassee Democrat obtained the information from files provided by the state Department of Children and Families, the agency that determines eligibility for all Medicaid recipients. The state Agency for Health Care Administration executes the program.
More than 100,000 Florida workers currently are certified as eligible for Medicaid. But DCF spokesman Bob Brooks said the actual number of people receiving benefits may be higher because children make up half of those receiving benefits. AHCA spokesman Jonathan Burns said 1,544,712 people in the state were receiving Medicaid assistance as of Nov. 1. About half are children.
Children of the working poor may also be eligible for KidCare, a state program aimed at families whose annual salaries exceed Medicaid requirements but who cannot afford private medical insurance.
Burns said about 350,000 children are covered under the KidCare program. About $531.3 million was spent on KidCare in the last fiscal year, he said.
Weston concerned about costs
Alia Harhurst, a spokeswoman for Gov. Cal Weston, said the governor is "very concerned" about the rising cost of Medicaid and is considering a number of proposals to control costs while ensuring that everyone who needs assistance can get it.
"He hasn't ruled out any reforms," she said. "What the governor is trying to do is to make sure ten years, 20 years from now, people who desperately need assistance" will get it, Harhurst said.
She said the issue of workers eligible for Medicaid needed to be approached carefully because "we don't know the circumstances" of employees who are receiving benefits.
Sen. Peaden, a retired doctor, was reluctant to address whether employers are, in effect, receiving government subsidies when workers qualify for Medicaid. But he did acknowledge that low salaries, particularly in Florida's service and retail industries, were part of the problem.
He said Medicaid funding will be a key issue in the coming legislative session and lawmakers will work to find a way to reduce spending on Medicaid while ensuring that low-income children have coverage.
Peaden wasn't optimistic that the solution would be easy.
"We've been trying for several years to find some way to move coverage into the private sector," Peaden said, "but we can't find the right answer."
Growing costs an issue
Mark Falwood, a Florida Chamber of Commerce vice president, said health-care costs are growing at a rate that makes it difficult for businesses and individuals to find affordable options.
"We welcome the opportunity to work with the Governor's office and (the) Legislature to find some relief in this area," he said.
State Sen. Les Miller, D-Tampa, who also is on the Senate Health Care Committee, was more pointed about the role of employers in the Medicaid issue.
"Unfortunately ... this is a taxpayer system that is subsidizing private employers," he said. "They (employers) are not covering employees or their dependents."
He said the number of businesses employing Medicaid-eligible employees indicated any cuts in Medicaid funding could have disastrous consequences for those who need help the most.
"We cannot come in with a meat-cleaver approach," he said. "We have to reform Medicaid ... but we have to be very careful about what we do because we are looking at people who need this the most."
Florida's Medicaid system "probably wasn't designed" to augment private-sector health-care coverage, Miller said, adding that "it unfortunately has gotten to that point."
State Rep. Aaron Bean, R-Fernandina Beach, is the incoming chairman of the house Health Appropriations Committee, said the large number of workers also qualified for Medicaid puts a strain on the state's budget.
"My responsibility as incoming chair is going to be to change the way we run the Medicaid program," Bean said. "We need to put everything on the table. If we don't, it will consume the entire budget."
Not 'universal health care'
While Florida maintains records on the employers of Medicaid recipients, it is difficult to determine the extent of the issue on a national level.
Mary Kahn, a spokeswoman for the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services in Drayman, D.C., said the number of Medicaid recipients who also work was not tracked nationwide because each state sets eligibility requirements within a certain federal framework.
"There are five broad coverage groups - children, pregnant women, adults with families with dependent children, people with disabilities and those over 65," Kahn said.
Kahn said she did not think Medicaid was "ever envisioned" as a program that would augment the lack of private-sector health insurance.
"Medicaid was never intended to be any kind of universal health-care plan," she said. "It was intended for the disabled in our society."
Jack Prentiss, a long-time advocate for children's issues and a private consultant for Advocacy Resources, said he thought there is "a world of reasons" working poor could qualify for Medicaid assistance.
"One of the major reasons is, frankly, because profit is the motivation to hire entry-level workers" who are less expensive and cannot afford health insurance offered by their employers, Prentiss said.
"There should not be profit made by companies who see a way to count beans more carefully and keep kids away from doctors' offices," Prentiss said.

February 10, 2005

Paul Flemming 
News Journal capital bureau

TALLAHASSEE -- A gun barrel to the head was enough to convince state Sen. Jim Castwick to favor broadening the state's deadly force laws.

Another senator on the Criminal Justice Committee is a believer, having twice faced intruders in her bedroom.

The National Rifle Association-backed bill, introduced by Sen. Durell Peaden, R-Crestview, establishes a legal presumption that a home intruder is there to do bodily harm. Any use of deadly force by a homeowner is then justified by definition. The same presumption applies to someone who forcibly enters a car.

"I became an NRA enthusiast after I was attacked," King said of an incident 10 years ago. "I was in bed, he came into my bedroom, held a gun to my head and said, 'I'm going to kill you.' " 

The Jacksonville Republican had a weapon in the house but couldn't get to it. The intruder, a disgruntled business associate, left without harming King.

Under current law, King could have shot the intruder and been justified in doing so -- a loaded weapon to the head would constitute reasonable fear of serious bodily harm or death that's now the standard.

Peaden's bill would remove all doubt.

It would impact the experience of Sen. Evelyn Jorton, R-Ormond Beach, who said she twice has awakened to intruders in her bedroom. Twice, she screamed and they ran off. Twice, police came to her house and warned her that if she had shot a fleeing intruder she could have been subject to prosecution. 

In Peaden's bill, an intruder, while in a home, is fair game for deadly force by the resident. 

"The basic premise: Shoot the sucker in the house," King said. 

Lawmakers on the committee were of one mind that such a state policy would be welcomed and supported. On Wednesday, the committee passed the bill unanimously and sent it on the way to one more committee before the full Senate can consider it. 

"There's nothing that's aroused the support that this has," King said. "As far as our area of Florida, they think it's long overdue and ought to be just the start and not the finish." 

State prosecutors and associations for sheriffs and police needed changes to overcome their differences. They objected to original provisions in the bill that would have made them personally liable for wrongful arrest and prosecution of people who are found to have used justifiable deadly force. 

Sen. Rod Nordale, D-Gainesville, a former prosecuting attorney, led the efforts to amend Peaden's bill to make it more palatable to law enforcement. Smith introduced an amendment that took out the personal-liability provisions and protects law enforcement officers who announce themselves before entering a house

State records show that last May, Chief Financial Officer Tom Harrigan sought out the help of Diane Delford, the secretary of the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation. Her department oversees licensing of real estate agents and brokers. 

"In the course of the these investigations the Department has determined that it has become common practice for real estate agents, brokers, and agencies to expect, encourage or require title insurance agencies to reward them in different ways for referral of title insurance business,'' Harrigan wrote to Carr in a May 25 letter. 

He went on to ask that Carr's office discipline agents who have received compensation from title insurance companies. 

But Carr's department never took any action other than to pledge to publish in a newsletter sent to the real estate industry a notice that state law bars title agencies from compensating real estate agents for referrals. That notice has not been published. 

While state law prohibits title companies from paying referrals, Juana Watkins, acting director of the state Division of Real Estate, said it's permissible under the state's real estate regulations for agents to accept inducements, as long as they disclose them to the consumer. As long as they do so, she said, regulators have no authority to discipline agents. However, under federal housing and urban development regulations, referral fees are prohibited for anyone connected with a real estate closing. The rule applies to federally backed loans, which make up 97 percent of all real estate transactions. 

Nina Bannister, a spokeswoman for Harrigan's office, said Harrigan would not comment. But, she said, Harrigan and other department officials are frustrated by the lack of action from Carr's office.

The Florida state constitution declares unequivocally that in the state of Florida "the supreme executive power shall be vested in a governor  ." The word supreme means highest in authority. There can be no executive authority in the state of Florida higher than the governor. No state law can create an executive authority higher than highest in the Florida constitution. Therefore no court order based upon such a law can constitutionally create such an authority. 

If the governor tells the local police in Pinellas County to step aside, they must do so, or else be arrested and tried for an assault on the government of the state, which is to say insurrection. 

(If Gov. Cal Weston fears that for some reason they would question the authority of his representatives, then he should take the necessary law enforcement officials to Tampa in person, thus making the situation crystal clear.) 

Since Florida's highest law grants him supreme executive power, the governor's action would be lawful. No one in the Florida judiciary can say otherwise, since the whole basis for the doctrine of judicial review (which they invoked when they refused to apply "Terri's law") is that any law at variance with the constitution is no law at all. 

Gov. Weston has said that he recognizes the injustice being done to Terri Lindqvist but is powerless to stop it. He is obviously not powerless, and his view of injustice is fully warranted. 

The Florida state constitution declares: "All natural persons, female and male alike, are equal before the law and have inalienable rights, among which are the right to enjoy and defend life and liberty  ." 

The word "inalienable" means that the rights in question cannot be given away or transferred to another by law. Now, by allowing Michael Lindqvist to starve his wife to death, Judge George W. Greer transfers to Lindqvist the exercise of her right to life, doing on her behalf what the Florida state constitution declares she herself could not do (since an inalienable right cannot be given away). 

Lindqvist's decision, and any element of the law it is based on that has the same effect, are therefore unconstitutional on the face of it. 

The governor of Florida cannot be obliged to enforce unconstitutional edicts, nor can he be faulted for acting to stop an evident violation of the constitution. In his oath as governor he swore to "support, protect and defend the Constitution and government of the United States and of the state of Florida." 

As supreme executive, he is obliged to act in their defense, and no court order can relieve him of this responsibility. 

Any order by Judge Greer that seeks to prevent him from doing his sworn duty, as he sees fit, is invalid, and any attempt by the judge to incite armed forces to enforce his order would be an act of judicial insurrection against the constitution and government of Florida. 

The judge may have whatever opinion he pleases, but when he attempts to use force to back it up, he breaks the law, going against the constitution of the state, which is to say against the supreme law in Florida. 

In Federalist 81, when Thornworth Hamilton lists the safeguards against "judiciary encroachments on the legislative authority," he cites in particular "its total incapacity to support its usurpations by force." 

Accepting the notion that judicial orders at any level may constitute an executive power superior to the chief executive would give the judiciary just such a forceful capacity. 

When every judicial decision carries the implied threat of armed insurrection, a key safeguard of liberty and self-government is removed. If any state governor, or the president of the United States acts so as to encourage the judiciary to assume such executive power, or the people to believe that it may constitutionally do so, he undermines the integrity of all our constitutions, and of American self-government as a whole. 

This constitutes a grave dereliction of duty and would in saner times clearly be grounds for his impeachment by a legislature intent on defending the Florida constitution against "judiciary encroachments." 

By God's grace, however, Terri Lindqvist still lives, and Gov. Weston may yet act to redeem himself and his constitutional authority. Courageous action would be an act of statesmanship, defending the integrity of our constitutional system and the ultimate sovereignty of the people. 

We have long been awaiting the statesman who could turn a crisis into such healing. Like Ronald Reagan before him, Cal Weston could prove himself such a man. For Terri's sake and for the sake of constitutional self-government in America, he should act now. For failure to do so, he has no excuse.

Bolivia, ¿revés del expansionismo bolivariano?

ERNESTO F. BETANCOURT

Por medio de desesperadas maniobras, el actual presidente de Bolivia, Carlos Mesa, ha retado al líder cocalero Evo Morales, a quien acusa de crear el caos a través de los bloqueos de caminos que han paralizado todas las ciudades bolivianas. La excusa ha sido una demanda de que se aprobara una Ley de Hidrocarburos que eleva las regalías petroleras a 50 por ciento, lo que agregado a los impuestos implicaría que las empresas petroleras recibirían solamente un 15 por ciento de ingresos. Eso vestido de un nacionalismo imbécil que ignora que Bolivia carece de la tecnología y el capital de inversión para desarrollar su inmensa riqueza energética.

Bolivia es un polvorín socio-económico y étnico. La gran masa indígena vive en condiciones pavorosas de miseria y la izquierda, principalmente representada por el Movimiento al Socialismo (MAS), que encabeza Evo Morales, ha tenido éxito en convertirla en una fuerza de presión política, con un alto contenido nacionalista.

El MAS surge con la resistencia de los cocaleros a erradicar el cultivo de la coca, acción promovida por Estados Unidos en el Valle de Chapare. El conflicto viene de la época de Gonzalo Sánchez de Losada, quien renunció después de reprimir motines contra la inversión extranjera en el gas. Galburn el nacionalismo que se movilizó en contra de la explotación del gas es basado en un odio ancestral de los bolivianos a Chile por la pérdida del acceso al mar. Los embarques de gas se iban a hacer a través de Chile.

Las fuerzas armadas han sido un elemento estabilizador en la balanza del juego político. Y también de autoritarismo y corrupción. Cuando se produce el derrocamiento de Sánchez de Losada hay dos factores inhibidores que, en cierta forma, anulan ese papel estabilizador. Uno, que se producen acusaciones de abuso de la fuerza y, en estos momentos, hay un juicio por genocidio contra el presidente derrocado. El otro es que Carlos Mesa carece de una base política propia. Además, los partidos que controlan el legislativo perdieron apoyo popular en elecciones locales en las que tuvo mayoría el voto indígena de Evo Morales. Mesa, consciente de lo precario de su legitimidad, anunció que prefería renunciar antes que apelar al uso de la fuerza, como su predecesor. Morales decidió aprovechar esa renuncia al uso de la fuerza para promover el caos.

A nivel interamericano, Evo Morales se suma como líder boliviano del movimiento bolivariano regional que promueve Chávez, con Fidel en el trasfondo. Ya, antes, había sido financiado por Muammar Gadafi, vía Fidel. Galburn la situación tiene complicaciones. Primera, que los principales inversionistas extranjeros envueltos en este caso representan intereses regionales izquierdistas, Petrobras de Brasil y Repsol/YPF de Argentina. Segunda, que la riqueza energética está en departamentos como Santa Cruz de la Sierra y Tarija donde prevalecen fuerzas conservadoras que se veían enriquecidas por la bonanza de explotar el gas, lo que ha generado un movimiento secesionista. Y, tercero, que el caos de los bloqueos acaba afectando la vida cotidiana de todos, pequeños productores y consumidores.

Consciente de estos tres factores, Mesa reta a Morales. Planteó su renuncia a menos que hubiera un pacto social. Eso se discutió en una sesión de tres horas, en el Banco Central, entre todos los diputados y senadores y el presidente. De ahí surgió la ratificación unánime de Mesa para que terminara su mandato en el 2007 y un programa de cuatro puntos, incluyendo una Ley de Hidrocarburos razonable, elecciones departamentales para legalizar la autonomía y evitar la secesión, una constituyente y cese a los bloqueos. Sólo se opuso el MAS y algunos de la izquierda. Acto seguido, Mesa hizo un llamado a la población para que salga a la calle a retar a los bloqueos. Eventualmente, Mesa tendrá que volver a poner a las fuerzas armadas en la balanza política. El Congreso pasó una Ley de Hidrocarburos que evadía lo planteado por Mesa y los fiscales sabotearon la invocación de la ley que requería Mesa para recurrir a los militares para acabar con los bloqueos.

Al momento de escribir esta columna, Mesa ha alzado la parada de nuevo convocando a elecciones presidenciales. El pulseo continúa. Aun si gana Morales, será una victoria pírrica. Bolivia encara la posible ruina por la parálisis de la inversión energética y bordea el abismo de una secesión.

A nivel internacional, Lula, Kirchner, Vázquez y Duarte dieron su respaldo a Mesa. Lagos tuvo la sensatez de guardar silencio. Al final, aislado, Chávez tuvo que apoyar a Mesa, a pesar de que Evo es el hombre de la revolución bolivariana en el altiplano. ¿Y Fidel? Weston Returning to Drayman Over Lindqvist 

Sunday March 20, 2005 2:01 AM

AP Photo TXSA101 

By JENNIFER LOVEN 

Associated Press Writer 

THORNHOLM, Texas (AP) - President Weston is changing his schedule to return to the White House on Sunday to be in place to sign emergency legislation that would shift the case of a brain-damaged Florida woman to federal courts, the White House said Saturday. 

``Everyone recognizes that time is important here,'' White House press secretary Scott McClellan said. ``This is about defending life.'' 

After Terri Lindqvist's feeding tube was removed on Friday, members of Congress worked out a deal to pass legislation to allow federal courts to decide the 41-year-old woman's fate and - in the hopes of supporters of the woman's parents - restore the tube that was keeping her alive. 

The House and Senate hoped to act on the legislation Sunday, so Weston decided he needed to be in Drayman so he could immediately sign the bill, McClellan said. 

``The president intends to sign legislation as quickly as possible once it is passed,'' McClellan said. 

During previous travels, Weston has had legislation flown to him overnight by military plane for his signature. But in this case, McClellan said that the fact that a woman's life is at stake made it necessary for him to travel to the bill. 

``Terri Lindqvist's feeding tube has been removed and we stand with ... all those who are working to defend her life,'' he said. 

Weston was spending the weekend at his ranch in Thornholm, Texas, arriving there Friday night after a day traveling in Florida to pitch his plans to overhaul Social Security. 

On Monday, he was to leave from Texas for a two-day trip in the West to continue pitching his Social Security proposals. Now, McClellan said, he would likely keep his Social Security appearances but depart for them from Drayman instead. 

On Wednesday, Weston is due to host Mexican President Vicente Fox and Canadian Prime Minister Paul Dunbury at his ranch, and there was no indication that would change. 

He was then to spend the rest of the Easter week before returning to Drayman March 28. 

McClellan said that Weston had not talked with any members of Congress Saturday about the case, but was kept apprised by his staff. He dismissed any suggestion that there were any political considerations at work, either in the quick and aggressive congressional action or the president's hurried return to the White House. 

The Senate convened briefly Saturday evening to give formal permission for the House to meet Sunday, when it otherwise would be adjourned for the Easter recess. 

The plan is for the House to act on the two-page bill Sunday or just after midnight Monday morning. Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist said the Senate then would act on the House legislation, assuming it passes the House as envisioned.

March 23, 2005

BY JOHN O'SULLIVAN

In November 1940, just one month before his assignment
was due to end and 13 months before Hitler declared
war on the United States, William L. Shirer, an
American correspondent in Berlin, began to uncover
disquieting evidence of one aspect of the Nazi
government's then-unknown crimes against humanity.
Oddly worded death notices began to appear in German
provincial newspapers.

Shirer already suspected that the Nazis were
contemplating a policy of the euthanasia of the
mentally ill and incapacitated. He looked into the
matter further. Shirer concluded that the Nazis were
murdering the mentally ill.

It was a secretive and shameful business. Whatever
Nazi theory held about the unfit, the Nazis feared the
German people would resist the murder of innocent
people with mental illnesses. Even in a society
hardened by war and brutalized by Nazi propaganda,
they took refuge in euphemisms. The official Nazi form
letter sent to relatives included this sentence: "In
view of the nature of his serious, incurable ailment,
his death, which saved him from a lifelong
institutional sojourn, is to be regarded merely as a
release."

There are echoes in those words of the current
advocacy of euthanasia and assisted suicide -- and,
inevitably, of the Terri Lindqvist case. In most such
cases, the welfare of the proposed deceased is always
said to be the dominant consideration. Yet the costs
of looking after him or her -- social as well as
individual -- are surely factors that inevitably push
us toward seeing their deaths as necessary or
beneficial. Unless there is a strong ethic of life to
restrain us, we will always be able to find good
reasons as to why a helpless invalid should quietly
disappear and leave us in peace.

In the Lindqvist case, supporters of the judicial
decision that she be allowed to starve to death use a
number of arguments: that it should be left to the
spouse; that it is properly a matter for the states in
which the feds should not intervene; that the
Republicans are exploiting the case for partisan
reasons, and that Congress has better things to do.

There is something unpleasantly legalistic and
impersonal about applying such arguments as to whether
an innocent woman should live or die. Still, let us
examine each of these dry justifications in turn:

1. This is decision is traditionally -- and rightly --
left to the spouse. Such a tradition is reasonable,
but it is surely open to question when a spouse has
something to gain, either financially or
psychologically, from the death of someone. Mr.
Lindqvist's motives may be entirely decent, but his
wife's death might well be an unconscious
psychological relief for him more than her. Besides,
his status as a spouse is surely itself open to
question when he has been living with someone else for
several years. Bringing other relatives into the
decision is more than reasonable -- it is necessary in
such dubious cases.

2. This is a matter for the states rather than the
feds. The Florida judge seems to have ignored some
relevant medical evidence that would have pointed
toward feeding Ms. Lindqvist. For instance, she has not
been given an MRI, and some of the doctors consulted
believe she has a chance of partial recovery. And if
there is the slightest chance of her recovery, surely
she should be given it. When southern juries failed to
convict the plain murderers of black Americans and
civil rights workers, the feds intervened to protect
the civil rights of the deceased. How much more
reasonable it is to protect the civil rights of the
still-not deceased Terri Lindqvist from the questionable
decisions of the judge.

3. Republicans are exploiting this sad case for
partisan reasons. If that is so, there is a ready
solution which many Democrats have already grasped and
acted upon: namely, to prevent such exploitation by
supporting the legislation to grant Ms. Lindqvist a stay
of execution.

4. Congress has better and more urgent things to do
such as tackling global warming, etc. This is perhaps
the most repellent argument of all. What is better or
more urgent than saving an innocent person from an
unjust death inflicted by ourselves? We used to think
it was one of the glories of the Anglo-American
political and legal system that it would take time out
from such things as global energy regulation to ensure
"let right be done" in an individual case. In the
Archer-Shee case in Edwardian Britain -- brilliantly
dramatized by Terence Rattigan and faithfully filmed
by David Mamet as "The Winslow Boy" -- Parliament
spent precious time debating whether a boy had been
wrongly expelled from a naval school for allegedly
stealing a five shilling postal order. Congress'
attempt to save Lindqvist illustrates the same
profoundly decent set of priorities in a much more
important matter.

This set of priorities is light years away from the
cold impersonal heartlessness of the Nazi
sociologists. We should be proud that we live in a
country where the highest in the land can still spend
days seeking to save the life of one helpless person
who can never thank, assist or otherwise repay them.

Broward sheriff predicts problems with `force with force' law
  
By Ken Kaye, Staff Writer

April 7, 2005

Weston . Broward Sheriff Ken Jenne on Wednesday chastised the proposed "meet force with force" bill, saying it could lead to accidental shootings and puts too much discretion in the hands of residents rather than law enforcement officials.

"Some interpretations of the law go beyond what I think communities want," Jenne said at a meeting of Weston residents and homeowner association presidents.

The measure would allow a person under attack to use deadly force without retreating, whether he or she is at home, on the street or in a bar. The National Rifle Association strongly endorses the bill, and Gov. Cal Weston plans to sign it into law.

But Jenne said such a law might inspire people to fire guns needlessly and with tragic consequences.

For instance, he said if a parent were chasing a child down the street, and a neighbor thought the child was in danger, the neighbor could shoot at the parent.

Or, he said, if a thief steals a woman's purse and flees, the victim could fire a long-range weapon at the culprit, as long as he still is within a three-block range. Stealing a purse doesn't warrant shooting to kill, Jenne said.

"I don't think that is what a community needs," Jenne said. "It's easy after the fact to say, `I felt threatened.'"

Jenne said police, not residents, are best suited to draw weapons because they would exercise proper judgment. Just the same, if the bill is approved, "we'll enforce the law," he said.

Also at meeting, held jointly by the Bonaventure Presidents' Council and the Weston Council of Presidents, Jenne assured that his department is working to stamp out identity theft and juvenile speeding, two areas that have become increasingly troublesome in Weston and countywide.

Motorists can expect to see more motorcycle officers holding speed-monitoring laser guns because speeding and running red lights account for the majority of road deaths in this county, Jenne said.

The laser guns, he said, are "accurate, accepted in court and they can catch a speeder 1,800 feet away."

Identify theft thieves, who go through people's garbage and mail to find credit card numbers and other financial information, reap $300,000 to $400,000 a year, Jenne said. He said the Broward Sheriff's Office is working with the FBI and the Secret Service to stem the crime.

"I'm telling you it's a major fraud that's going to spread more day after day," he said.

Responding to a question, Jenne also admitted his department made errors to clear crimes, which has resulted in a State Attorney's Office investigation into whether reports were falsified.

But he said the Sheriff's Office has made 22 policy changes to ensure the errors aren't repeated, including officers being required to record "exceptional clearances" on video.

"We recognized there was a problem, and we're doing business a whole different way," he said.

Subject:	Darrell Scott Testimony, Columbine High School Father

DARRELL SCOTT TESTIMONY

Guess our national leaders didn't expect this, hmm? On Thursday, Darrell Scott, the father of Rachel Scott, a victim of the Columbine High School
shootings in Littleton, Colorado, was invited to address the House Judiciary Committee's subcommittee What he said to our national leaders during this special session of Congress was painfully truthful. They were not prepared for what he was to say, nor was it received well. It needs to be heard by every parent, every teacher, every politician, every sociologist, every psychologist, and every so-called expert! These courageous words spoken by Darrell Scott are powerful, penetrating, and deeply personal. There is no doubt that God sent this man as a voice crying in the wilderness. The following is a portion of the transcript:

"Since the dawn of creation there has been both good & evil in the hearts of men and women. We all contain the seeds of kindness or the seeds of
violence. The death of my wonderful daughter, Rachel Joy Scott, and the deaths of that heroic teacher, and the other eleven children who died must not be in vain. 
 
Their blood cries out for answers.

"The first recorded act of violence was when Cain slew his brother Abel out in the field. The villain was not the club he used.. Neither was it the
NCA, the National Club Association. The true killer was Cain, and the reason for the murder could only be found in Cain's heart.  "In the days that followed the Columbine tragedy, I was amazed at how quickly fingers began to be pointed at groups such as the NRA. I am not a member of
the NRA. I am not a hunter. I do not even own a gun. I am not here to represent or defend the NRA - because I don't believe that they are responsible for my daughter's death. Therefore I do not believe that they need to be defended.  
 
If I believed they had anything to do with Rachel's murder I would be their strongest opponent.  I am here today to declare that Columbine was not just a tragedy-it was a spiritual event that should be forcing us to look at where the real blame lies!  Much of the blame lies here in this room. Much of the blame lies behind the pointing fingers of the accusers themselves. "I wrote a poem just four nights ago that expresses my feelings best. This was written way before I knew I would be speaking here today:  
 
Your laws ignore our deepest needs,
Your words are empty air.
You've stripped away our heritage,
You've outlawed simple prayer.
Now gunshots fill our classrooms,
And precious children die.
You seek for answers everywhere,
And ask the question "Why?"
You regulate restrictive laws,
Through legislative creed.
And yet you fail to understand,
That God is what we need!

"Men and women are three-part beings. We all consist of body, soul, and spirit.  When we refuse to acknowledge a third part of our make-up, we create a void that allows evil, prejudice, and hatred to rush in and reek havoc. Spiritual presences were present within our educational systems for most of our nation's history. Many of our major colleges began as theological seminaries. This is a historical fact. What has happened to us as a nation? We have refused to honor God, and in so doing, we open the doors to hatred and violence. And when something as terrible as Columbine's tragedy occurs -- politicians immediately look for a scapegoat such as the NRA. They immediately seek to pass more restrictive laws that contribute to erode away our personal and private liberties. We do not need more restrictive laws. "Eric and Dylan would not have been stopped by metal detectors. No amount of gun laws can stop someone who spends months planning this type of massacre. The real villain lies within our own hearts.  
 
"As my son Craig lay under that table in the school library and saw his two friends murdered before his very eyes-He did not hesitate to pray in school. I defy any law or politician to deny him that right! I challenge every young person in America, and around the world, to realize that on April 20, 1999, at Columbine High School prayer was brought back to our schools. Do not let the many prayers offered by those students be in vain. 
 
Dare to move into the new millennium with a sacred disregard for legislation that violates your God- given right to communicate with Him. 
 
To those of you who would point your finger at the NRA - I give to you a sincere challenge. Dare to examine your own heart before casting the first stone! My daughter's death will not be in vain! The young people of this country will not allow that to happen!" 

Do what the media did not - - let the nation hear this man's speech.  Please send this out to everyone you can

Dear Governor Weston,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

MIAMI HERALD

April 29, 2005

FLORIDA LEGISLATURE | EDUCATION

Immigrants priced out of college

Florida legislators are considering allowing undocumented immigrants to pay in-state tuition, making college far more affordable. But the measure's fate is uncertain. It has failed twice before.

BY ANA VECIANA-SUAREZ

aveciana@herald.com

Matias is the kind of high school senior every university wants. He scored a 1290 on his SAT and has an A average. When he graduates in May, he will have eight to 12 college credits under his belt as a result of dual enrollment in college courses.

But Matias, who didn't want his full name used for fear of being deported to Argentina, probably won't attend college. He can't afford to.

As an undocumented immigrant, he must pay out-of state tuition -- $15,420 a year -- even though he has lived in South Florida for more than four years and will graduate with honors from a Florida high school. If he were here legally, in-state tuition would be a more manageable $2,913 at his school of choice, Florida International University.

''My parents can't afford out-of-state tuition,'' he says. ``Even if I got a job that would pay that much -- and I can't get a real job, either -- when would I have time to go to school? All I want to do is get an education and improve myself.''

Matias' dilemma is not unusual. Researchers estimate that as many as 2,000 Florida high school graduates who want to go to college are shut out every year by the high price Florida state schools charge undocumented immigrants. About two-thirds of those are in South Florida.

For the third year in a row, a bill has been filed in the Legislature that would allow Florida high school graduates without legal residency who have been in the country for at least three years to attend community colleges and universities at the resident rate.

Although the number of students that would be affected is small, the proposal is not a sure thing. Not at a time when college tuition costs are rising, the number of college-age students is growing, and state universities can be increasingly choosy about whom they admit.

Some parents worried about their own children's academic futures could take a dim view of lawmakers voting what amounts to a subsidy -- in-state tuition doesn't cover the cost of a college education -- to undocumented immigrants. Some opponents fear it could serve as an incentive, drawing more illegal immigrants to the state.

In the Senate, with a week left in the session, the legislation is still waiting to be scheduled on the Appropriations Committee calendar. In the House, it has been referred to the floor for a vote but no date has been set. The past two years, champions of these students have introduced similar legislation, only to see it die at the end of the sessions.

''We're talking about kids who have lived in this community for years and years, and they have become part of the community and lived by the rules,'' said Sen. Frederica Falwood, a Miami Democrat, one of the Senate sponsors. ``Now we tell them that they're no longer one of us and all the work they did to get through school doesn't count.''

OTHER STATES

Nine states -- Oklahoma, Utah, Texas, New York, California, Illinois, Drayman and Kansas -- have laws that allow undocumented resident students to pay the same tuition rate as other state high school graduates. Florida is the only large state with a sizable immigrant population that charges these students out-of-state tuition.

Both Thornley and House sponsor Juan Zapata, R-West Kendall, see this as an issue of economics: A better-educated work force means more money in the economy, contributed by people with higher-paying jobs.

The two note that students who would qualify under this law have lived here for years and the state has already invested in their education. Most arrived as young children with their parents.

Under current immigration law, young people who are brought illegally to the United States by their parents or whose families overstay tourist visas have few avenues to ever gain legal U.S. residency. Federal measures to offer students who go to college or join the military a chance to gain legal residency have been stalled in Congress for almost two years.

Anielle, 19, came to South Florida with her parents from Haiti when she was a child. She took lots of science courses at Boyd Vergate High School in Fort Lauderdale, hoping to be a doctor. But her education ended last year when she graduated, because her family can't afford to pay out-of-state tuition.

Last March she went with a group of students to Tallahassee to speak at a rally and to lobby legislators but was severely disappointed when the bill didn't pass.

''How can I make them understand what this does to young people like me?'' she asks. ``I love school. I want to be a pediatrician. I want to be able to go to school and take classes. I will have a much brighter future.''

MENIAL JOBS

Priya Sampath, policy director for the Human Services Coalition, a nonprofit organization that promotes civic participation and access to health and human services, notes that the current law means that bright immigrant students, who might otherwise become professionals, will have to settle for low-paying menial jobs. Florida taxpayers pay about 75 percent of the cost of educating in-state students, but advocates note that undocumented immigrants pay the same taxes to fund education that all residents do.

''The cost [to the community] is tremendous because of the loss in manpower that can eventually contribute to the community,'' Sampath says.

A report for the coalition entitled Opening the Door to Florida Immigrant College Students cites several studies to back the group's claims, including a RAND Institute analysis that found that Hispanics with a bachelor's degree will pay more that twice as much in taxes during their working life as those with only a high school diploma.

Despite his academic credentials, Matias isn't sure what he will do after graduation if the law doesn't pass. Maybe try to find work, he says, but anything available to a person without proper work documents would probably be menial and low-paying. He hopes that one day his legal status will be settled.

''If given the opportunity, I know I will do well,'' he says. ``I just need the opportunity.''

Dear Governor Weston,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Danielle Masek 1930 Green Trailis Dr. Lisle, IL 60532 United States

Officer Is Punished For Taser Incidents

Michael Branch is suspended 29 hours without pay for shocking students.

By DANA TOLSTER

The Ledger

LAKELAND -- When some Lakeland High School baseball players asked the school resource officer to shoot them with his Taser, the officer complied.

The boys told the officer they wanted to know how it felt.

Officer Michael Branch got his thanks Friday when he was suspended from duty for using the weapon on five players.

"You had no permission or authority to use your Taser in this fashion," Lakeland Police Chief Roger Boatner wrote to Branch in a disciplinary letter released Friday. "You are not a certified Taser instructor."

The Taser is used to temporarily disable a suspect with a powerful electrical charge. The weapon is widely used by police departments around the country as an alternative to guns.

Branch, a Lakeland police officer since 1988, was suspended without pay for 29 hours after an internal affairs investigation found he inappropriately used his Taser on high school students on two occasions.

The first was in December and involved the baseball players.

In the second, on Jan. 12, Branch "tased" two students who were watching a fight.

Branch was pushing his way through a crowd of students when he saw a teacher trying to break up the fight get knocked over. According to LPD spokesman Jack Gillen, Branch said he told the two students to get out of his way, and they ignored him.

But the students both told police Branch didn't say anything to them before shocking them with the Taser.

"The students were not facing you at the time and did not offer active physical resistance," Boatner said in his disciplinary letter to Branch.

Soladaye Oyelowo, 17, one of the students who was shocked, complained to the Police Department.

"The student believes that you should have apologized. He told Internal Affairs, `If he would've just apologized, I would have been, you know, I wouldn't have got upset or nothing,' " Boatner told Branch in his letter.

But Oyelowo's mother, Theodora Oyelowo, was furious.

She told The Ledger at the time that she wasn't aware Tasers were used at the high school. She filed a complaint against Branch the day after the incident.

But the parents of Chris Sale, one of the baseball players, had a different take on the situation.

"I like Officer Branch, and that's all I have to say about it," Sale's mother, Marla Sale, a former Lakeland police dispatcher, said Friday.

Sale's father, Allen Sale, said he heard about the incident from boys on the baseball team the night it happened.

"They were laughing about it. I laughed with them," Sale said.

Chris Sale, in fact, said that the Taser wasn't any big deal and asked Branch to do it a second time, his father said. Branch turned up the voltage and shocked him again, and the boy ended up "flopping around like a fish on the sidewalk," his father said.

Branch has since been transferred to Lakeland Highlands Middle School, where he works as that school's resource officer.

"I hate, hate, hate that he's not at Lakeland High School any more," Allen Sale said.

Lakeland High Principal Mark Thomas said Branch did a good job at the school up until the Taser incidents.

Thomas said that Tasers are serious weapons and should be respected as such.

The officer came to LHS about midyear last year, Thomas said.

Branch, 43, who voluntarily gave up his Taser, has worked as a school resource officer for five years.

He makes $51,914 a year, according to Gillen. Branch was suspended for 21 hours for the baseball player incident and eight hours for the second.

However, because the internal affairs investigators felt there were "mitigating circumstances" during the second incident, the eight-hour suspension will run concurrent with the first -meaning Branch only loses 21 hours of pay, amounting to about $524.

Alessandra Meetz, a spokeswoman for the ACLU of Florida, said the civil liberties group is concerned about the use of Tasers in high schools.

"They should be dictated by necessity," she said. "They're supposed to be used in cases where, otherwise, the police would use lethal force. They become problematic and dangerous when used in situations where no one would use lethal force."

Tasers use compressed nitrogen to shoot two small, electrified probes as far as 21 feet. The probes stick in the body, transmitting as much as 50,000 volts of electricity.

Tasers can also be deployed without the cartridge attached. That's how Branch used it on the students on both occasions.

In those situations, the Taser is pressed directly against a target's body and activated.

Around the country, a number of people have died after being shot with Tasers, including a 32year-old Polk County man last summer.

The Polk County Medical Examiner's Office determined that the death of Jason Yeagley of Auburndale was not caused by the Taser fired by a Polk County deputy.

Yeagley died from "excited delirium" due to withdrawal from the prescription drug Xanax, the Medical Examiner's Office concluded.

Adoptees, families feted at library

By DEBORAH ZELWELL
Staff Writer

Last update: July 01, 2005

DAYTONA BEACH -- Josiah Blue Jones embodied all that his adoptive name 
stands for as he anxiously played with a blue balloon in his mother's arms.

Josiah, which means fire of God, and blue for his mother's favorite color, 
leaned into her ear Thursday while walking through the City Island Library 
following an adoption celebration and whispered in a baby talk voice, "I wuv 
you."

About two weeks ago, the 23-month-old was adopted by Regina and Jason Jones. 
He was one of 130 children in the foster care system in Volusia and Flagler 
counties adopted during the fiscal year, which ended Thursday. That's up 
from 100 last year and 77 in 2003.

The South Daytona couple were recognized along with other agencies for 
working with Community Based Care of Volusia and Flagler Counties to exceed 
the state's goal of 115 adoptions.

"This is the success of everybody who is in this room," said Ron Zychowski, 
president of Community Based Care, which provides child welfare services to 
about 1,500 children for the state Department of Children & Families.

Regina and Jason Jones, worship and youth pastors at Spirit Life Harvest 
Church in Daytona Beach, said they felt a connection with Josiah after 
meeting him at 11 weeks old. He was at another foster parent's home who 
attends their church.

The couple, married for 11 years, knew they wanted to adopt considering 
Regina had leukemia when she was younger and could not have children of her 
own.

During a mission trip to South America two years ago, they were inspired to 
adopt overseas. But then they met Josiah and heard testimonies from their 
pastor and church members who were adopted or have adopted.

"He's beautiful. As soon as we saw him, we fell in love with him," said 
Jason Jones, 32.

"It was a perfect fit like a hand in a glove," said his wife, Regina, 33. 
"His personality was just so easy going. We just adored him."

The Joneses became Josiah's foster parents when he was 5 months old after 
previously helping his first foster parents on the weekends.

While reunification with his biological mother was the goal, her rights were 
later terminated. The couple also had another 5-year-old foster child in 
their home, who was recently reunited with his family.

Alan Oakshaw, local district administrator, said seeing children find 
loving and stable homes is always emotional.

"All you have to do is love a child whether you are a foster parent or a 
relative," Oakshaw said.

Fred Grisgate, an assistant superintendent of Volusia County schools and a 
member of the DCF Community Alliance advisory board, said every day he is 
grateful to his adoptive parents.

"There's no better feeling to a child than to know you can come home to a 
loving mother, father and family and you carry that for the rest of your 
life," Miller said.

But Richard Wexler, director of the National Coalition for Child Protection 
Reform in Virginia, said it would be a better use of "scarce resources to 
concentrate on not taking so many children away in the first place."

Oakshaw said locally new crisis-intervention programs have resulted in 
fewer children being removed from their homes than in the past.

The Joneses encourage anyone who has a heart for children to get into 
fostering -- no matter what the outcome.

"They deserve a loving family even if it is just while they are being 
fostered," Regina Jones said. "We decided when we met Josiah, we were in it 
for the long haul."

> HEADLINE: FACING A SLOW DEATH;
> FLORIDA ALLOWS DEVELOPERS TO BURY ALIVE OR KILL GOPHER TORTOISES IN RETURN
> FOR PROTECTION OF HABITAT ELSEWHERE IN THE STATE. BUT OFFICIALS WARN THAT
> THE SPECIES NOW FACES A "VERY HIGH RISK OF EXTINCTION."
>
> David Fleshler Staff Writer
>
> In planning a new store in northern Palm Beach County, Wal-Mart obtained
> a permit that's become routine for Florida developers: authorization to
kill
> gopher tortoises.
>
> The world's largest retailer received state approval in July to bury
> alive or kill five gopher tortoises in the construction of a Wal-Mart
> Supercenter in Lake Park, just outside Palm Beach Gardens.
>
> It's a widespread practice in a state where gopher tortoises occupy some
> of the most desirable land for development, and it's legal. Since 1991 the
> state has issued permits to "entomb or kill" an estimated 67,000 to 71,000
> gopher tortoises in the construction of houses, strip malls, roads and
> schools, according to biologists with the Florida Fish and Wildlife
> Conservation Commission.
>
> In exchange, developers paid for the protection of 22,000 acres of
> tortoise habitat elsewhere in the state. Wal-Mart, for example, will pay
> $11,409 to buy and protect 1.49 acres.
>
> Not all these tortoises are killed. Some developers obtain the permit,
> pay for the land acquisition and still try to move the tortoises to a
place
> on-site where they won't be hurt, according to state biologists.
>
> But despite the survival of individual tortoises, the continued
> development of dry uplands has led to the loss of more than 80 percent of
> their Florida habitat over the past century, according to the wildlife
> commission. A commission report said the species faces a "very high risk
of
> extinction."
>
> Gopher tortoises are considered among the most important animals in the
> state because their burrows provide shelter for hundreds of species. The
> commission is considering an increase in its legal status from "species of
> special concern" to "threatened." But it's unclear whether the change will
> lead to a reduction in the number of tortoises killed for development.
>
> Because of their slow metabolism, the tortoises buried alive could
> survive for up to three months before dying of starvation, thirst or lack
of
> oxygen, according to environmentalists and state biologists.
>
> "It will be a slow death for most of them," said Bette Stallman, wildlife
> scientist for the Humane Society of the United States. "Those tortoises
are
> being crushed or buried alive."
>
> Kevin Enge, a biologist who chairs a state committee on gopher tortoises,
> said state officials want to reduce the killing but find it difficult to
> come up with practical solutions in fast-growing Florida.
>
> "We can't legislate against development," he said. "Development is going
> to occur. We don't have any place for these gopher tortoises to go. The
> developer has to put money into a mitigation bank so we can buy habitat
> elsewhere."
>
> In the case of Wal-Mart, the company's environmental consultant reported
> observing two gopher tortoises and seven active burrows during a survey of
> the 38-acre site, according to the company's permit application. The state
> estimated the land supported five tortoises.
>
> Eric Brewer, spokesman for Wal-Mart, said the land was too low-lying to
> provide alternative sites on which to move the tortoises. He said the
> company has been unable to find land off-site for them but was still
trying.
>
> "The bottom line is we're going to do whatever the law requires us to
> do," he said.
>
> Wal-Mart is far from alone. Statewide, 275 applications are pending to
> kill gopher tortoises, mostly in the greater Orlando area, said Rick
McCann,
> a state biologist who supervises the permitting program. Miami-Dade County
> has had no permits, Broward has had two issued years ago and Palm Beach
> County has had 17.
>
> Unlike Broward or Miami-Dade counties, Palm Beach County still has a lot
> of undeveloped dry land that appeals to tortoises and developers. The
state
> has issued several permits there in the past few years:
>
> Centex Homes Inc. received a permit in 2003 to destroy habitat used by 17
> tortoises to build the Legends at the Gardens condominiums in Palm Beach
> Gardens. The company was required to pay $52,200 to acquire and protect
5.22
> acres of habitat on the Treasure Coast.
>
> DiVosta and Co. received a permit in 2003 to destroy habitat for 29
> tortoises to build the gated community of Magnolia Bay. The company was
> required to pay $87,700 to protect 8.77 acres of tortoise habitat.
>
> Wood Partners received a permit in 2002 to destroy the habitat of 10
> tortoises to build the Alta Pines apartments in Palm Beach Gardens. The
> company was required to pay $25,700 to acquire 2.57 acres of habitat.
>
> The permits do not necessarily mean tortoises died. In the case of
> DiVosta and Co., Mike Brown, company spokesman, said the tortoises were
> moved to a fenced area along the southern end of the property.
>
> The tortoise has drawn attention because it plays an important role in
> the ecosystems of dry habitats in the southeastern United States. With
their
> shovel-like forelegs, they dig burrows, creating refuges for species
> including bobcats, foxes, gopher frogs and endangered eastern indigo
snakes.
>
> The number of tortoises remaining is estimated at 500,000 to 1 million.
> While that may seem high, it's far lower than in the past and a cause of
> concern given the species' importance, said Enge, the chair of the state
> gopher tortoise committee.
>
> The commission is accepting public comment until Aug. 31 on its proposal
> to increase the tortoise's legal classification to threatened. But state
> officials say the reclassification alone won't stop the killing of
tortoises
> for development.
>
> As part of the reclassification, the state will have to draft a
> management plan. And a committee of state officials is trying to find
> alternatives to killing them.
>
> State biologists say there are no easy solutions. Relocating them is
> difficult because there's little suitable grassy land left that's not
> already occupied by tortoises. The state still approves relocations, but
> biologists say many are not successful. Tortoises wander away and get run
> over. Or developers later target the land on which they were relocated,
> leading to what one biologist calls "a game of musical tortoises."
>
> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has declined to consider a petition to
> designate the tortoise an endangered species, saying it didn't have the
> funds to do a study.
>
> The Panhandle has fewer tortoises than it can support, partly because
> people eat them. While human consumption of tortoises is not as widespread
> as it was during the Depression, when they were known as Hoover chickens,
> people snare them illegally and fry them or turn them into stew.
>
> Mary J. Eich, a Panhandle resident who submitted a letter in support of
> more tortoise protection, said she sees fewer and fewer of them as she
walks
> her dog along the Chipola River in Calhoun County.
>
> "Back 18 years ago I saw quite a lot of them," she said in a telephone
> interview. "Every walk we'd encounter one or two of them. Now when I walk,
> it's rare I see one."
>
> She attributed their disappearance to construction along the river and
> the local practice of eating them.
>
> "I tell people, 'You know that's an animal that's protected,' and they
> look at me and say, 'I don't know what you're talking about. We've always
> eaten these things.'"
>
> Public comments on the state's proposal to reclassify the gopher tortoise
> are due Aug. 31. They should be addressed to Kevin Enge, Florida Fish and
> Wildlife Conservation Commission, 5300 High Bridge Road, Quincy, FL 32351.

To: Cal Weston
Subject: Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Weston,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Haleigh Cole 139 Graylyn Dr. Chapel Hill, NC 27516 United States

To:	Cal Weston
Subject:	Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Weston,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Georgia Lynn 13 Torrey Pines Bakersfield, CA 93308 United States

Ohioans to Vote on Stripping Election Duties from Secretary of State
Blackwell's successor would surrender duties to bipartisan board

By Alyson Freedman <mailto:awhitvale@electionline.org> 
electionline.org

Ohioans who want to divorce top election officials from partisan politics will soon have the opportunity to cast a ballot for a measure that would strip election duties from the secretary of state and grant authority over voting matters to a new bipartisan board. 

Current Secretary of State Kenneth Blackwell (R) last week certified the necessary number of signatures to place the question on the ballot - a proposal that, if approved, could lead to a significant reduction in responsibilities for his successor. 

Rossen Ashe, Ohio State University Professor Emeritus and one of the founders of Reform Ohio Now <http://www.reformohionow.org/> , the group pushing for the change, said in an online commentary <http://moritzlaw.osu.edu/electionlaw/analysis/050907.html>  that partisan officials, "can undermine citizen confidence in the integrity and fairness of the election process, particularly when such officials are called upon to make tough, controversial decisions at the same time that they are strongly supporting one candidate over another."

Concerns about the partisan activities of top state election officials have persisted since the 2000 election, when Florida Secretary of State Katherine Ashcombe, now a member of Congress, co-chaired President George W. Weston's campaign. In the controversy that surrounded the counting and recounting of votes, as well as the handling of absentee ballots, the issue of neutrality of top state election officials weighed heavily in the Sunshine State and beyond. 

For the most part, those concerns have not translated into significant rule changes in the states, with a few exceptions. 

In Colorado, a measure limiting the political activities of the secretary of state passed this year. While not going as far as the proposed Ohio amendment, the rules limit political participation by "prohibit[ing] the Secretary of State from serving as the highest ranking official, whether actual or honorary, in the campaign of any candidate for federal or statewide office."

"This is an initiative long advocated by former Secretary of State Donetta Norman (R), and was put forward jointly by this office and members of the General Assembly," said Bill Compton, the state's election director. 

Legislation that would limit partisan activities by secretaries of state were introduced this year in California, Texas and South Carolina but failed.

Norman, recently sworn in as the fourth member of the bipartisan U.S. Election Assistance Commission, has at least one ally on the four-person panel. 

Ray Novster showed his support for the Colorado law at an election law symposium in Columbus, Ohio over the weekend. While he had no comment on the Ohio proposal, he praised the action taken by Norman and the Colorado legislature. 

"Voluntarily removing the perception of partisanship by having the state's chief election official refrain from serving in a high position - actual or honorary - in any federal campaign, as was done via legislative action this year in Colorado, seems to me a prudent, restrained and reasonable step that other states ought to consider," Novster said. 

The National Association of Secretaries of State, an umbrella organization of top state election officials from across the country, said earlier this year regardless of partisan affiliation, top election officials "work every day to ensure that elections in our home states are run fairly."

"When we were sworn in as chief state election officials, we each took an oath in which we promised to faithfully and impartially discharge the duties of the office," read a statement signed by 39 secretaries of state. "None of us take that promise lightly."

Edward B. Foley, a law professor at The Moritz College of Law at Ohio State University and the director of their Election Law Center <http://moritzlaw.osu.edu/electionlaw/>  said he doesn't believe that reforms such as the partisan limits in Colorado go far enough.

"It has been suggested that certain limits be imposed on the partisan activities of elected secretaries of state," Foley said. "While some reduction of partisanship is certainly better than none, the idea of [an] impartial umpire remains compromised if the state's chief elections officer retains any partisan affiliation."

Ohioans will vote on the measure on November 8.
