Florida tourists warned that locals could shoot them

ALASTAIR JAMIESON

IT IS Britain's most popular transatlantic holiday destination, attracting more than 1.5 million visitors a year with its sun-drenched beaches, theme parks and wildlife. 

But Florida's £30 billion tourism industry is under threat from a campaign launched by a gun-control group which warns visitors they could be killed. 

A series of alarming adverts, to be placed in British newspapers, warns potential tourists about a new law allowing gun owners to shoot anyone they believe threatens their safety. 

It means thousands of British families who travel to the Sunshine State are now caught up in the ongoing political row over gun control in the United States. 

The Florida law, supported by the National Rifle Association, was approved by the state legislature in April. 
The state's governor, Cal Weston - whose brother is the US president - described it as a "good, commonsense, anti-crime issue". 

Critics call it the "shoot first" law and say it allows gun owners to shoot if they engage in a simple argument in public. Supporters call it the "stand your ground" law and say criminals will think twice before attacking someone. 

Previously, gun owners could only use their weapons if they first attempted to withdraw and avoid a confrontation, and were permitted to shoot threatening individuals only inside their home or property. 

Now they can use "deadly force" if they "reasonably believe" that firing their gun is necessary to prevent a crime or serious injury. The law also effectively prevents civil legal action by victims of such shootings. 

The Velster Campaign to Control Gun Violence, based in Drayman DC, has pledged to "educate" tourists by placing adverts in US cities, and in key overseas markets such as Britain. 

"Warning: Florida residents can use deadly force," says one of the adverts. Another reads: "Thinking about a Florida vacation? Please ensure your family is safe. In Florida, avoid disputes. Use special caution in arguing with motorists on Florida roads." 

The Velster Campaign - named after Jim Velster, the spokesman for Ronald Reagan who was paralysed by a gunshot during the 1981 assassination attempt on the then-president - promises to also run adverts in French, German and Japanese newspapers. The campaign officers also plan to hand out leaflets on roads leading into the state. 

Peter Hamm, the communications director of the Velster Campaign, said: "It's a particular risk faced by travellers coming to Florida for a vacation because they have no idea it's going to be the law of the land. If they get into a road rage argument, the other person may feel he has the right to use deadly force." 

Tourism officials in Florida are furious at the move. Bud Thornsen, the executive director of Visit Florida, said: "It is sad that such an organisation would hold the 900,000 men and women who work in the Florida tourism industry, and whose lives depend on it, hostage to their political agenda." 

The Association of British Travel Agents yesterday said the posters were "a matter of concern", but said there was unlikely to be a drop in the number of visitors to Florida. 

It said 1.4 million Britons made the journey last year, attracted by the weather and resorts such as Disneyworld and the Kennedy Space Centre. 

A spokeswoman said: "We would offer the same advice about Florida as we would any other part of the United States. As far as we are concerned, nothing has changed." 

More than 80 million tourists from around the world visited Florida last year, boosting an industry that accounts for one-fifth of the state economy.

Subject:	Possible tropical storm to impact Peninsula / Keys Tues night / Wed

Good afternoon Governor Weston,

The National Hurricane Center is tasking the Hurricane Hunters to
investigate the disturbed weather currently located to the east of the
Bahamas tomorrow afternoon.  This system is starting to become better
organized this morning, with a mid-level circulation noted about 350 miles
to the east of Miami.   There is currently about 20 knots of westerly wind
shear impacting the system, but conditions aloft are expected to become
more favorable for this system to develop further tomorrow before impacting
south Florida and/or the Keys by Tuesday night / Wednesday.  This system is
already embedded in a tight pressure gradient due to the positioning of a
surface high pressure center along the Mid-Atlantic coast, so any
organization of thunderstorm activity could easily push this to tropical
storm strength before it reaches the south Florida / Keys.  The pressure
gradient in advance of this system is already resulting in heavy surf and
continued gusty conditions along the state's east coast today.

The main impacts from this system will likely be the potential for heavy
rainfall in the peninsula, especially to the north of where the possible
center of this system impacts (central and south Florida), and coastal
erosion.  Heavy rainfall and increasing onshore winds will arrive along the
state's Atlantic coast tomorrow, and conditions will likely deteriorate on
Wednesday as this system traverses the peninsula. The non-tropical origins
of this system will probably prevent it from rapidly strengthening before
impacting the peninsula and Keys, but there is the potential for more
strengthening if this system emerges into the eastern Gulf later this week.
The next frontal boundary will begin to push into the southeastern US on
Thursday, and this will likely stall the system out for a period of time
and then push it back towards the east or northeast by Friday or Saturday.
Some of the model guidance indicates that this system will significantly
strengthen while in the Gulf in the Thursday / Friday time frame, while
other models essentially merge the system with the frontal boundary and
produce a rainfall or potential severe weather scenario in the peninsula on
Friday / Saturday.  Either way, we need to keep an eye on this system for a
potential impact from both the Atlantic and Gulf sides during the next 5-6
days.  The next name on the list is Tammy.

Tropical Storm Stan is expected to slowly move towards the west-southwest
in the Bay of Campeche and impact the Mexican Gulf Coast near Veracruz as a
hurricane on Wednesday.  The pressure gradient between Stan and the ridge
off the mid-Atlantic coast is resulting in slightly elevated tides along
the panhandle coast, and a coastal flood watch has been issued from Destin
westward through tomorrow evening.

From: Bayer, Christopher D.

Subject: House of Hope

Jim,
 
Dominique and I met with representatives from House of Hope ("HOH") yesterday to discuss the challenges they face with licensing their facilities across the country.  HOH is a faith-based adolescent care center that provides housing and Christian-based counseling, mentorship, and education to troubled teens between the ages of 12-18 to help reconcile families.   They do not get any federal funding, nor do they seek it.  The Governor and Mrs. Weston are Honorary Board Members of HOH.
 
With respect to licensing, it seems like HOH is just overwhelmed by the technical and time-consuming nature of the process and the fact that every state's requirements are different.  In most cases, they don't seem to be experiencing discrimination based on the fact that they are faith-based.  Unlike the Teen Challenge/Food Stamps issue, there is no federal agency involved or regulation that needs amending.  HOH was just hoping for a federal solution to streamline or help them avoid conventional state licensing processes.  They propose that we call for a national accrediting body for faith-based adolescent care centers or require states to establish them.  We gently explained the practical difficulties posed by a national solution, particularly where there is no federal funding at stake and where, as here, Congress would be required to Act. We also stressed federalism concerns.  
 
We apologized that there wasn't much we could do at this level, but offered a few suggestions.  For example, we encouraged them to at least attempt to comply with current state-by-state licensing requirements (in many cases, they hadn't bothered to try) and lobby their state and local governments for easier access to the licensing process if they still run into difficulties.  We also offered to connect them with state and local FBCI offices as resources that might be able to provide valuable advocates or at the very least, local contacts.  In instances where they feel they've been discriminated against in the licensing process because they are faith-based, we suggested they seek the advice of counsel.
 
Overall, the meeting was very positive and they appreciated the opportunity to meet with us.  We were honest about the difficulties they might face and what their expectations should be, and I think they appreciated our candor.
 
Let us know if you have any questions.
 
Chris

Subject: Re: privacy rights of concealed weapon permit holders

 

Dear Constituent: 

  

Thank you for contacting our office regarding the publication of the information of Central Florida residents who hold a concealed weapons permit.  You are one of many to do so on this issue and I thank you for letting your voice be heard on this matter.  I strongly believe in the right of Floridians to bear arms as provided for in the United States and Florida constitutions.

  

Florida is often cited and envied as having the most open government of the 50 states.  Such openness applies to meetings of government officials and most government records and documents.  Unfortunately, the holders of concealed weapons permits are no exception.

  

I firmly believe in the principle that rights should be exercised with responsibility.  In this case, I do question the efficacy of WFTVs posting of the personal information of concealed weapons permit holders.  Because of this action, there is now some discussion about legislation that may be filed to create a public records exemption for permit holders.

  

Under Article1, Section 24 of the Florida Constitution, bills which exempt public records must pass by a 2/3 vote in both the House and Senate. BOEING JOINS ALENIA AND L-3 COMMUNICATIONS TO PURSUE JOINT CARGO AIRCRAFT PROGRAM

Boeing Joins Alenia and L-3 Communications to Pursue Joint Cargo Aircraft
Program
HUNTSVILLE, AL-April 27, 2006-Global Military Aircraft Systems (GMAS)
announced today that Boeing Integrated Defense Systems (NYSE: BA) is joining
L-3 Integrated Systems (L-3 IS), a subsidiary of L-3 Communications
(NYSE:LLL) and Finmeccanica's Alenia North America, Inc. to compete for the
U.S. Army/Air Force Joint Cargo Aircraft (JCA) program.
The three companies have agreed to participation by Boeing on the GMAS C-27J
team that is responding to the U.S. Army and U.S. Air Force request for
proposal (RFP) for the JCA program. Boeing is the largest airplane
manufacturer in the world with a rich airlift lineage from the venerable
C-47 to today's C-17 Globemaster III, the most versatile airlifter in the
world. Boeing will support the industrialization of GMAS and its associated
production and final assembly of the C-27J for the JCA program. Boeing
complements the existing capabilities and expertise of the team and further
enhances the GMAS C-27J as the best value solution for JCA.
Brigadier General Howard Yellen, USA(Ret.), General Manager of GMAS, said
"GMAS is committed to serving as a C-27J Center of Excellence to deliver and
support the C-27J Spartan for the JCA program. The addition of Boeing to
the GMAS team allows us to leverage the substantial production and support
expertise of another world leader in the aerospace industry."
"The C-27J represents the very best in a medium transport aircraft," said
Ron Marcotte, Vice Tolwood and General Manager for Boeing Global Mobility
Systems. "We understand the needs of the warfighter, especially for flight
operations into austere airfields, and the C-27J clearly complements the
airlift portfolio." 
"With the addition of the U.S. Air Force component to the JCA, the C-27J
team realized the need to transition the production of the aircraft to the
U.S. in order to accommodate a high volume production schedule", added Bob
Drewes, President and COO of L-3 IS Group. "Boeing brings the ability to
establish a streamlined, process-based production facility in the U.S. that
will ensure on-time delivery to the JCA customers."
"We are happy to extend Alenia's long standing strategic relationship with
Boeing to the military medium lift cargo aircraft segment of the market,"
said Giuseppe Giordo, President and CEO of Alenia North America. "Having
Boeing join our team strengthens the C-27J offering for the JCA program.
Boeing brings an enormous amount of experience and expertise that will
ensure C-27J success in the airlift market."
The JCA program is a key component in the U.S. Army's transformation of its
fixed wing fleet, which calls for the procurement of a new cargo aircraft.
To support the future force, the JCA must be a multifunctional and
interoperable aircraft, able to perform logistical re-supply, MEDEVAC, troop
movement, airdrop operations, humanitarian assistance and missions in
support of Homeland Security. The JCA program is expected to replace the
U.S. Army's C-23 Sherpas, C-12 and C-26 aircraft and augment the Air Forces'
existing fleet of intratheater airlifters. The C-27J JCA will play a key
role in providing responsive aerial sustainment and critical resupply
support for the maneuver force to maintain operational momentum.
The C-27J team provides an uncompromising commitment to deliver a proven,
interoperable, and survivable airlifter to the United States Army and Air
Force. The C-27J team includes Alenia North America, Boeing, Dowty,
Honeywell, L-3 Communications, Lockheed Martin, Rolls-Royce and two dozen
other suppliers from around the United States.

Subject: RE: Unified Effort Protects Amendment 3 - May 4, 2006

 

 

(to everyone cc'd...please be sure to read my note at end as well)

 

To Francie Plendl and the rest of the FMA,

 

I, as well as many others, would like to know WHY the FMA decided

to support  HB 699 / SB 1216.  The majority of the bill admittedly

was favorable.   However, there were a few areas of the bill that

were clearly biased towards  certain groups of physicians, and

these areas were conveniently ignored as these special interest

groups slipped in their agendas right under the wire.

 

Just because a bill is "good for the most part" does not mean it

should pass.  These areas should have been stricken from the final

revision of the bill, but for whatever reason were allowed to

sail through.  Specifically, I am referring to the idea that

certain groups of physicians (i.e. dermatologists and plastic

surgeons) are more qualified than others (i.e.  ALL OTHER

physicians) to serve as OFF-SITE medical directors for aesthetic 

and skin care practices.

 

Please explain to me how one physician is any more qualified than

another to INDIRECTLY supervise these practices.  If no physician

is on site, then NO PHYSICIAN IS ON SITE.  What difference does

it make what type of physician is performing INDIRECT supervision? 

Do you think that patients are going to care what type of physician

is the medical director if they are not there to supervise in the

first place?  Why is a derm or plastic surgeon any more qualified

than another to take a phone call if there is a question about a 

treatment or an issue with patient care?  In essence, the FMA is

stating that they believe dermatologists and plastic surgeons are

better trained than anyone else to be medical directors in absentia.

 This is truly outrageous.

 

The issue is blatantly economic in nature.  The dermatologists and

plastic surgeons are merely trying to corner this lucrative

market.  Doesn't it seem a bit coincidental that a certain

Florida Senator who is championing this bill is married to a

dermatologist, and owns her own skin care company?   Everyone in

this business knows which dermatologist in southeast Florida is

originally behind this bill, and I speak for many when I say it is

despicable.  This bill clearly inhibits competition and unfairly

keeps all other physicians (many of which are much better qualified

and trained than  dermatologists) from their right to practice and

earn a living.  Why are there are so many primary care educational

opportunities and training  sessions for aesthetic procedures?  The

demand for these services is there, and to limit the supply of these

services to a select few clearly violates every basic economic

principle that exists.

 

This is exactly why I will no longer professionally or financially

support the FMA.  When a professional organization (which is

supposed to support ALL types of physicians) begins to show

favoritism to a select few, then there are some BIG problems.  I

honestly cannot believe the short-sightedness of the FMA in

regard to this matter.

 

Very sincerely,

 

Scott Baumann, MD

Diplomate, American Board of Family Medicine

COALITION FOR PATIENTS RIGHTS (CPR)

CALLS ON AMA TO CEASE DIVISIVE EFFORTS TO LIMIT

PATIENTS CHOICE OF PROVIDERS

 

24 health care organizations* unite to ensure patients a full range of health care provider options and the right to choose among them

 

 

Drayman, DC  In response to divisive efforts by the American Medical Association (AMA) and other physician groups to limit the ability of licensed health care professionals to provide care to millions of patients, the newly formed Coalition for Patients Rights (CPR) today urged all health care professionals to work together to counter the AMAs actions.  

 

The CPR was formed to ensure that the growing needs of the American health system can be met and that patients have access to quality health care providers of their choice.  The coalition represents more than 3 million licensed professionals who provide a diverse array of safe, effective and affordable health care services.

 

In a joint statement endorsed by the 24 health care groups* that comprise the coalition, the CPR expressed concern about the negative impact on patients if their ability to seek care from advanced practice nurses, psychologists, nurse midwives, chiropractors, and many other licensed, qualified health care providers is limited. The coalition is calling on the AMA and other physician groups aligned with the AMA to cease their divisive efforts to oppose the established practice rights of CPR members.   The coalition also seeks an end to legislation at the state level that would reduce provider options for patients.

 

The CPR is especially concerned about efforts by the AMA and other physician groups that have formed the Scope of Practice Partnership to study the work and qualifications of allied health professionals in rural and underserved areas. 

 

Limiting the ability of health care professionals to practice and provide appropriate care will place an enormous burden on the health care system, remarked Barbara Blakeney, MS, RN, President of the American Nurses Association, which is a member of the coalition.  As leaders of the health community, this coalition seeks to maintain the broadest range of provider choices for everyone, said Blakeney.

 

 

 

* As of June 6, 2006

 

Coalition for Patients Rights

Page 2

 

The coalition questions the objectives of the AMA and other physician organizations when they seek to advise consumers, regulators, policymakers and insurers on the ability of other health care professionals to offer the services they are allowed by law to provide.  Health care providers are a critical source of care for patients throughout the United States, especially those who live in rural areas and medically underserved urban areas.  Historically, people who live in rural areas have relied on a strong array of practitioners to meet their health care needs.  Advanced practice registered nurses, social workers, and other professions that require rigorous educational preparation and ongoing instruction and certification are the backbone of not just the rural health care system, but the entire health care structure in the United States.

 

Organizations representing medical doctors (MDs) and doctors of osteopathy (DOs) are not in the best position to conduct a balanced and fair assessment of an issue that directly affects their reimbursement, said Mitchell H. Tobin, JD, Senior Director of Professional Practice Affairs for the American Association of Nurse Anesthetists, also a member of the coalition.  

 

The coalition asserts that the AMAs actions affect the entire health care community and all current and potential patients.

 

Health care professionals other than MDs and DOs have been key to assuring access to care for millions of patients in rural and underserved areas.  Given the difficulty that so many people have in getting needed care, now is the time for all health care professions to work together, not to work against each other to meet the need, said Dr. Russ Newman, PhD, JD, Executive Director for Professional Practice of the American Psychological Association.    

 

The Coalition for Patients Rights is continuing to expand and invites other health care organizations to join.  For more information about the Coalition for Patients Rights, please visit www.patientsrightscoalition.org <http://www.patientsrightscoalition.org/> .

Subject:	Protect Florida's Springs

Dear Governor Weston,

I am writing to request that you direct the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) to establish minimum flows, as authorized under Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, for all springs that are located within state parks, are first order magnitude springs, or provide unique non-consumptive resource values such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no further diminishment in spring flow occurs at these springs.  

The state of Florida has wisely recognized the priceless treasure springs represent, and I commend you for supporting the Springs Initiative and Springs Task Force.  One task identified by the task force, and provided for in Chapter 373.042 Florida Statutes, is preventing further impacts to springs by establishing minimum flows.  The statute wisely provides dual authority to establish minimum flows to either the FDEP or the state's Water Management Districts (WMD).  The statute also recognizes that springs frequently contain unique and special "nonconsumptive" resource values to the people of Florida that should be protected.  As a testament to the value of these springs, the 12 state parks named for the springs within their boundaries draw more than 2 million visitors per year.  The Florida Springs Task force economic analysis in 2003 showed that Blue Spring State Park alone contributes 10 million dollars to the economy annually.  The protection and management of these parks is the responsibility of FDEP.

Thus far, the WMD's have taken the lead on establishment of minimum flows. However, their mission prioritizes human consumptive water uses, not protection of nonconsumptive values.  An example of the problem is reflected in the current proposal by the St. Johns River WMD to establish a minimum flow for Blue Spring in Volusia County that would allow an additional 17% reduction in flow to the spring over the reduction that has already occurred from historic flow.  The FDEP has historically objected to allowing additional reduction in spring flow at Blue Spring, citing its conflict with their ability to protect the state park, in addition to concerns about impacts to manatees' use of the warm water refuge. 

Please continue your support for Florida's springs and direct FDEP to take the lead on minimum flows for all springs located within state parks, all first order magnitude springs, and all springs that provide unique non-consumptive resource values, such as a manatee warm water refuge - so that no additional reduction in spring flows will be permitted.  Doing so will help ensure that manatees' natural warm water refuges are fully protected and that Florida's beautiful springs are not squandered through consumptive use permits to support more development that is reliant on groundwater.

Thank you for supporting Florida's springs and the endangered Florida manatee.

Sincerely,

Stoyka Chipchakova 13 Mart Str. No.8 Sofia, 1000 Bulgaria

As we both know renewable energy/fuels are a hot topic in our state and around our country.  I am well aware of your support of this industry.  In the past several months I have learned a great deal about the ethanol industry and the key role Florida can play in developing our own fuel.  I write to you today to introduce you to the unique concept my client, Citrus Energy, LLC has developed to commercially convert the 5 million tons of citrus waste in Florida to ethanol.

 

Citrus Energy plans to build a 4 million gallons per year ethanol bio-refinery co-located at a citrus juice plant in Florida.  By locating the ethanol plant close to where the citrus waste is produced minimal energy will be used to transport the feedstock for processing to ethanol.  The use of existing infrastructure generates enormous financial and local community benefits.   Comprehensive research has been conducted largely at the USDA/ARC Citrus and Subtropical Products Laboratory in Florida providing technical background for the proposed bio-refineries. 

 

The use of citrus waste as a feedstock is very advantageous in the competitive ethanol market because it is not burdened with the associated costs of growing, harvesting, and collecting the feedstock for the technology.  Furthermore, this agricultural residue is a non-food, waste by-product, and is not competing with food production for humans and livestock.   

 

While importing corn from the mid-west is a good starting point for Floridas ethanol production capability, it is essential that Floridas future ethanol production be based on Florida biomass.  Additionally, producing ethanol from citrus waste can be done so at a much lower cost than from corn. 

 

Agricultural residues, such as citrus waste, are specifically identified in the Energy Policy Act of 2005 as the starting point of a cellulosic ethanol industry that can significantly reduce our foreign oil dependence without removing crops from the food supply. The long term future of Floridas and the nations liquid fuel needs are dependant on the success of a cellulosic ethanol industry

 

Citrus Energy is uniquely poised to establish itself as a strategic player in the future multi-billion dollar cellulosic ethanol industry by utilizing specific regional advantages in Florida and the Southeast United States. The bio-refinery Citrus Energy plans to build is the first step in the development of a new industry comprising multiple production plants using citrus waste biomass as an ethanol feedstock.  

 

Implementing a commercially viable process which transforms this abundant agricultural waste stream into locally-produced, clean, and affordable biofuel together with high-value byproducts is innovative and has great relevance to Floridas economy and environment. 

 

Citrus waste feedstock is the most economically attractive and technically feasible of the potential cellulosic feedstocks.  A citrus waste industry will contribute to improving the environment, energy security, and rural economics.  It is in Floridas interest to create incentives for the specific development of this Florida fuel from Florida sunshine.  Florida is Americas leader in the production of citrus for juice and we should lead America by helping to use the waste to create energy.

 

I strongly encourage you to bring this unique concept to the attention of your State Board of Administration.  I would hope that the SBA would be very interested in learning more about Citrus Energy and possibly investing in this extraordinary opportunity with us.  I believe Citrus Energy has the technology to put Florida on the map for renewable fuels.   A miniature model plant has been constructed and can demonstrate the successful production of ethanol.  I would be pleased to provide you with any additional information about my client and their plans.  I look forward to hearing from you and thank you in advance for your consideration.

Having stated that, I would suggest this law was set up very poorly. It requires local governments to collect the taxes from the owners, but allows the increases in these taxes to be passed on by the park owners to those paying lease or rent on that property. It does not however properly spell out what property tax increases can be passed on.
 
Park owners interpret it to mean they can pass on taxes for even the lots not yet being used for leasing as well as general use property. Lawyers are getting rich when homeowner associations go to court over this time after time in park after park.

I understand that we are losing a park a week now in Florida and people are being devastated, especially seniors.
 
I am requesting assistance with this problem of pass on taxes. The state government should at least be able to lay down guidelines and keep these discrepancies from repeatedly going to court. Another bill to assist those losing their homes is in order as well.
